hook: The most valuable storage engineer in a design review rarely knows the most internals. What do they know?
title: The right question, asked before the default spreads
body: Storage mistakes don't stay small. A wrong default, a missing deletion path or a bad partition key gets copied into a hundred services, and then the data sits on disk for years. A **senior staff engineer** is rarely the person who knows the most internals. They are the person who asks the right question early, while the fix is still one line in one design doc instead of a migration across every team.
takeaway: Bytes outlive code: the cheapest fix is the question asked on day one.
deeper:
**Why timing dominates:** A service can be rewritten in a quarter. Data written with no owner, no deletion path or the wrong key has to be migrated, not redeployed, and that takes months.

**The toolkit:** Six mental models (temperature, repair speed, metadata, blast radius, defaults, migration), a way to pick a store from the data's shape, a 16-section design-doc checklist, 36 review questions and a trade-off catalog. Each exists to surface an expensive choice while it is still cheap.

**The pattern to spot:** A retention default, a change data capture stream, an open format, a version on every record. Each is nearly free on day one and a multi-month project in year three. The skill is recognizing which early decision will harden into policy.

**The catch:** Asking early means asking before anyone has good numbers. So the best questions are about shape: how many objects, who deletes it, how would we leave.

quiz.q: Two engineers review a new service. One spots a subtle locking issue in the storage engine; the other asks who deletes the data. Which question is likely worth more by year three, and why?
quiz.a: Usually the deletion question. With no owner, data is kept and paid for forever, and adding a deletion path later means touching years of stored data across many services.

mcq.q: Why is an early question worth more in storage design than in most service design?
options: Stored data stays on disk for years and must be migrated to fix
Storage engines cannot be upgraded once deployed
Storage design reviews happen only once per system
Storage code is harder to read than service code
mcq.why: Bytes outlive code. A bad choice baked into stored data needs a slow migration, while code can simply be redeployed.

hook: Most of the photos you store will almost never be read again. Why keep paying for them as if they were hot?
title: Data cools with age, so its storage should too
body: Paying hot-tier prices for every byte forever is wasteful. Data has a lifecycle: born, read a lot, read less, then archived or deleted. How often it is read is its **temperature**: hot (many reads per second), warm (sometimes), cold (rarely, kept for a reason) and frozen (kept only for law or insurance). For most user content, access drops sharply with age. Meta's f4 paper showed photo reads falling fast after upload, which is why Meta built a separate warm tier.
takeaway: Measure the read curve before you pick the tier.
deeper:
**Two operators, one curve:** Meta built a warm tier beside its hot photo store once read rates fell. Google's Colossus places new data on flash and moves it to bigger disks as it cools. Both follow the same shape: a short hot period, then a long tail of rare reads.

**Measure, don't guess:** Plot read rate at 1 day, 30 days and 1 year. The knee of that curve tells you when to move data. Move too early and you pay retrieval costs; move too late and you pay hot prices for cold bytes.

**Temperature picks redundancy too:** Hot data is usually replicated for fast reads. Warm and cold data is erasure-coded to save bytes. Frozen data can sit in archival storage with slow retrieval, because its only reader may be an auditor years later.

**The catch:** Temperature belongs to a dataset, not a company. Photos, messages and logs each cool on their own curve.

quiz.q: Your team keeps three years of user photos on one SSD-backed tier. Reads of photos older than a month are near zero. What is the cheapest change, and what must you measure first?
quiz.a: Move older photos to a cheaper warm or cold tier, erasure-coded or archival. First measure read rate by age to find the knee of the curve, so data moves only after reads drop.

mcq.q: Why did Meta build a separate warm tier for photos?
options: Photo read rates fall quickly after upload
Photos needed stronger consistency after upload
Its hot store could not hold videos
Regulators required old photos to be stored apart
mcq.why: The f4 paper showed photo reads drop fast with age, so older photos could move to cheaper warm storage.

hook: Adding a fifth storage tier can cost more than it saves. Where does the money go?
title: Every tier boundary is a move that can lose data
body: Tiers save bytes, so more tiers should save more. They don't. Every **tier boundary** is a data move, and every move is a chance to lose or duplicate data. Each needs a mover, a check that the copy landed before the source is deleted, and handling for objects changed mid-move. Past a few tiers, the operations cost more than the bytes saved. The sharper question is simpler: who deletes this data? If nobody can answer, it's kept forever and paid for forever.
takeaway: If nobody owns deletion, the retention policy is forever.
deeper:
**What one move involves:**
1. Copy the object to the new tier.
2. Verify that it landed intact.
3. Handle writes or deletes that arrived mid-copy.
4. Only then delete the source.
Each step can fail, and each needs monitoring and on-call knowledge.

**The three questions:** What does the read rate look like at 1 day, 30 days and 1 year? What is the retention rule? Who deletes it? The first sets tier boundaries. The last two set the size of the bill.

**Why ownership matters:** Without an owner, infinite retention becomes the default. The dataset grows until it turns into a cost incident or a compliance incident. Naming an owner on day one is cheap, because the dataset is still small.

**The catch:** Deletion is the final move. It deserves the same care as tiering, which is why a lifecycle section belongs in every storage design doc.

quiz.q: A team proposes six storage tiers to shave cost on a log dataset that has no retention rule. What two objections should a reviewer raise?
quiz.a: Each tier boundary is a move that can lose or duplicate data, so six tiers add operational risk that may exceed the savings. And with no retention rule or owner, the logs will be kept and paid for forever.

mcq.q: Which question best predicts whether a dataset will be paid for forever?
options: Who deletes it?
Which object store holds it?
How many replicas does it have?
Which compression codec does it use?
mcq.why: Without a named owner for deletion, data defaults to infinite retention, so its cost grows without limit.

predict.q: A team adds a fifth storage tier to cut cost. What usually grows fastest?
options: Operational risk from data moves
Read latency on hot data
Metadata per object

hook: You can buy more durability without adding a single disk. How?
title: Halve repair time, cut data-loss risk by 4×
body: Adding copies is the obvious way to protect data. Speed matters more. You lose data only when too many copies fail before the first failure is repaired. With three replicas, loss needs the other two to die inside that **repair window**. The odds scale roughly with (repair time / disk lifetime) squared, so halving repair time cuts loss risk about 4×. For a code surviving m failures, the effect is roughly to the power m.

stat.label: lower loss risk from halving repair time

takeaway: Durability is bought with repair speed as much as with copies.
deeper:
**Why squared:** After one disk dies, two more specific disks must fail before repair finishes. Each chance is proportional to the window length, so the joint chance scales with the window squared. Halve the window and you get about a quarter of the risk.

**The assumption:** Disks fail independently at an annualized failure rate (AFR) of about 1 to 2 percent. That figure is an assumption, not a measurement; Backblaze publishes real drive statistics.

**Parallel repair:** Dropbox's Magic Pocket spreads reconstruction across hundreds of storage nodes at once, so many sources feed many destinations instead of one replacement disk becoming the bottleneck. Repair starts after a node has been offline for 15 minutes.

**The consequence:** Mean time to repair (MTTR) is a first-class design metric. A durability estimate that ignores repair time is decoration.

quiz.q: Your 3-replica cluster rebuilds a failed disk in 8 hours. A change cuts that to 2 hours. Roughly how much does the chance of data loss fall, and why?
quiz.a: About 16×. Loss needs two more failures inside the repair window, so risk scales with the window squared: (8 / 2)² = 16.

mcq.q: For an erasure code that tolerates m failures, halving repair time cuts loss risk by roughly how much?
options: 2 to the power m
Exactly 4, whatever m is
About 2×, the same as the window
Not at all, since parity covers it
mcq.why: Loss needs m further failures inside the repair window, so risk scales roughly with the window to the power m.

hook: Repairing lost data as fast as possible sounds like pure upside. Who pays for it?
title: Repair traffic competes with your users for bandwidth
body: Rebuilding a lost disk reads and writes huge amounts of data over the same disks and network links that serve users. Run repair flat out and user latency suffers. So repair traffic must be **rate-limited**. But throttle it too hard and the repair window grows, and since loss risk scales with the window squared or worse, durability drops fast. The job is to find a rate that protects users without letting the window stretch.
takeaway: Throttle repair, but never so hard that the window grows.
deeper:
**Two models collide:** The durability model says window length matters enormously. The performance model says background traffic hurts tail latency. A senior engineer quantifies both instead of picking a side.

**A common answer:** Give repair a guaranteed minimum rate so the window stays bounded, and let it burst when user load is light.

**Parallelism softens it:** When reconstruction is spread across hundreds of nodes, as in Dropbox's Magic Pocket, each node gives only a small slice of bandwidth. No single disk or link saturates, yet the total repair rate stays high.

**The grace period:** Magic Pocket starts repair only after a node has been offline for 15 minutes. A delay like this can avoid rebuilding data for a machine that is only briefly down, such as during a reboot. It is a trade-off too: a longer wait saves needless repairs but lengthens exposure when the failure is real.

quiz.q: To protect p99 latency, your team caps repair at 5 percent of disk bandwidth. Rebuilds now take four times longer. What happened to durability under 3-way replication?
quiz.a: Loss risk rose about 16×, because it scales with the repair window squared. The cap bought latency with durability; a higher floor or wider parallel repair is needed.

mcq.q: Why does spreading repair across hundreds of nodes ease the latency trade-off?
options: Each node gives a small slice, so nothing saturates
Repair traffic moves to a separate backup network
Fewer fragments need reading for each repair
User reads are paused while repair runs
mcq.why: Spreading work thin keeps the total repair rate high while no single disk or link is overloaded for users.

hook: One scheme stores under half the bytes of triple replication and survives twice the failures. The catch?
title: RS(10,4) beats 3× copies, until you have to repair
body: Triple replication stores 3 bytes per byte and survives 2 failures. **Reed-Solomon** RS(10,4) splits data into 10 data fragments plus 4 parity fragments: 1.4× overhead, and any 4 can be lost. The bill arrives at repair time. Rebuilding one lost fragment means reading 10 fragments. That cost is why Azure invented **LRC**, codes with cheaper single repairs, and why hot data is often replicated while cold data is erasure-coded.

stat.label: storage overhead of RS(10,4), vs 3× copies

takeaway: Erasure coding saves bytes at write time and spends them at repair time.
deeper:
**How it works:** Erasure coding splits data into k data and m parity fragments; any k of them rebuild the original. Reed-Solomon is the classic code. RS(10,4) stores 14 fragments for every 10 of data.

**Three costs:**
1. Writes need CPU to compute parity and network to spread 14 fragments across failure domains.
2. Small reads may touch several nodes, adding latency.
3. Repair reads 10 fragments to rebuild 1, which slows repair and stretches the window durability depends on.

**Azure's fix:** Local reconstruction codes (LRC) make the common single-fragment repair cheaper.

**The rule of thumb:** Replicate hot, small, latency-sensitive data. Erasure-code warm or cold, large objects where cost matters. Meta's photo path follows it: replicate new photos for fast reads, then re-encode to wider codes as they cool.

quiz.q: A team wants to erasure-code a hot, small-object tier to save disk. What would you warn them about?
quiz.a: Small reads may span several nodes, adding latency, and each repair reads 10 fragments under RS(10,4). For hot, small, latency-sensitive data, replication is usually the better trade.

mcq.q: Rebuilding one lost fragment under RS(10,4) requires reading how many fragments?
mcq.why: Any 10 of the 14 fragments can reconstruct the data, so rebuilding one lost fragment means reading 10.

hook: GFS and HDFS could always add more disks. They still hit a wall. What ran out?
title: Bytes scale with disks. Metadata doesn't.
body: Storing bytes is easy to scale: add disks. Knowing where each byte is, who owns it and what it is called is not. GFS hit limits because one master held all **metadata** in memory. HDFS hit the same wall with its NameNode. Google and Meta fixed it the same way: put metadata in a sharded key-value store. Colossus keeps it in Bigtable. Tectonic keeps it in ZippyDB.
takeaway: Disks rarely run out first. The map of where bytes live does.
deeper:
**Why one master breaks:** Every file costs memory on that one machine, and every open, list, rename and stat hits it. As file counts climb into the billions, the master runs out of RAM or request capacity long before the disks fill.

**The shared fix:** Treat metadata as its own database problem. Shard it across a replicated key-value store, and the metadata tier scales out the way the data tier always could.

**Where it recurs:** The trade-off is central master versus sharded metadata store: a master for small scale and simplicity, a sharded store for billions of files. A billion-file metadata service applies the same pattern: separate the namespace from block locations, and shard directories by hash of parent ID.

**The catch:** A central master is not a mistake at small scale. GFS and HDFS started there because it is simple. The mistake is not knowing when you will outgrow it.

quiz.q: Your in-house file system has plenty of free disk, but file creates are timing out and the master node sits at 95 percent memory. What is the diagnosis and the long-term fix?
quiz.a: Metadata is the bottleneck: one master holds every file's entry in RAM. Move metadata into a sharded, replicated key-value store, as Colossus did with Bigtable and Tectonic with ZippyDB.

mcq.q: Where does Meta's Tectonic keep its file system metadata?
options: In ZippyDB, a sharded key-value store
In one master's memory, like GFS
In Bigtable, like Colossus
In a NameNode, like HDFS
mcq.why: Tectonic scaled metadata by sharding it into ZippyDB, the same move Colossus made with Bigtable.

hook: Two datasets hold the same number of bytes. One brings the storage system to its knees. What's different?
title: A million 1 KB files cost more than one 1 GB file
body: Capacity planning usually starts with terabytes. That's the trap. A million 1 KB files cost far more metadata than one 1 GB file, though the bytes match. Each object brings **per-object overhead**: an entry, a location record, often a per-request charge, and work in every LIST, repair and cleanup pass. Small files kill systems sized by bytes. So ask how many objects, how often list, rename and stat run, and which operation is O(number of files).
takeaway: Size a storage system by object count, not only terabytes.
deeper:
**The per-object tax:** Every object carries fixed overhead no matter how small it is. With tiny objects, the overhead dominates the data.

**A concrete case:** Storing 5 billion 2 KB records as separate objects looks cheap by bytes, about 10 TB. The real risk is object count: metadata, LIST cost and per-request cost swamp the storage bill. The fixes are to pack small records into larger files, as Haystack did for photos, or to use a key-value store built for small items.

**Review questions that catch it:** Does anything scale with the number of files rather than bytes? Which resource runs out first: IOPS, capacity, CPU, memory, or metadata?

**The rule:** Object count drives metadata design. Bytes drive cost and tiering. A capacity plan that reports only one of them has done half the math.

quiz.q: An IoT team plans to write every 1 KB sensor reading as its own object in S3, billions a month. The byte bill looks tiny. What will actually hurt, and what would you suggest?
quiz.a: Object count: per-request charges, LIST cost and metadata load dominate. Batch readings into larger files, for example hourly Parquet, or use a key-value store built for small items.

mcq.q: Which operation should worry you most in a system sized only by bytes?
options: One whose cost grows with the number of files
A sequential read of one large file
A single write of a 1 GB object
A checksum over a single fragment
mcq.why: Anything O(number of files) grows with object count, which byte-based sizing never measures.

hook: A bad deploy goes out at AWS. Why does it hit only some customers instead of all of them?
title: Split the system so one failure stays one slice
body: Put every customer on one giant cluster, and a single bad config push can take them all down together. **Blast radius** is how much breaks when one thing breaks. Good designs limit it by splitting into independent units: cells, stamps, shards, regions. AWS uses **cell-based architecture**. Azure uses **storage stamps**. Either way, a bad deploy or a hot tenant hits one slice, not everyone.
takeaway: Name the unit that fails, and its size, before it fails.
deeper:
**How the analogy maps:** A cell works like a watertight compartment in a ship's hull. A breach floods one compartment while the bulkheads keep the rest dry. A cell is an independent copy of a service stack serving a subset of users, so a bug or overload inside it stays inside it.

**Different unit sizes:** AWS cells are full service stacks. Azure stamps are fixed-size storage clusters. Shards and regions apply the same idea at finer or coarser grain. Rolling a deploy out one unit at a time means a bad release is caught in one slice.

**The review question:** What is the blast radius of one bad deploy? A good answer names the unit and its share of customers. 'We will be careful' is not an answer.

**The catch:** Isolation is not free. Every small unit keeps its own headroom, so capacity sits idle, and units need rebalancing as load shifts.

quiz.q: Your storage service runs as one cluster for all 5,000 tenants, and a misconfigured deploy just caused a full outage. What structural change limits the next one, and what does it cost?
quiz.a: Split into independent cells or stamps, each serving a subset of tenants, and deploy one unit at a time. The cost is stranded capacity: each unit needs its own headroom and rebalancing.

mcq.q: What is an Azure storage stamp?
options: A fixed-size storage cluster that bounds failure
A checksum stored alongside each blob
A lease granted to a primary replica
A marker for point-in-time restore
mcq.why: Stamps are Azure's fixed-size storage cluster unit, so a bad deploy or hot tenant affects one stamp, not the whole service.

hook: Meta merged storage into giant clusters. Azure split it into small stamps. Which one got it wrong?
title: Meta pooled, Azure split, and both were right
body: Small units bound failure but waste capacity: each keeps its own headroom and needs rebalancing. Big units pool resources but fail bigger. Meta chose big Tectonic clusters to fix **stranded capacity**, resources that exist but can't be used by the workloads that need them. Azure chose stamps to bound failure. Neither got it wrong. Each picked the risk that dominated its own constraints.
takeaway: Pick the unit size by asking which risk you fear more.
deeper:
**Stranded capacity:** With many small cells, free disk sits in one while another is full. Add up every cell's safety margin and the idle share of the fleet can be large. Big shared clusters let spare capacity go to whichever tenant needs it.

**Azure's call:** Stamps are fixed-size on purpose, with a headroom target of staying under 70 percent. Capacity sits idle by design, and a failure inside one stamp can't spread.

**The catalog rule:** Pick small cells or stamps when blast radius is the top risk. Pick a giant shared pool when stranded capacity is the top cost.

**The catch:** A shared pool needs other armour. Without per-tenant quotas and priority classes, one tenant's batch job saturates disks and every online service slows down. Tectonic's traffic classes exist for exactly this.

quiz.q: One company runs 40 tiny storage cells, each at 45 percent use, and keeps buying disks. Another runs one giant pool and a noisy tenant just slowed everyone. What should each consider?
quiz.a: The first has stranded capacity: fewer, larger units would pool headroom. The second needs per-tenant quotas and priority classes, or smaller cells if blast radius is its top risk.

mcq.q: Why did Meta build large Tectonic clusters instead of small isolated units?
options: To fix stranded capacity by pooling resources
To bound the blast radius of bad deploys
To meet data residency rules per region
To avoid the overhead of erasure coding
mcq.why: Big pools let spare capacity serve any tenant. Meta's top cost was capacity stuck where the workloads needing it couldn't use it.

hook: One setting almost nobody touches can double your storage bill. Which one?
title: The default is the policy
body: Most teams keep whatever the platform does by default. So the **default** is the real policy. If default retention is forever, storage grows forever. If default replication is cross-region, cost doubles for data that never needed it. In 2023, AWS made encryption at rest the S3 default, and after that nobody had to remember it. A senior staff engineer spends more time on defaults than on edge cases.
takeaway: Make the safe, cheap choice the one teams get by doing nothing.
deeper:
**Why defaults win:** Teams are busy. A setting that needs an explicit choice gets left alone. So a default governs most of the company's data, while a clever edge case might help one team.

**Leverage both ways:** A bad default multiplies cost or risk across every dataset. Forever-retention piles up bills and personal data. Cross-region synchronous replication by default makes every write pay a cross-region round trip. A good default deletes a whole class of mistakes: once S3 encrypted new objects automatically, there was no checklist item left to forget.

**The three questions:** What happens if the team does nothing? Is that safe? Is it cheap?

**Putting a number on it:** Ask what the default retention costs in 3 years. A growing dataset with no expiry is a line item that only goes up.

quiz.q: Your platform's new-bucket template sets retention to forever and replication to cross-region, and most teams will never change it. What does that cost, and what would you change?
quiz.a: Storage grows forever, and cross-region copies double cost for data that never needed them. Make bounded retention and single-region the defaults, with cross-region an explicit, justified choice.

mcq.q: What changed once AWS made encryption at rest the S3 default in 2023?
options: Nobody had to remember to turn it on
Customers had to manage their own keys
Unencrypted buckets were deleted
Encryption became a paid add-on
mcq.why: A default covers everyone who does nothing, so encryption no longer depended on each team remembering it.

predict.q: A platform makes cross-region replication the default. What happens to cost for data that never needed it?
options: It doubles
It rises about 10 percent
Nothing, since replicas are free

hook: The storage system you pick this quarter already has an expiry date. When is it?
title: Every storage system is replaced within 5 to 10 years
body: Teams choose storage as if it were permanent. It never is. Every system you choose today will be replaced within 5 to 10 years. Meta replaced Haystack and f4 with Tectonic. Amazon retail left Oracle. Uber is moving its lake to the cloud. Dropbox left S3. **Migration** isn't a failure of the original design. It's the normal lifecycle, so a good design plans its own exit from day one.

stat.label: until today's storage choice gets replaced

takeaway: Price the exit on day one. You will pay it eventually.
deeper:
**Every direction:** The examples cover all of them. Separate in-house stores merged into one (Meta). Off a commercial database (Amazon retail). On-premises to cloud (Uber). Cloud to in-house (Dropbox). No choice is safe from replacement.

**Why it keeps happening:** Common pressures include growth by orders of magnitude, shifting costs and new hardware. A system that fits year one rarely fits year eight.

**How long it takes:** At 100 Gbps sustained, moving 50 PB takes about 46 days of pure transfer. Add verification, dual writes and a rollback window, and real migrations run for months.

**The catch:** A migration you never planned for is a rewrite. One you did plan for, with a routing layer, change data capture and versioned records, is merely a project.

quiz.q: A team argues its new database choice is final, so an abstraction layer in front of it is wasted effort. How do you respond?
quiz.a: Storage systems get replaced within 5 to 10 years; Meta, Amazon retail, Uber and Dropbox all migrated. A stable API and CDC now turn that future move into a project instead of a rewrite.

mcq.q: Which move did Dropbox make?
options: It left S3
It left Oracle
It merged Haystack and f4
It moved its lake to the cloud
mcq.why: Dropbox left S3. Amazon retail left Oracle, Meta merged Haystack and f4 into Tectonic, and Uber is moving its lake to the cloud.

hook: Four decisions cost almost nothing on day one and save months in year five. What are they?
title: Four day-one habits that make migration cheap
body: Migrations hurt most when apps talk to the engine directly, data is locked in one format, and nobody can tell which copy is newer. Four habits fix that. Put an abstraction layer or stable API in front of the store, like Netflix's KV layer. Emit **change data capture** (CDC) from day one. Keep data in **open formats** such as Parquet and Iceberg. Make every record carry a version or timestamp.
takeaway: The cheapest migration is the one you designed for before launch.
deeper:
**The abstraction layer:** Apps call the API, not the engine, so the engine can be swapped behind it without touching hundreds of callers.

**CDC:** A stream of every change lets a new store be filled and kept in sync. Backfill history, then replay the stream until cutover, instead of freezing writes.

**Open formats:** The next engine reads existing files directly. Proprietary formats allow deep optimization for one engine, but ten-year data in a format only one engine can read turns the next migration into a full rewrite.

**Versions on every record:** During dual writes and backfills, both systems receive data, and a backfilled copy can race a fresh update. A version or timestamp settles it: the newer one wins. It is the smallest field in the schema and the one that makes cutover provable.

quiz.q: During a migration, the backfill copies record 42 into the new store one second after a user updated it through dual writes. Which day-one habit decides which copy is correct?
quiz.a: A version or timestamp on every record. Comparing versions shows the dual-written update is newer, so the stale backfilled copy loses.

mcq.q: Why emit change data capture from day one?
options: So a new store can be filled and kept in sync
So queries run faster on the primary
So backups can safely be skipped
So the schema never needs to change
mcq.why: CDC streams every change, letting a future store catch up and stay current until cutover.

hook: One question in a design review exposes a cost nobody has priced. What is it?
title: Ask how you would leave before you move in
body: Lock-in rarely shows up in a design doc. It shows up in year five, as a migration nobody budgeted. So a senior staff engineer asks one question in review: how would we leave this system? If the answer is 'we could not', the design carries a **hidden cost** nobody has priced. Lock-in can be fine, but only as a conscious, costed choice, never as an accident.
takeaway: 'We could not leave' is a cost, not an answer.
deeper:
**Why it works:** It turns lock-in from a vague worry into a line item. If leaving would take a year of engineering, a full data rewrite or downtime, that bill will come due, because every storage system gets replaced within 5 to 10 years.

**Where it shows up:** The design-doc migration plan ends with how we would leave this system later. Review question 24 asks how we would migrate off in 5 years. Deletion and migration are the two design-doc sections most often missing.

**Why it speeds approval:** Showing the exit when presenting a decision lowers the stakes. Reviewers approve faster when a wrong choice is recoverable.

**What a good answer names:** A stable API in front, CDC out, open formats and a version on every record. Four answers, all cheap on day one.

quiz.q: A team proposes a vendor database with a proprietary format and no change stream, and says migration is not on the roadmap. What do you ask for?
quiz.a: Ask how they would leave, and price it. Then push for an API layer, CDC and exportable open formats, or an explicit sign-off that the lock-in cost is accepted.

mcq.q: What does the answer 'we could not leave' reveal in a design review?
options: A hidden cost nobody has priced
A design that is ready to approve
A need for more replicas
A consistency bug in the data model
mcq.why: Every system is migrated eventually, so an impossible exit is a real future cost missing from the design.

section: Part 2: Choosing storage for a new system
hook: Someone says 'we should use Cassandra' before anyone has described the data. What should come first?
title: Start from the data's shape, not a product name
body: Picking a product first means defending it later. Start with the shape of the data and its access pattern. The first cut is a short decision chain. Large immutable blobs over 1 MB go to an **object store**: S3, GCS, Blob, Ambry or a Tectonic blob tenant. Append-only events or logs go to a **log**: Kafka for streaming, then lake tables. Everything else continues down the chart.
takeaway: Describe the data before you name the database.
deeper:
**Why blobs split first:** Large, immutable objects behave nothing like records. They suit erasure coding, CDN caching and cheap flat storage, and they bloat any database that holds them. The 1 MB line is the heuristic for 'large'.

**Why logs split second:** Events are written sequentially, rarely updated and read in bulk. Kafka gives durable ingestion, ordered per partition, and the data then lands in lake tables on object storage for analysis.

**What the chart is:** A first cut, not a rule. Every arrow hides a trade-off, and modifiers such as latency, consistency and retention can overturn the answer.

**The consequence:** One app ends up with several stores. Photos, profiles, messages and logs each take a different branch, and that is the point.

quiz.q: A team wants to store 5 MB user-uploaded PDFs, which never change, as binary columns in Postgres. Which branch of the first cut applies, and why?
quiz.a: Large immutable blobs over 1 MB go to an object store. Keep only a pointer and checksum in Postgres, so backups, replication and caches don't carry the files.

mcq.q: Where does the first cut send append-only events and logs?
options: A log such as Kafka, then lake tables
An object store such as S3 or GCS
A relational database such as Postgres
A cache such as Redis or Memcached
mcq.why: Append-only events are written sequentially and read in bulk: Kafka for streaming, then lake tables for analysis.

section: Part 2: Choosing storage for a new system
hook: Your data needs joins and transactions. When is Postgres no longer the answer?
title: Scans go columnar; transactions go SQL, sized by region
body: Not blobs, not logs? Next question: mostly scans and aggregates? Then use a **columnar** lake or warehouse: Iceberg, BigQuery, Redshift. If not, do you need multi-row transactions or joins? If the data fits one primary region and under a few TB, use a relational database: Postgres, MySQL, Aurora. If it is bigger or multi-region, move to **distributed SQL**: Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB.
takeaway: Stay on one relational primary until size or geography forces you off.
deeper:
**Why columnar for scans:** Storing each column together means an aggregate over three columns reads three columns, not every row. Similar values sit together, so they compress well.

**Why relational first:** A single-region relational database is the simplest, most mature option. When the data fits, it is the default, and reaching for more adds operational cost with no benefit.

**When distributed SQL earns it:** Spanner, CockroachDB and TiDB shard data and replicate with consensus. You keep transactions and joins at larger scale or across regions, but pay in complexity, and cross-region writes pay a round trip.

**The catch:** 'A few TB' is a heuristic, not a hard limit. The real test is whether one primary can carry the write load and data size over the planning horizon, which is why size in 3 years is one of the modifiers.

quiz.q: An inventory service needs multi-row transactions, holds 800 GB and serves one region. A teammate proposes CockroachDB for future scale. What does the first cut suggest?
quiz.a: It fits one primary region and under a few TB, so a relational database such as Postgres or Aurora is the default. Revisit if 3-year size or multi-region needs change.

mcq.q: Which condition sends transactional data to distributed SQL rather than Postgres?
options: It won't fit one primary region and a few TB
It needs single-key reads under 10 ms
It is mostly scans and aggregates
It is append-only events or logs
mcq.why: Transactions that outgrow one region or a few terabytes need sharding with consensus, which Spanner, CockroachDB and TiDB provide.

section: Part 2: Choosing storage for a new system
hook: A cache in front of every database sounds like free speed. What two things must be true first?
title: Huge-QPS lookups go key-value; caches need staleness
body: No transactions or joins needed? Then ask: single-key reads under 10 ms at huge QPS? If yes, use a **key-value or wide-column store**: DynamoDB, Cassandra, Bigtable. If not, a document store or the relational default is fine. A cache such as Memcached, Redis or EVCache comes last, and only if the workload is read-heavy and can tolerate **staleness**. Miss either condition and the cache becomes a liability.
takeaway: A cache is a copy that can be wrong. Add one only if that's fine.
deeper:
**Why key-value:** These stores trade query flexibility for predictable latency. Access is by key, data is partitioned across many nodes, and each read touches one partition.

**When not to bother:** At moderate scale, stay with a document store or the relational default. A specialized store without need is just more to operate.

**The two cache conditions:** Read-heavy means a hit saves real load. Tolerating staleness matters because a cache can serve an old value after a write. If readers must always see the latest data, you need reliable invalidation or a write-through cache.

**What good looks like:** A read-heavy profile service uses a look-aside cache keyed by user ID, invalidated by CDC from the database so no writer can forget, with leases or request coalescing to stop thundering herds on popular keys.

quiz.q: A payments ledger is read 50 times per write, and a stale balance would allow overdrafts. A teammate puts Redis in front of it. What's wrong?
quiz.a: It is read-heavy but cannot tolerate staleness. A look-aside cache may serve an old balance after a write, so balance checks must read the source of truth or use a strictly fresh design.

mcq.q: Which workload best fits a key-value or wide-column store?
options: Single-key reads under 10 ms at huge QPS
Multi-row transactions with joins
Mostly scans and aggregates
Large immutable blobs over 1 MB
mcq.why: Key-value stores partition by key, so each read touches one partition, which gives predictable latency at high QPS.

section: Part 2: Choosing storage for a new system
hook: Your p99 target is 1 ms. Most storage options just disappeared. Which ones survive?
title: The p99 target picks your media before your product
body: The first cut ignores two questions that can overturn it. **Latency**: what is the p99 target? Under 1 ms means memory or local flash. Under 10 ms means SSD-backed key-value storage. 100 ms and up allows object storage. **Consistency**: can a reader see stale data? If not, you need a single leader or consensus per key, and cross-region writes get slower.
takeaway: Strong consistency is a latency bill paid on every cross-region write.
deeper:
**Why the ladder holds:** Sub-millisecond p99 needs data in RAM or on local flash, with no network hop to a remote service. Ten milliseconds leaves room for a networked, SSD-backed store. Object storage, reached over HTTP, fits workloads that tolerate 100 ms or more.

**Why consistency costs:** If a reader must always see the latest committed write, each key needs one authority that orders writes: a single leader or a Paxos or Raft group. Across regions, that authority talks over long links, so writes pay a cross-region round trip.

**Who needs which:** Strong consistency for money, identity, inventory and uniqueness. Eventual consistency for feeds, counters, caches and analytics.

**The catch:** Getting it wrong hurts in both directions. Unneeded strong consistency buys latency for nothing. Missing it buys subtle correctness bugs.

quiz.q: A like-counter team insists every read show the exact latest count worldwide, with writes in three regions. What will that cost, and would you push back?
quiz.a: Strong consistency needs one leader or consensus per key, so every write pays a cross-region round trip. Counters are a classic eventual-consistency case, so push back.

mcq.q: What does 'readers must never see stale data' require of a storage design?
options: A single leader or consensus per key
A cache in front of every read
Erasure coding across regions
A columnar storage format
mcq.why: Only one authority ordering each key's writes guarantees readers see the latest one, and it slows cross-region writes.

predict.q: Your service needs p99 reads under 1 ms. Which storage can meet that?
options: Memory or local flash
An SSD-backed key-value store
Object storage over HTTP

section: Part 2: Choosing storage for a new system
hook: A dataset is small today and fits anywhere. Which three questions show it won't in three years?
title: Size in 3 years, retention, compliance: the slow modifiers
body: A store that fits today can be the wrong choice by year two. Three modifiers stretch the decision across time. **Size**: total bytes and object count in 3 years. Object count drives metadata design; bytes drive cost and tiering. **Retention**: how long, and who deletes? Long retention needs tiering and archival; short retention favours TTL-based stores. **Compliance**: personal data, which regions? That means deletion by user ID, residency pinning and per-tenant keys.
takeaway: Size for year three, and decide deletion before the first write.
deeper:
**Why 3 years:** Sizing for today picks a system you'll migrate within a year. Splitting object count from bytes catches billions of tiny items breaking metadata while capacity looks fine.

**Retention picks machinery:** Data kept for years must move to cheaper tiers or archival storage. Data kept for days belongs in a store with a TTL, so expiry is automatic and nobody writes a cleanup job.

**Compliance adds hard walls:**
1. Deletion by user ID: every dataset must know which column holds the user ID.
2. Residency pinning: data stays in allowed regions, which constrains replication.
3. Per-tenant keys: one customer's key can be revoked, or their data crypto-shredded.

**The catch:** All three are cheap to design in and brutal to retrofit. GDPR deletion across every store is a full design problem on its own.

quiz.q: A session store keeps data for 24 hours; an audit log must be kept for 7 years. What does the retention modifier suggest for each?
quiz.a: Sessions: a TTL-based store, so data expires automatically. Audit log: tiering and archival, moving it to cheaper storage as it cools, with a named owner for deletion.

mcq.q: Which modifier mainly drives metadata design?
options: Object count in 3 years
Total bytes in 3 years
The p99 latency target
The write pattern
mcq.why: Every object needs its own metadata entry, so object count, not bytes, sets metadata load. Bytes drive cost and tiering.

section: Part 2: Choosing storage for a new system
hook: Your search index sits on the same triple-replicated, backed-up tier as your users' photos. What's wrong?
title: Overwrite or append? Rebuildable or not?
body: Two last questions change both the engine and the bill. **Write pattern**: heavy overwrites favour B-trees, which update pages in place. Heavy writes and appends favour LSM trees, which buffer writes in memory and flush sorted files. **Rebuildable**: can the data be recomputed from other data? **Derived data** can accept lower durability and bulk-load paths, as LinkedIn's Venice does. A search index is not a user's photo.
takeaway: Protect what you can't recompute; rebuild what you can.
deeper:
**B-tree vs LSM:** B-trees modify pages where they live, giving fast point reads, range scans and in-place updates. LSM trees turn random writes into sequential ones and compress well, which suits write-heavy workloads and flash, but they pay with background compaction.

**Primary vs derived:** A user's uploaded photo is irreplaceable: full durability and backups. A search index, recommendation features or aggregate tables can be regenerated from the source. They may use fewer replicas, skip backups, and refresh by bulk-loading whole datasets instead of row-by-row writes. LinkedIn's Venice is a derived-data platform built around that bulk-load path.

**The review question:** Is this data primary or derived? Can it be rebuilt? The answer decides how much durability, replication and backup the data needs. Guess wrong one way and you waste money; guess wrong the other way and you lose data for good.

quiz.q: A team triple-replicates and nightly backs up a feature table that is recomputed from event logs every day. What would you question?
quiz.a: It is derived data that can be rebuilt from the logs. It likely needs less durability, perhaps no backups, and a bulk-load refresh path instead of full primary-data protection.

mcq.q: Which write pattern favours an LSM tree?
options: Heavy writes and appends
Heavy in-place overwrites
Read-heavy range scans
Rare writes with many joins
mcq.why: LSM trees buffer writes in memory and flush sorted files, turning heavy writes into sequential I/O.

section: Part 3: Reference architectures for the running example
hook: One app with 1 billion users stores profiles, photos, messages and logs. How many databases does it need?
title: A billion-user app needs many stores, not one
body: A global app with 1 billion users stores profiles, photos and videos, messages, logs and events, and analytics data. No single product fits all of them. Photos go to an erasure-coded **object store** behind CDN edge caches. Profiles go to sharded or distributed SQL behind Memcached or Redis. Messages go to a wide-column or LSM store partitioned by conversation. **Change data capture** feeds Kafka, then a Parquet and Iceberg lake, then an archive.
takeaway: Each data type gets the store that matches its shape.
deeper:
**Matching shape to store:** Small transactional records go to SQL. Large immutable media goes to object storage. Write-heavy, time-ordered messages go to LSM-based stores. Bulk analytical data goes to columnar lake tables.

**The connective tissue:** CDC streams every database change into Kafka. That decouples online stores from analytics: the lake fills from events, not from queries against production databases. Lake data sits as Parquet files in Iceberg tables on object storage, in open formats many engines can read.

**The edges:** The CDN in front of the object store absorbs hot reads near users, so the origin mostly serves misses and older content. After the retention window, data moves to an archive tier instead of living on expensive storage forever.

**The catch:** Several stores means several things to operate. The payoff is that each can scale, fail and migrate on its own.

quiz.q: An analytics team wants to run heavy nightly queries directly against the production profile database. What does the reference architecture offer instead?
quiz.a: Use CDC: stream every change into Kafka and land it in the Parquet and Iceberg lake, so analytics reads the lake and never loads production.

mcq.q: In the reference architecture, how does the lake get its data?
options: CDC streams changes to Kafka, which feeds it
Nightly queries copy tables from production
The CDN writes access logs straight into it
Applications write every record twice
mcq.why: Change data capture decouples online stores from analytics: every change flows through Kafka into Parquet and Iceberg tables.

section: Part 3: Reference architectures for the running example
hook: Profiles are tiny records. Why do Google, AWS and Meta all keep them in transactional stores?
title: Profiles: a transactional store for truth, a cache for reads
body: Profiles look like a key-value problem: small records fetched by user ID. But they are read by other fields too, and updated with some transactions, so they need **secondary indexes** that stay consistent. The row goes to a transactional store: Spanner at Google, Aurora or DynamoDB at AWS, MySQL (MyRocks) behind TAO and Memcache at Meta, Postgres or MySQL with Vitess, CockroachDB or TiDB in open source. Caches absorb the flood of reads.
takeaway: Let the database be correct and the cache be fast.
deeper:
**Why transactions:** A profile is looked up by several fields, and each index must stay consistent with the row. Changing a username while keeping it unique is the kind of update transactions exist for.

**Why caches:** Profiles are read far more often than written, since feeds, messages and comments all display them. At Meta, TAO and Memcache sit in front of MySQL, so the database mostly sees writes and misses.

**How the options scale:** Aurora and Postgres are single-primary. Vitess shards MySQL horizontally. Spanner, CockroachDB and TiDB are distributed SQL with transactions across shards. DynamoDB fits when access is mostly by key.

**The cache design:** Look-aside, keyed by user ID, invalidated via CDC from the database so no writer can forget, with leases or request coalescing against thundering herds. Alert on stale-read rate, not only latency.

quiz.q: A team stores profiles in a pure key-value store keyed by user ID. Product then asks for login by email and unique usernames. What breaks?
quiz.a: They need secondary indexes that stay consistent with the data, plus uniqueness checks. A transactional SQL-style store handles both, with a cache in front still absorbing reads.

mcq.q: What does Meta put in front of MySQL to serve profile reads?
options: TAO and Memcache
EVCache and Redis
CloudFront and S3
Kafka and Iceberg
mcq.why: Meta's profile rows live in MySQL (MyRocks), and TAO plus Memcache absorb the heavy read traffic.

section: Part 3: Reference architectures for the running example
hook: Photos are the heaviest data a social app stores. Why are they also among the easiest to store cheaply?
title: Photos never change, and that makes them cheap
body: Photos and videos are the heaviest data in the app: large blobs, hot at first, then cold. The property that saves you is **immutability**. Nothing overwrites a photo, so erasure coding and CDN caching work well, and data can be tiered by age. Google uses Colossus via GCS. AWS uses S3 plus CloudFront. Meta uses a Tectonic blob tenant, formerly Haystack and f4. Open source has Ceph RGW and MinIO.
takeaway: Data that never changes can be coded, cached and moved freely.
deeper:
**What immutability removes:** No in-place updates, so no overwrites to coordinate across erasure-coded fragments. A CDN copy is never an old version of the photo itself; at most, related metadata such as privacy settings can go stale.

**Meta's evolution:** Haystack served hot photos and packed many into large files to cut metadata cost. f4 added a warm tier with cheaper erasure coding once read rates fell. Both were later replaced by Tectonic, where photos live as a blob tenant.

**The CDN's job:** Edge caches serve popular content near users, so the object store's job becomes durability and the long tail.

**Where the money is:** Photos for 1 billion users come to roughly 128 PB of raw storage a year. At that growth, the tiering policy matters more than which object store you pick.

quiz.q: A product change lets users edit photos in place, overwriting the original object. What does that break in the storage design?
quiz.a: Immutability. Overwrites must be coordinated across erasure-coded fragments, and CDN caches can serve old versions. Better to write each edit as a new object and update the pointer.

mcq.q: Why do erasure coding and CDN caching suit photos and videos so well?
options: The blobs never change once written
The blobs are small and rarely read
The blobs need strong consistency
The blobs are rewritten on every view
mcq.why: No overwrites means no fragment coordination and no stale versions of the object sitting in caches.

section: Part 3: Reference architectures for the running example
hook: Chat is write-heavy, and users read one conversation at a time, newest first. What should the keys be?
title: Messages: partition by conversation, cluster by time
body: Scatter message rows and 'show the last 50' becomes dozens of lookups. So the keys follow the reads. The **partition key** is the conversation ID, putting a chat on one partition. The **clustering key** is time or a sequence number, keeping its messages in order. Now 'last 50' is one range scan. Messages are write-heavy, and LSM engines suit heavy writes. Typical picks: Bigtable or Spanner, DynamoDB, MySQL/MyRocks, Cassandra, ScyllaDB.
takeaway: Let the most common read decide the keys.
deeper:
**Why LSM:** LSM trees buffer writes in memory and flush sorted files, turning a flood of small random writes into sequential I/O.

**The full write path:**
1. Append the message to an LSM-based store.
2. Replicate within the region with quorum writes.
3. Order messages by per-conversation sequence numbers issued by a single leader.
4. Cache recent messages and tier old ones to cheaper storage.

**The encryption twist:** With end-to-end encryption, the server stores only ciphertext. It cannot index what it cannot read, so search must happen on the device.

**The catch:** The keys are tuned to the dominant read, one conversation at a time. A query that cuts across conversations, like global search, has to be served some other way.

quiz.q: A team partitions chat messages by day instead of by conversation ID. What happens to reads and writes?
quiz.a: Reading one chat touches many partitions, and all of today's writes pile onto one hot, growing partition. Conversation ID spreads writes and keeps each chat's reads on one partition.

mcq.q: Why cluster chat messages by time or sequence number?
options: Recent messages come back in one ordered range scan
The database can expire old messages automatically
Writes spread evenly across every node
Search can run on the server side
mcq.why: Clustering stores a conversation's messages in order, so 'the latest N' is a single sequential range read.

section: Part 3: Reference architectures for the running example
hook: Logs pile up faster than almost any other data, and nobody reads them line by line. How should they live?
title: Logs and analytics: cheap objects, columns, separate compute
body: Logs and events are append-only, huge and read in bulk. So they want sequential writes, cheap object storage and **columnar** files for scans. The path is a durable log first, then files: Kafka to Iceberg in open source, Kinesis or MSK to S3 at AWS, Scribe to the Tectonic warehouse at Meta, Colossus files and BigQuery at Google. Analytics then **separates compute from storage**, so query engines scale on their own.
takeaway: Keep the data cheap and open; let engines come and go.
deeper:
**Why a log first:** Kafka, Kinesis, MSK or Scribe absorbs bursty producers and gives consumers ordered streams. Consumers then write compressed Parquet files to object storage every few minutes, committed as Iceberg snapshots.

**Why columns:** Analytical queries read a few columns across huge numbers of rows. Storing each column together, as Capacitor at Google and Parquet do, reads only what the query needs and compresses similar values well.

**Why separate compute:** Data sits in cheap, durable object storage, and engines such as Trino, Spark and Presto scale independently on top. Open table formats like Iceberg and Delta let many engines read the same tables, which avoids lock-in and eases the next migration.

**The upkeep:** Compact small files into large ones, partition by date and event type, and keep raw events 30 to 90 days, aggregates longer.

quiz.q: A team writes one tiny Parquet file per event to object storage, millions an hour, and queries crawl. What went wrong, and what fixes it?
quiz.a: Too many small files, so metadata and per-file overhead dominate. Buffer through Kafka, write files every few minutes, and compact small files into large ones.

mcq.q: Why do open table formats like Iceberg matter for analytics?
options: Many engines can read the same tables
They store each row beside its index
They remove the need for object storage
They make single-key reads under 1 ms
mcq.why: Open formats let Trino, Spark and Presto share one copy of the data, avoiding lock-in to a single engine.

section: Part 3: Reference architectures for the running example
hook: One database for everything is the simplest design on day one. What does it look like in year three?
title: One database for all data: easy now, stuck by year three
body: One database for every data type is simple on day one. By year three, logs are crowding out profile queries, photos are bloating backups, and every migration touches everything. The data types want opposite things: logs are write-heavy bulk scans, profiles need fast point reads, photos are big blobs. Split storage **by data type** early, even if each store is small, so each can scale, fail and migrate on its own.
takeaway: Split by data type while splitting is still cheap.
deeper:
**How it fails:**
1. A log ingestion spike competes for the same disks, buffer cache and locks as user-facing profile queries, and tail latency suffers.
2. Blobs ride inside rows, so every backup, replica and snapshot carries them.
3. Migration becomes all-or-nothing: you can't move logs to a lake without touching the database that serves profiles.

**Why early is cheap:** Each store starts small, so splitting costs little. Splitting later means a zero-downtime migration, and at 100 Gbps even the pure transfer of 50 PB takes about 46 days.

**The general rule:** Start from data shape and access pattern, not product names. The same app needs several stores, and 'one database' is a product choice made before anyone looked at the shapes.

quiz.q: A startup's single Postgres holds users, event logs and uploaded images. Backups take 9 hours and profile p99 spikes nightly. What do you split first, and why?
quiz.a: Move images to an object store, since they bloat every backup and replica, and logs to Kafka and a lake, since their writes compete with profile queries. Keep Postgres for profiles.

mcq.q: Why does one shared database hurt as an app grows?
options: Workloads with opposite access patterns interfere
It cannot hold more than a few terabytes
Databases cannot store images at all
It forces eventual consistency on every table
mcq.why: Logs, profiles and blobs compete for the same disks, cache and locks, and every migration has to touch all of them.

section: Part 3: Reference architectures for the running example
hook: 10 percent of 1 billion users post one photo a day. How much raw disk does that eat in a year?
title: Photos for 1 billion users: about 128 PB a year
body: Every input is labelled, so anyone can challenge one. Assume 10 percent of 1 billion users upload one photo a day, 2 MB on average, plus 25 percent for resized versions. That is 100 million × 2.5 MB = 250 TB a day logical. With RS(10,4) at 1.4×, it is about 350 TB a day raw, roughly 128 PB a year. At that growth, the **tiering policy** matters more than which object store you pick.

stat.label: raw photo storage added per year

takeaway: State every assumption, so a wrong estimate is fixable.
deeper:
**The chain:**
1. 1 billion × 10 percent = 100 million uploads a day.
2. 2 MB + 25 percent = 2.5 MB each.
3. 100 million × 2.5 MB = 250 TB logical.
4. × 1.4 for RS(10,4) = 350 TB raw a day.
5. × 365 ≈ 128 PB a year.

**Why labelling matters:** A reviewer who disagrees changes one input and recomputes, instead of arguing with the conclusion. Reviewers trust a wrong estimate with clear assumptions more than a vague claim, because they can fix the assumptions.

**The conclusion:** Moving cooling photos to cheaper tiers, or re-encoding them with wider codes, saves far more than a few percent off the object store's price. With 3× replication instead of 1.4×, raw growth would be more than twice as large.

quiz.q: Using the same photo sketch, the team switches from RS(10,4) to triple replication. Roughly what happens to yearly raw storage?
quiz.a: It rises from about 128 PB to about 274 PB: 250 TB a day × 3 × 365, a little over twice as much raw storage for the same logical data.

mcq.q: In the photo sketch, what turns 250 TB of logical data a day into 350 TB raw?
options: RS(10,4) erasure coding at 1.4× overhead
Resized versions adding 25 percent
Triple replication across regions
CDN edge caches copying hot photos
mcq.why: Erasure coding with 10 data and 4 parity fragments stores 1.4 bytes per logical byte: 250 × 1.4 = 350.

predict.q: 10 percent of 1 billion users upload one 2 MB photo a day. Roughly how much raw storage is that per year?
options: About 128 PB
About 13 PB
About 1,300 PB

section: Part 4: How to write a storage design doc
hook: A bad service design can be fixed next sprint. Why can't a bad storage design?
title: In a storage design doc, bytes outlive code
body: A bad service design gets redeployed. A bad storage design stays on disk for years, because **bytes outlive code**. So the checklist opens with four sections. Context and goals, with a single primary goal, such as the predictable p99 latency DynamoDB chose. Non-goals, such as cross-region transactions. A data model with entities, keys, sizes and a schema evolution plan. Access patterns: each query's QPS, read/write ratio, latency target and consistency need.
takeaway: One primary goal settles a hundred arguments later.
deeper:
**One goal, not five:** DynamoDB's design centred on predictable latency, and that one goal guided countless smaller decisions. A doc with five equal goals gives reviewers no way to resolve conflicts between them.

**Non-goals prevent drift:** Saying 'we will not support cross-region transactions' stops scope creep and tells future users to pick a different store if they need it.

**Schema evolution:** The schema will change, and old records stay on disk in the old shape. The review question is blunt: how will the schema change without downtime?

**Access patterns decide everything:** Each query's rate, read/write mix, latency target and consistency need determine the partition key, indexes, caching and engine. Listing them early exposes hot keys and queries that need secondary indexes before they surprise you in production.

quiz.q: A design doc lists five equal goals: low latency, strong consistency, lowest cost, multi-region writes and simple operations. What is the problem, and what would you ask for?
quiz.a: The goals conflict and none outranks the others, so trade-offs can't be settled. Ask for a single primary goal, such as predictable p99 latency, and demote the rest to secondary goals or non-goals.

mcq.q: Why does a storage design doc need a schema evolution plan?
options: Old records stay on disk in the old shape
Schemas cannot change after launch
Access patterns depend only on the schema
Backups can only hold one schema version
mcq.why: Bytes outlive code: records written years ago remain, so the schema must change without downtime.

section: Part 4: How to write a storage design doc
hook: Three replicas protect you from dead disks. What do they do with a corrupt write?
title: Durability math, headroom and failure modes, in numbers
body: The middle of the checklist turns claims into numbers. **Capacity plan**: bytes and object counts today, in 1 year and in 3, with a headroom target such as staying under 70 percent, as Azure stamps do. **Durability math**: redundancy, failure domains, repair time, annual loss probability, backups and restore time. Availability: the SLO and behaviour during a partition. **Failure modes**, including corrupt writes and operator error, because replicas copy those faithfully.
takeaway: Replication protects you from hardware, not from yourself.
deeper:
**Headroom with an owner:** The target sets when to add capacity. Its partner review question: who gets paged when it is crossed?

**Durability as a number:** Given the redundancy scheme, the failure domains copies sit in and the repair time, estimate the yearly loss probability. Add backup restore time, because a backup that takes a week to restore may not meet the need.

**The failure list:** Disk, node, rack, zone and region loss. A hot key. A bad deploy. A corrupt write. Operator error. For each one, the doc states:
1. How it is detected.
2. What the impact is.
3. How the system recovers.

**Why software faults belong here:** Three replicas of a corrupt write are three corrupt copies. Redundancy can't undo a mistake; checksums, soft delete and tested restores can.

quiz.q: A design doc covers disk, rack and zone loss in detail and nothing else. Then an engineer's bad migration script overwrites a column. What was the doc missing?
quiz.a: Operator error and corrupt writes. Replication copied the bad data everywhere, so the doc needed detection, impact and recovery for those: checksums, soft delete or tested restorable backups.

mcq.q: Which headroom target does Azure's stamp design illustrate?
options: Stay under 70 percent utilization
Stay under 90 percent utilization
Stay under 50 percent utilization
Stay under 99 percent utilization
mcq.why: Azure stamps keep utilization below 70 percent, leaving room for failures and growth.

section: Part 4: How to write a storage design doc
hook: A user asks to be deleted, but legal says their records must be kept. Which design-doc section settles it?
title: The design-doc sections that outlive launch day
body: Launch is one day. The obligations after it last for years, so four sections pin them down. **Security**: encryption at rest and in transit, key management, access control, audit logs. **Compliance review**: personal data inventory, residency, retention, a deletion path by user ID, and legal hold. Those last two sit together on purpose: one removes data, the other forbids removing it. **Lifecycle**: temperature, tiering, TTLs, archival, deletion. Operations: upgrades, schema changes, resharding, runbooks, dashboards.
takeaway: Every deletion path needs a brake: legal hold.
deeper:
**Security vs compliance:** Security asks who can read the data and how it is protected. Compliance asks what the law requires about where it lives, how long it stays and how it is removed. Different questions, often different reviewers.

**Deletion needs an inventory:** A deletion path by user ID only works if every dataset declares whether it holds personal data and which column holds the user ID. Legal hold, a block on deletion for legal reasons, must be respected by that same machinery.

**Lifecycle makes temperature concrete:** It states when data turns warm or cold, which tier it moves to, when TTLs expire it and who deletes it.

**Operations assumes years:** Engine upgrades, schema changes and resharding will all happen. Runbooks and dashboards must exist before the first incident, not get written during it.

quiz.q: A deletion orchestrator removes all of a user's records within a day, but that user is under a litigation hold. What should the design have included?
quiz.a: A legal hold check in the compliance design: the deletion path must skip or defer data under hold, because legal hold blocks deletion for legal reasons.

mcq.q: Which design-doc section holds the deletion path by user ID and legal hold?
options: Compliance review
Security
Operations
Access patterns
mcq.why: Compliance review covers the personal data inventory, residency, retention, deletion by user ID and legal hold.

section: Part 4: How to write a storage design doc
hook: A design doc names one option and explains why it's great. What is missing that makes reviewers nervous?
title: Migration, cost, alternatives: the reviewable half of a doc
body: A doc that presents one option asks reviewers to trust it. The last four sections make it checkable instead. **Migration plan**: backfill, dual-write or CDC, verification, cutover, rollback, and how you would leave later. **Cost model**: storage, requests, egress, replication, backup and people, per user or per GB-month. **Alternatives considered**: at least two, with why they lost. Open questions and risks: what nobody knows yet.
takeaway: An option with no rivals on paper was assumed, not chosen.
deeper:
**Migration is a sequence:**
1. Backfill existing data.
2. Dual-write, or stream changes with CDC.
3. Verify with checksums and counts.
4. Cut over, with a rollback path ready.
The same section says how you would leave this system, because every system is migrated eventually.

**Cost includes people:** Storage and requests are obvious. Egress, replication, backups and the engineers who run the system are not. A per-user or per-GB-month figure puts designs on one scale.

**Alternatives show judgment:** Two rejected options with reasons prove the choice was made, not defaulted into. They also give reviewers something concrete to push against.

**Open risks build trust:** Naming unknowns up front invites the right help and keeps the doc from looking falsely certain.

quiz.q: A doc's cost model counts only storage per GB. The system serves most reads cross-region and keeps three backups. What will the estimate miss?
quiz.a: Network egress on the read path, the cost of replicas and backups, and people. A full cost model covers storage, requests, egress, replication, backup and people.

mcq.q: How many alternatives should a storage design doc consider?
options: At least two, with why they lost
Exactly one, the chosen design
Every product on the market
None, if the team knows the store
mcq.why: Two rejected options with reasons show the choice was deliberate and give reviewers something to challenge.

section: Part 4: How to write a storage design doc
hook: Two design-doc sections are easy on day one and brutal to add in year three. Which two?
title: Write deletion and migration first, while they're cheap
body: **Deletion** and **migration** are the two design-doc sections most often missing. On day one each is a small change: a user-ID column, a per-user key, a TTL, a CDC stream, an abstraction layer. In year three, with petabytes on disk and dozens of dependent teams, the same capability means scanning, rewriting and migrating everything. Both are easy to design early and very hard to add late. So write them first.
takeaway: The sections teams skip are the ones they can't add later.
deeper:
**Why they get skipped:** Neither affects launch. The service works without a deletion path, and nobody plans to leave a system they are still building. Both costs land years later, often on someone else.

**What day one looks like:** Declare which column holds the user ID. Encrypt each user's data with a per-user key, so deleting the key makes backups unreadable for that user. Set a TTL. Emit CDC. Put an API in front of the engine.

**What year three looks like:** A GDPR request that must reach databases, caches, object stores, search indexes, logs, the lake, ML training sets and backups. Or a 50 PB move that takes about 46 days of pure transfer at 100 Gbps, before any verification.

**The short version:** Deletion and migration are cheap as design and ruinous as retrofit.

quiz.q: Three years in, legal asks you to delete one user's data from nightly backups kept for a year. There are no per-user keys. What are your options, and what would have made this easy?
quiz.a: Rewrite or expire every backup holding the user, which is slow and costly. Per-user encryption keys from day one would allow crypto-shredding: delete the key and the backups become unreadable for that user.

mcq.q: Which two design-doc sections are most often missing?
options: Deletion and migration
Security and cost
Capacity and durability
Access patterns and data model
mcq.why: Both are easy to design on day one and very hard to add in year three, so they should be written first.

predict.q: Which design-doc sections are most often missing?
options: Deletion and migration
Security and compliance
Capacity and cost

hook: Your biggest item is 2 MB today. What happens to the design when one arrives at 200 MB?
title: Review questions that hunt the extremes in your data
body: Designs are built for the average item and break on the extreme one. The 36 design-review questions come in eight groups, and the first, **data model and access**, hunts extremes. What is the largest single item, and what if it is 100× larger? What is the hottest key, and its peak QPS? Which queries need a **secondary index**, and is it transactional with the data? How will the schema change without downtime? Is this data primary or derived?
takeaway: Design for the largest item and the hottest key, not the average.
deeper:
**The 100× question:** A store tuned for 2 MB items may cap row sizes, cache entries or request bodies. Asking about 100× finds those limits in review instead of in production.

**The hottest key:** Averages hide skew. One celebrity profile or one viral photo can take far more traffic than the rest, and a single shard has to serve it.

**The index question:** If data and index are written separately with no transaction, a crash between the two writes leaves them inconsistent forever. Pinterest named this a key reason for moving its graph store to TiDB.

**Primary or derived:** Rebuildable data can take lower durability and bulk-load paths. Irreplaceable data cannot.

**The other seven groups:** Capacity and scaling; durability and reliability; consistency and correctness; operations and change; security and compliance; cost; organization.

quiz.q: A design indexes posts by hashtag in a separate table, updated by a second write after the post is saved. Which review question catches the risk, and what is it?
quiz.a: Is the index transactional with the data? Without atomic writes, a crash between them leaves posts missing from the index, or entries pointing at nothing, forever.

mcq.q: How many groups do the 36 design-review questions fall into?
options: Eight
Six
Five
Twelve
mcq.why: Data model and access, capacity and scaling, durability and reliability, consistency and correctness, operations and change, security and compliance, cost, and organization.

hook: Your cluster has 40 percent free disk and is about to fall over. What ran out?
title: Find which resource runs out first, before production does
body: Teams watch disk space and get surprised by something else. The **capacity and scaling** questions drag the first bottleneck into the open. What are the object count and byte count in 3 years? What is the resharding plan, and has it been tested? Which resource runs out first: IOPS, capacity, CPU, memory, or metadata? What is the headroom target, and who gets paged when it's crossed? Does anything scale with file count rather than bytes?
takeaway: An untested resharding plan is a wish, not a plan.
deeper:
**Five resources, one winner:** IOPS, capacity, CPU, memory and metadata each have a ceiling, and one hits first. Small files exhaust metadata while disks sit half empty. Hot random reads exhaust IOPS long before capacity.

**Resharding, tested:** Every growing dataset needs resharding eventually. A plan that has never run is a guess about one of the hardest operations the system will perform, and it will run under load.

**Headroom with a pager:** A target such as staying under 70 percent, as Azure stamps do, only helps if crossing it pages a named person. Otherwise it is a number on a dashboard nobody watches.

**The file-count question:** Anything O(number of files), such as listing, renaming or scanning a namespace, grows with object count, which byte-based capacity plans never see.

quiz.q: A thumbnail store is at 40 percent disk use, yet latency climbs and the metadata servers are pinned. Which review question should have caught this, and what's the fix?
quiz.a: Which resource runs out first, and does anything scale with file count rather than bytes? Metadata hit its limit first. Pack small thumbnails into larger files or shard the metadata.

mcq.q: Why ask whether the resharding plan has been tested?
options: Resharding is hard and will eventually run under load
Resharding is needed only when changing vendors
Untested plans break compliance rules
Resharding lowers the object count
mcq.why: Growing datasets must reshard eventually. An untested plan is a guess about a risky operation performed on live traffic.

hook: The team says 'we have backups'. Which single question tells you whether that's true?
title: When did you last restore, and how long did it take?
body: 'We have backups' and 'we have three replicas' sound like answers. The **durability and reliability** questions test them. What is the repair time after a disk or node loss? How many failures can one item survive, and are copies in independent failure domains? How is silent corruption detected; are checksums end-to-end? When did we last restore from backup, and how long did it take? Can an operator or a bug delete everything? What is the blast radius of one bad deploy?
takeaway: Redundancy you haven't tested is a belief, not a property.
deeper:
**Repair time first:** Loss risk scales with the repair window squared for 3-way replication, so repair time is the durability number that matters most.

**Independent domains:** Three copies on one rack share one fate. Racks, zones and regions each fail as a unit, and copies must be spread across them.

**End-to-end checksums:** Silent corruption raises no errors. A checksum computed at the writer and verified at the reader catches bit flips anywhere along the path.

**The deletion question:** Replicas copy a mass delete faithfully. What stops it: soft delete, delayed purge, object lock?

**The restore question:** A backup never restored in a drill is a hope, not a backup. Asking when, and how long, turns faith into a measured number.

quiz.q: A service keeps three replicas in one zone and nightly backups nobody has ever restored. Which two review questions expose it, and why?
quiz.a: Are copies in independent failure domains? No, a zone loss takes all three. When did we last restore? Never, so the backups are a hope until a drill proves them.

mcq.q: What protects against an operator or a bug deleting everything?
options: Soft delete, delayed purge or object lock
A third replica in another zone
Faster repair after a node loss
End-to-end checksums on every read
mcq.why: Replicas faithfully copy a mass delete. Only mechanisms that delay or forbid deletion can undo or block it.

hook: The worst storage bugs sail through every happy-path test. When do they finally show up?
title: The bugs that only appear during failover
body: Happy-path tests miss the worst storage bugs, because they appear only under failure or concurrency. The **consistency and correctness** questions go looking for them. What does a reader see during a failover? How are concurrent writes to the same key resolved? What happens to in-flight writes if a region is lost, and what is the **RPO**, the data you may lose? Are cache invalidations reliable, or can the cache stay stale forever?
takeaway: Ask what the system does in its worst second, not its average one.
deeper:
**Failover reads:** During a leader change, a reader might see stale data, an error, or a value that later disappears. The design should pick one on purpose and document it, so clients can handle it.

**Concurrent writes:** Two writers, one key. A single leader orders them. Last-writer-wins with timestamps keeps one and silently drops the other. CRDTs merge without coordination. Each is a different promise to the user.

**Region loss:** With asynchronous replication, in-flight writes may be lost. The RPO names how much. Zero needs synchronous replication; a few seconds allows async.

**Stale caches:** An invalidation that depends on every writer remembering will eventually be forgotten. Driving it from the database's change stream means no writer can forget, and alerting on stale-read rate catches what slips through.

quiz.q: Two regions accept writes to the same shopping cart and resolve conflicts by last-writer-wins. A user adds an item in each region at nearly the same moment. What can happen, and which question should have caught it?
quiz.a: One addition can silently vanish, because LWW keeps only the later write. The question: how are concurrent writes to the same key resolved? A CRDT merge would keep both.

mcq.q: What does RPO measure?
options: How much data you may lose in a disaster
How long recovery may take
How many replicas must acknowledge
How stale a cache may become
mcq.why: Recovery point objective is the data-loss budget. Recovery time objective, RTO, is how long recovery may take.

hook: A new engine version wrote a week of data in a new format, then turned out to be buggy. Can you roll back?
title: Can you roll back after the new version wrote data?
