body: Rolling back code is easy. Rolling back code that already wrote data in a new format is not, and **operations and change** asks exactly that. It also asks: how do we upgrade the engine without downtime? Are the top three alerts actionable? How would we migrate off in 5 years? **Security and compliance** asks: can we find all personal data by user ID? How long until a deletion reaches caches, replicas, backups and the lake? What enforces residency? Can one tenant's key be revoked? Are access logs reviewed?
takeaway: Rollback ends where the new format begins. Plan for that line.
deeper:
**The format trap:** Once a new version writes data the old version can't read, rolling back the binary strands those records. Common answers are to ship readers that understand both formats before any writer switches, or to put the new format behind a flag that can be turned off.

**Alerts that mean something:** Three actionable alerts beat thirty noisy ones. Each should point at something the on-call engineer can actually do.

**Deletion reaches further than you think:** Primary stores, caches, replicas, backups and the lake all hold copies. The question asks how long until the data is gone from every one.

**Keys and residency:** Which regions may the data live in, and what enforces it, beyond a promise? Who holds the encryption keys, and can one tenant's key be revoked? Per-tenant revocation calls for customer-managed keys.

quiz.q: A release changes the on-disk record format on Monday. By Wednesday it corrupts some reads, and the old binary can't parse the new records. What should the design have planned?
quiz.a: A rollback path for data already written in the new format: readers that understand both formats before writers switch, or a flag to stop writing the new format.

mcq.q: Why does rollback get hard after a new version writes data?
options: Old code may not read the new format
Rollbacks always require downtime
New data is copied to backups instantly
Alerts stop firing after a version change
mcq.why: Once records exist in a format only the new version understands, reverting the binary strands that data.

hook: One number tells you how much of your storage bill buys nothing at all. Which number?
title: The 90-day question and the simplest version that works
body: Storage bills rarely come from the data people use. The **cost** questions find the rest. What is the cost per GB-month and per million requests, including replicas and backups? What share of stored data hasn't been read in 90 days? What is the egress cost of the main read path? What does default retention cost in 3 years? The **organization** questions ask who owns the data, who depends on it, and what the simplest working version is.
takeaway: Every dataset needs an owner, a price and a reason to exist.
deeper:
**Full cost, not list price:** A GB-month figure that ignores replicas and backups undercounts by at least the replication factor. On a busy read path, requests and egress can outweigh storage itself.

**The 90-day number:** Data untouched for 90 days is a tiering or deletion candidate. Its share tells you how much of the bill buys nothing.

**Ownership:** Which team owns this data, and who approves schema changes? Without an owner, nobody deletes, and nobody can say yes to a change.

**Dependents:** How many other teams will depend on it, and through what interface? A stable API keeps them from coupling to the engine, which keeps the future migration possible.

**The humility question:** What is the simplest version that could work, and why is it not enough? It makes the design justify its own complexity.

quiz.q: A team's storage bill doubled in a year while active usage stayed flat. Which two cost questions would you ask first?
quiz.a: What share of stored data hasn't been read in 90 days, and what does default retention cost in 3 years? Flat usage with rising cost points to data kept forever on expensive tiers.

mcq.q: What does 'what is the simplest version that could work?' test?
options: Whether the design's complexity is justified
Whether the team owns the data
Whether egress costs are included
Whether backups have been restored
mcq.why: Asking why the simplest version isn't enough forces every added component to earn its place.

hook: Engineers argue for years over replication versus erasure coding. Why can neither side win?
title: Replication or EC, B-tree or LSM: the workload decides
body: Asking which technique is better misses the point: each wins for a different workload. **Redundancy**: replicate hot, small, latency-sensitive data; erasure-code warm or cold, large objects where cost matters. **Engine**: a B-tree for read-heavy work with in-place updates and range scans; an **LSM tree** for write-heavy work, compression and flash. Describe the workload first, and each choice mostly makes itself.
takeaway: Name the workload and the trade-off usually answers itself.
deeper:
**Why replicate hot data:** A read hits one full copy on one node, and repair copies one replica. Erasure coding would spread small reads across several nodes and make each repair read 10 fragments under RS(10,4).

**Why erasure-code cold data:** At 1.4× instead of 3×, RS(10,4) cuts raw storage by more than half and survives 4 failures instead of 2. For large objects read rarely, slower reads and repair are a fair price.

**Why B-trees for reads:** Pages are updated in place, so a point read or range scan walks one tree.

**Why LSM for writes:** Writes are buffered in memory and flushed as sorted files, turning random writes into sequential ones that compress well and suit flash. The cost is background compaction, and a read may check several files.

**The pattern:** Many systems use both, replicating data while it is hot and re-encoding it as it cools.

quiz.q: A metrics service ingests millions of small writes per second and rarely updates old points. Which engine fits, and what does it cost?
quiz.a: An LSM tree: it suits write-heavy workloads, compresses well and fits flash. The cost is background compaction and reads that may have to check several files.

mcq.q: When does the trade-off catalog favour erasure coding over replication?
options: Warm or cold, large objects where cost matters
Hot, small, latency-sensitive data
Data that needs multi-row transactions
Any data kept in more than one region
mcq.why: Erasure coding saves bytes but makes small reads and repair costlier, which suits large, rarely read objects.

hook: Every multi-region database promises something. What does it quietly give up in return?
title: Strong or eventual, one leader or many, sync or async
body: Each of these choices buys one property by paying with another. **Consistency**: strong for money, identity, inventory and uniqueness; eventual for feeds, counters, caches and analytics. **Topology**: a single leader for simple reasoning and transactions; leaderless or multi-leader for always-writable, multi-region writes. **Cross-region replication**: synchronous when RPO must be zero; asynchronous when latency matters more than the last few seconds of data.
takeaway: Every guarantee is paid for in latency, availability or lost writes.
deeper:
**Strong costs latency:** One authority must order each key's writes, and across regions that means a round trip per write.

**Multi-leader costs conflicts:** Every region accepts writes and replicates asynchronously. Concurrent updates need resolving, with last-writer-wins timestamps or CRDTs, and last-writer-wins can silently drop a write. Dynamo and Cassandra follow this family.

**Synchronous costs every write:** Zero RPO means no acknowledgment until another region has the data. Making that the default for all data is an anti-pattern; it should be an explicit choice per dataset, backed by an RPO requirement.

**How to choose:** Match the guarantee to what breaks. A double-spent balance or a duplicate username is a correctness incident, so pay for strong. A like count that lags a second is invisible, so don't.

quiz.q: A shopping-cart service must accept writes even when regions can't reach each other. Which topology fits, and what risk comes with it?
quiz.a: Leaderless or multi-leader, so every region stays writable. The risk is conflicting concurrent updates: last-writer-wins can lose one, while CRDTs can merge them instead.

mcq.q: When does the catalog call for synchronous cross-region replication?
options: When RPO must be zero
When latency matters most
When data is eventually consistent
When all writes come from one region
mcq.why: Only synchronous replication guarantees no acknowledged write is lost with a region, at the cost of a cross-region round trip per write.

hook: Three storage choices are cheap on a whiteboard and nearly impossible to change later. Which three?
title: Cells or pools, master or shards, local or network disk
body: Some storage choices are settings. These three are architecture. **Failure domain**: small cells or stamps when blast radius is the top risk; a giant shared pool when stranded capacity is the top cost. **Metadata**: a central master for small scale and simplicity; a sharded metadata store for billions of files. **Storage and compute**: coupled, on local disk, for lowest latency and predictable workloads; disaggregated, over network storage, for elastic compute and independent scaling.
takeaway: Make architecture choices for the scale you'll reach, not today's.
deeper:
**Cells vs pools:** Azure chose stamps to bound failure. Meta chose big Tectonic clusters to fix stranded capacity. A pool then needs per-tenant quotas and priority classes, or one batch job slows everyone.

**Master vs shards:** GFS and HDFS started with one metadata master because it is simple, and both hit its limits. Colossus moved metadata to Bigtable; Tectonic moved it to ZippyDB.

**Coupled vs disaggregated:** Local disk avoids a network hop, so latency is lowest and predictable. Network storage lets compute scale up and down without moving data, which is why analytics keeps data in object storage and scales query engines separately.

**Why these resist change:** Each one shapes where data physically lives. Changing it means moving the data, and moving data is a migration.

quiz.q: An analytics platform's query load swings 10× between day and night, but its data lives on the compute nodes' local disks. Which trade-off applies, and what would you change?
quiz.a: Coupled versus disaggregated storage. Move the data to network or object storage so compute can scale up and down independently, accepting some extra latency.

mcq.q: When does the catalog favour a sharded metadata store over a central master?
options: At billions of files
At small scale
When simplicity matters most
When the data is mostly cold
mcq.why: A central master keeps all metadata on one machine; billions of files need metadata sharded across a key-value store.

hook: A bug deletes a thousand user photos. Whether you can undo it was decided months ago. By which choice?
title: Hard delete meets deadlines; soft delete forgives bugs
body: Three pairs trade safety or simplicity against freshness or control. **Deletion**: hard delete now when compliance deadlines are tight; soft delete, purge later, to protect against mistakes and bugs. **Cache**: look-aside for read-heavy data that tolerates staleness; write-through when the cache must stay fresh on write. **Tiering**: automatic by access when patterns are unknown; explicit by policy when lifecycles are predictable or legal rules apply.
takeaway: Soft delete is an undo button with an expiry date.
deeper:
**Soft delete in practice:** Mark the record deleted so it disappears for users, then purge it physically later. The photo-storage design works this way: the photo vanishes from metadata at once, and compaction removes the bytes within the compliance window. The gap between the two is your undo window.

**Look-aside vs write-through:** With look-aside, the app reads the cache, falls back to the database on a miss and fills the cache, so reads can be stale after a write. Write-through updates the cache on every write, trading write cost for freshness.

**Auto vs policy tiering:** S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves objects by observed access, which suits unknown patterns. Explicit lifecycle rules win when you know the lifecycle, or the law dictates it.

**The common thread:** Each pair asks what hurts more here: a stale read, a lost record or a missed deadline.

quiz.q: A team hard-deletes rows the moment a user clicks delete. A batch-job bug then marks 10,000 accounts deleted. Which choice would have helped, and when is hard delete still right?
quiz.a: Soft delete with a delayed purge, so the mistaken deletes could be reversed. Hard delete now still fits when compliance deadlines are too tight for a delay.

mcq.q: When does the catalog prefer explicit, policy-based tiering?
options: When lifecycles are predictable or legally set
When access patterns are unknown
When every object is under 1 KB
When the data is always hot
mcq.why: Automatic tiering suits unknown patterns. When you know the lifecycle or the law sets it, explicit rules are better.

hook: Dropbox left S3 to run its own storage. When does building your own storage actually make sense?
title: Build storage only if it's your product or top cost
body: Building storage is years of work. The rule: build only when storage is your product or your top cost; otherwise use a **managed service**. Two related choices trade control against effort the same way. Format: proprietary for deep optimization for one engine; open formats like Parquet and Iceberg for many engines and future migrations. Keys: provider-managed for simplicity; customer-managed for per-tenant revocation and **crypto-shredding**.
takeaway: Own the layer that sets you apart. Rent the rest.
deeper:
**Build vs buy:** Dropbox leaving S3 for its own Magic Pocket is an example that fits the build side of the rule. For most teams, storage is not what sets them apart, and a managed service is usually the better deal once the people who would run it are counted.

**Proprietary vs open:** A proprietary format can be tuned hard for one engine. But every storage system is replaced within 5 to 10 years, and long-lived data in a format only one engine reads turns the next migration into a full rewrite.

**Whose keys:** Provider-managed keys are simple. Customer-managed keys let you revoke one tenant's key, or crypto-shred: encrypt each user's data with its own key, then delete the key, so every copy, backups included, becomes unreadable.

**The thread:** Each choice trades effort now for control later. Take control only where you will use it.

quiz.q: A B2B SaaS must make a departing customer's data unreadable immediately, backups included. Which catalog choice matters, and why?
quiz.a: Customer-managed, per-tenant encryption keys. Revoking or deleting one tenant's key crypto-shreds their data everywhere, backups included, without rewriting anything.

mcq.q: When does the catalog recommend building your own storage?
options: When storage is your product or top cost
Whenever a managed service costs money
When you need open file formats
When the team has run the store before
mcq.why: Building pays off only where storage sets you apart or dominates cost. Otherwise a managed service wins.

section: Anti-patterns a senior staff engineer catches early
hook: A jobs table with a 'status' column works perfectly for a year. What breaks it?
title: Your jobs table is a queue in disguise
body: A table with a 'status' column that many workers poll is the easiest queue to build. It works at small scale. At large scale, **polling queries** and row locks fight with user traffic in the same database, and every new worker makes it worse. The fix: use a log such as Kafka, or a real queue, for work distribution, and keep the database for state.
takeaway: Databases hold state. Logs and queues move work.
deeper:
**Why it degrades:** Each idle worker keeps asking for rows with status 'pending'. More workers means more polling queries. Claiming a job takes a row lock, and workers contend for the same few rows at the head of the table. All of it runs on the database that also serves users.

**Why a log fits:** Kafka is durable and ordered per partition. Consumers read from an offset instead of scanning and locking rows, so adding consumers adds throughput rather than contention.

**How to argue it:** Don't only say no. Say what it will cost and when: 'This polling table will hit lock contention at about 5,000 workers, which is our plan for Q3.' A dated, numbered prediction changes minds faster than a principle.

**The catch:** It looks fine in review, which is exactly why it survives until year two or three.

quiz.q: A job table serves 200 workers fine today, and the roadmap says 5,000 workers by Q3. What will happen, and what would you propose now?
quiz.a: Polling queries and row locks will contend with user traffic on the same database. Move work distribution to Kafka or a real queue, and keep the table only for job state.

mcq.q: What fights with user traffic when a database is used as a queue?
options: Polling queries and row locks
Checksum verification
Cache invalidations
Schema migrations
mcq.why: Many workers polling a status column and locking rows compete with user queries on the same database.

predict.q: A jobs table polled by workers runs fine at 200 workers. What breaks first as the worker count grows?
options: Lock contention with user traffic
Disk capacity
Backup size

section: Anti-patterns a senior staff engineer catches early
hook: One 5 MB image stored in a database row gets copied far more often than you'd guess. Where do the copies go?
title: A blob in a row rides along in every copy of the row
body: Storing images or large JSON documents inside rows feels convenient: one system, one transaction. But every copy of the row carries the blob. Backups, replication and caches all slow down, because each one moves or holds those bytes. The fix is to store the **blob** in an object store and keep only a **pointer and checksum** in the row. The database stays small and fast for the queries it is good at.
takeaway: Put bytes in object storage and pointers in the database.
deeper:
**Where the copies go:** Every replica holds the blob. Every backup copies it again. Every cached row carries it into memory. One 5 MB image becomes many 5 MB copies, most of which exist only because the row does.

**Why the checksum:** The row and the blob now live in different systems. A checksum in the row lets a reader verify that the object it fetched is the one that was written, and lets scrubbers catch silent corruption.

**What object stores are good at:** Large immutable blobs suit erasure coding at 1.4× instead of 3×, CDN caching near users and cheap flat storage. None of that is available inside a database row.

**The ordering rule:** Write the object first, then commit the row that points to it. A crash then leaves at worst an unreferenced object for garbage collection, never a pointer to nothing.

quiz.q: A team stores 3 MB PDF attachments in a MySQL column, and replica lag and backup time keep climbing. What do you change, and in what write order?
quiz.a: Move attachments to an object store and keep a pointer and checksum in the row. Write the object first, then commit the row, so a crash leaves only an orphan object for garbage collection.

mcq.q: What should a database row keep once its blob moves to an object store?
options: A pointer and a checksum
The first megabyte of the blob
A compressed copy of the blob
Nothing, since the store tracks it
mcq.why: The pointer finds the object and the checksum verifies it, while backups and replicas stop carrying the bytes.

section: Anti-patterns a senior staff engineer catches early
hook: A partition key of 'day' looks tidy. Why does it melt one server every single day?
title: A 'day' partition key sends every write to one partition
body: Keys such as 'country' or 'day' look natural. That is the trap. An **unbounded partition** grows without limit and runs hot: all of today's writes land on today's partition, and one populous country holds a huge share of users. Soon it is too hot to serve and too large to move. Pick a key with **high cardinality**, many distinct values, or add a **bucket suffix** that spreads one logical key over several partitions.
takeaway: A partition key needs many values, and no value that dominates.
deeper:
**Why 'day' fails:** A time-based key puts all current writes on one partition while older ones sit idle. The hot partition takes the whole write load, and the rest of the cluster can't help.

**Why 'country' fails:** A few countries hold a large share of users. Their partitions grow without limit, and a partition that big can't be split or moved without a long, risky copy.

**The bucket suffix:** Append a small number, say 0 to 15, to the key, so one day becomes sixteen partitions. Writes spread across all of them; a read for that day fans out to the sixteen and merges the results.

**Where good keys come from:** Chat messages are partitioned by conversation ID and clustered by time. Time orders the data inside a partition instead of choosing the partition. That is high cardinality with a natural order.

quiz.q: An events table is partitioned by event date. Ingest is 100,000 writes a second, and one node sits at 100 percent while the others idle. What's the fix?
quiz.a: Add a bucket suffix so each day spreads over many partitions, or partition by a high-cardinality key such as user or device ID and cluster by time.

mcq.q: What does a bucket suffix do to a hot partition key?
options: Spreads one logical key across several partitions
Moves old partitions to cold storage
Merges small partitions into one
Adds a TTL to expire old rows
mcq.why: Appending a small bucket number splits one hot key into several physical partitions, so writes spread out.

predict.q: A busy table is partitioned by 'day'. Where do today's writes go?
options: All to one partition
Evenly across the cluster
To the least-loaded node

section: Anti-patterns a senior staff engineer catches early
hook: A crash lands between two writes. The record exists, but lookups can't find it. How long does that last?
title: Two writes, no transaction, inconsistent forever
body: Maintaining an index in application code means two writes, one for the data and one for the index, with no atomicity between them. If the process crashes between the two, they stay inconsistent forever: records that can't be found, or **index entries** pointing at nothing. Nothing repairs it on its own. Pinterest named this a key reason for moving its graph store to TiDB, where the database keeps indexes consistent with the data.
takeaway: If two writes must agree, one transaction must hold them.
deeper:
**The crash window:**
1. The app writes the record.
2. The process crashes.
3. The index write never happens.
The record exists but no lookup finds it. Reverse the order and the index points at a record that was never written.

**Why forever:** No process knows the two writes belonged together. Unless the client happens to retry the whole request, nothing re-runs the lost write. Only a full scan comparing data to index can find the mismatch.

**The review question:** Which queries need a secondary index, and is that index transactional with the data? Asked on day one, the answer is a database choice. Discovered in year three, it is a migration, which is what Pinterest took on.

**The short version:** An index that can disagree with its data is a rumour, not an index.

quiz.q: A service writes a user row, then a separate email-to-user lookup row, with no transaction. After a node crash, some users can't log in by email. What happened, and what's the fix?
quiz.a: The crash hit between the two writes, so the lookup row is missing. Write both in one transaction, or use a store with transactional secondary indexes.

mcq.q: What did Pinterest name as a key reason for moving its graph store to TiDB?
options: Application-maintained indexes without transactions
Blobs stored inside database rows
A database used as a job queue
Backups that were never restored
mcq.why: Two unlinked writes, data and index, drift apart after crashes; transactional indexes close that gap.

predict.q: An app writes data and its index separately, then crashes between them. How long does the mismatch last?
options: Forever, until something scans for it
Until the next compaction
About one replication delay

section: Anti-patterns a senior staff engineer catches early
hook: A service writes only to its cache and promises to flush later. What happens when that cache node dies?
title: A cache that can lose data is a bad database
body: Writing only to the cache and flushing to durable storage later makes writes fast and simple. It also means the newest data lives in one place that was never built to keep it. When the cache node dies, every unflushed write is lost. The rule: caches must be **rebuildable** from a durable store. If losing the cache loses data, it isn't a cache. It's an unreliable database.
takeaway: If you can't rebuild it from somewhere else, it isn't a cache.
deeper:
**Why it's tempting:** Cache writes are fast, and batching flushes reduces load on the database. On a normal day, everything works.

**Why it fails:** Caches are built to lose things: they evict under memory pressure and restart empty. A node crash, a deploy or an eviction before the flush all lose acknowledged writes, and nobody notices until a user does.

**The safe patterns:** Look-aside: write to the durable store, then invalidate the cache, so a miss refills from the truth. Write-through: update the store and the cache together on every write. Either way, the durable store stays the source of truth.

**The design test:** Delete the whole cache on purpose. If the system recovers with a latency blip, it was a cache. If data is gone, it was a database without durability.

quiz.q: To cut database load, a team makes a counters service increment only in Redis and flush every 10 minutes. What's the risk, and what's safer?
quiz.a: A Redis node failure loses up to 10 minutes of acknowledged increments. Write to a durable store first, keep the cache rebuildable, and accept loss only where the data truly tolerates it.

mcq.q: Which rule prevents the cache-as-source-of-truth anti-pattern?
options: Caches must be rebuildable from a durable store
Caches must flush writes in batches
Caches must hold every key in memory
Caches must replicate across regions
mcq.why: If the durable store always holds the truth, losing a cache node costs only latency, never data.

section: Anti-patterns a senior staff engineer catches early
hook: Nobody decided to keep this dataset forever. Nobody decided anything. How does it end?
title: Retention by nobody ends in a cost or compliance incident
body: No TTL, no lifecycle rule, no owner. Nobody chose to keep the data forever; nobody chose anything. That is **retention by nobody**, and the dataset grows until it becomes an incident. Either a cost incident, when someone finally notices the bill, or a compliance incident, when personal data outlives any legitimate need. The fix is cheap on day one: an owner and a retention rule when the dataset is created, with safe expiry as the default.
takeaway: Data with no owner is kept forever and paid for forever.
deeper:
**Why it happens:** Deleting data feels risky and keeping it feels free. With no owner, nobody takes the risk, so everything stays.

**Why forever is dangerous:** Storage and cost grow without limit. Compliance risk grows with every extra year of personal data. And nobody owns the cleanup, so each year it gets bigger and scarier.

**The questions that catch it:** Who deletes it? What is the retention rule? What does the default retention cost in 3 years? What share of stored data hasn't been read in 90 days?

**The fix at scale:** Make it a platform rule. Every new dataset declares an owner and a TTL or lifecycle rule, and one without them doesn't deploy. It is the same 'no declaration, no deploy' pattern used to find personal data for GDPR deletion.

quiz.q: An audit finds a 2 PB log bucket, created five years ago, with no TTL, no owner and almost no reads. What do you do now, and what stops the next one?
quiz.a: Assign an owner, set a retention rule, and tier or delete the unread data. Prevent the next one by requiring an owner and TTL on every new dataset: no declaration, no deploy.

mcq.q: Which two incidents does retention by nobody eventually cause?
options: A cost incident or a compliance incident
A latency incident or an availability incident
A consistency incident or a replication incident
A security breach or a regional failover
mcq.why: Unowned data grows until the bill gets noticed or personal data is kept past any legitimate need.

section: Anti-patterns a senior staff engineer catches early
hook: Every write on your platform waits on another region, and most data never needed it. How did that happen?
title: Synchronous cross-region should be a choice, not a default
body: Someone made cross-region **synchronous replication** the platform default, to be safe. Now every write pays a cross-region round trip, even for data that could tolerate a few seconds of loss. Latency and cost rise everywhere for durability most datasets never needed. The fix: make synchronous replication an explicit choice per dataset, backed by an **RPO** requirement, the amount of data you may lose in a disaster.
takeaway: Make every dataset earn its zero RPO.
deeper:
**What synchronous buys:** A write is acknowledged only after another region has it, so losing a region loses no acknowledged writes. RPO is zero.

**What it costs:** A cross-region round trip on every write, forever. For a clickstream, a cache fill or a derived table, that cost buys nothing.

**The asynchronous alternative:** Replicate after acknowledging. A region loss may drop the last few seconds of writes, which is fine when latency matters more than those seconds.

**How to decide:** Ask for the RPO per dataset. Money and identity may need zero; logs and feeds usually don't. A home-region design with async replicas elsewhere gives fast, consistent writes and a small RPO on failover.

**Why the default matters:** Most teams keep the default, so a synchronous default quietly taxes every write on the platform.

quiz.q: A platform replicates every write synchronously to a second region, and the analytics events team complains about write latency. What do you ask, and what do you likely change?
quiz.a: Ask for the dataset's RPO. Analytics events can usually tolerate a few seconds of loss, so switch them to asynchronous replication and keep synchronous only where RPO must be zero.

mcq.q: What should back a choice of synchronous cross-region replication?
options: An explicit RPO requirement for that dataset
A platform-wide default for safety
A cache hit rate above 99 percent
A replication factor of at least five
mcq.why: Synchronous replication taxes every write, so choose it per dataset, only when the RPO must be zero.

section: Anti-patterns a senior staff engineer catches early
hook: Your backup jobs have succeeded every night for two years. Why might you still have no backup?
title: A backup never restored is a hope, not a backup
body: Green backup jobs prove that something was written somewhere. They don't prove you can get data back. Jobs can silently skip files, formats drift, keys go missing, and a restore can take far longer than anyone assumed. A backup that has never been restored in a drill is a hope, not a backup. The SRE book's data-integrity guidance puts it plainly: what matters is the **restore**, not the backup.
takeaway: Measure restores, not backups.
deeper:
**What a drill proves:** That the backup exists, is complete, can be decrypted with keys you still have, and can be read by today's software. It also measures restore time, the number the business actually cares about.

**The review question:** When did we last restore from backup, and how long did it take? 'Never' and 'we don't know' are the same answer.

**Restore time is part of durability:** The design doc's durability section lists backups and their restore time. A backup that takes a week to restore may blow the recovery time objective (RTO), how long recovery may take.

**What backups are for:** Replicas protect against hardware failure but faithfully copy a bad write or a mass delete. Backups are the defence against your own mistakes, which makes them the one thing you can't afford to assume.

quiz.q: Nightly backups ran green for two years. The first real restore, after an operator error, takes four days, and a key needed for older backups is gone. What should have been in place?
quiz.a: Regular restore drills that measure success and duration, including key availability. They would have exposed the missing key and the four-day restore before a real incident.

mcq.q: What does a restore drill show that a successful backup job does not?
options: Whether data can be recovered, and how fast
Whether backup storage costs are rising
Whether the replication factor is high enough
Whether the backup job ran on schedule
mcq.why: Only a restore proves the data is complete and readable, and it measures the restore time recovery depends on.

section: Anti-patterns a senior staff engineer catches early
hook: One team's batch job just slowed every online service in the company. How was that even possible?
title: Pooling capacity without quotas also pools failure
body: A giant shared storage cluster is efficient: spare capacity goes wherever it's needed. Without quotas, it goes to whoever grabs it. One tenant's batch job saturates the disks, and every online service slows down with it. Shared storage needs **per-tenant quotas** and **priority classes**, as Tectonic provides with its traffic classes. Without isolation, pooling capacity also pools failure.
takeaway: A shared pool without quotas is one tenant away from an outage.
deeper:
**Why pools are worth it:** Meta chose big Tectonic clusters to fix stranded capacity, the free disk and IOPS that sit idle in one small cell while another is full.

**What quotas do:** Cap each tenant's share of IOPS and bandwidth, so one workload can't take everything.

**What priority classes do:** Latency-sensitive online traffic goes ahead of batch work when the disks are busy. The batch job still finishes; it just yields.

**The trade-off:** The alternative is Azure's model, small fixed-size stamps that bound failure by construction but strand capacity. Pick small cells when blast radius is the top risk, and a giant shared pool, with quotas, when stranded capacity is the top cost.

**The review question:** What is the blast radius of one bad tenant? In a pool without quotas, the answer is everyone.

quiz.q: An ML team's nightly scan of training data saturates the shared storage cluster, and user-facing p99 triples every night. What two mechanisms fix it without splitting the cluster?
quiz.a: Per-tenant quotas to cap the ML job's share of I/O, and priority classes so online traffic goes first, as Tectonic's traffic classes do.

mcq.q: How does Tectonic keep one tenant from saturating a shared cluster?
options: Traffic classes with quotas and priorities
A separate fixed-size stamp per tenant
A different erasure code per tenant
Moving batch tenants to archival storage
mcq.why: Tectonic pools capacity in big clusters and uses traffic classes to isolate tenants and put online work first.

section: Anti-patterns a senior staff engineer catches early
hook: Data that must live ten years will outlast the engine that wrote it. What happens to it then?
title: Ten-year data in a one-engine format means a full rewrite
body: Some data must live ten years. Every storage system gets replaced within 5 to 10. Put long-lived data in a **proprietary format** only one engine can read, and replacing that engine means a full rewrite of every byte. **Open formats** such as Parquet and Iceberg let many engines read the same files, so switching engines doesn't require rewriting the data.
takeaway: Data outlives engines, so store it in a format that outlives them too.
deeper:
**The timeline problem:** Retention rules can run for a decade, while engines turn over every 5 to 10 years. Long-lived data will almost certainly meet a second engine.

**What a rewrite costs:** At 100 Gbps sustained, 50 PB takes about 46 days of pure transfer, before verification, shadow reads and a rollback window. A format change adds a translation step to every byte.

**What open formats buy:** Trino, Spark and Presto can all read Iceberg or Delta tables on object storage. The engine becomes replaceable while the data stays put.

**When proprietary is right:** It allows deep optimization for one engine. That can be worth it for data that won't outlive the engine.

**The day-one habit:** Keep data in open formats where possible, alongside an API layer, CDC and a version on every record.

quiz.q: A team plans to archive 10 years of compliance records in their current database's native snapshot format. What's the risk, and what would you suggest?
quiz.a: The engine will likely be replaced within that decade, turning the archive into a full rewrite. Store the records in an open format such as Parquet or Iceberg on object storage.

mcq.q: When does the trade-off catalog allow a proprietary format?
options: For deep optimization for one engine
For data many engines must read
For data that must live ten years
For data that will be migrated soon
mcq.why: Proprietary formats can be tuned tightly to one engine; open formats win when many engines or future migrations matter.

section: Anti-patterns a senior staff engineer catches early
hook: You tell a team their design is an anti-pattern. They nod and ship it anyway. What should you have said?
title: A dated, numbered prediction beats a principle
body: 'Don't use the database as a queue' is a principle, and principles are easy to nod at and ignore. So don't only say no. Say what it will cost and when: 'This polling table will hit lock contention at about 5,000 workers, which is our plan for Q3.' A **dated, numbered prediction** changes minds faster than a principle, because it ties an abstract rule to the team's own roadmap.
takeaway: Say what it will cost and when, not just that it's wrong.
deeper:
**Why it works:** A principle invites debate about whether it applies. A prediction invites a check: is 5,000 workers really the Q3 plan? Once the team agrees on the inputs, the conclusion follows.

**How to build one:**
1. Name the resource that breaks: locks, IOPS, metadata, a partition.
2. Estimate the load where it breaks.
3. Find that load on the team's roadmap.
4. State the date.

**It matches how decisions get presented:** Lead with the requirement, show the numbers with assumptions labelled, name what you give up, show the exit. Reviewers trust a wrong estimate with clear assumptions more than a vague claim, because they can fix the assumptions.

**The catch:** A prediction can be wrong, and that's fine. A wrong number with visible inputs gets corrected. A vague warning just gets ignored.

quiz.q: You spot an unbounded 'country' partition key in a review. How would a senior staff engineer phrase the objection?
quiz.a: As a dated, numbered prediction tied to the roadmap, for example: after next quarter's launch in our biggest market, that partition takes most writes and becomes too large to move. Then propose a high-cardinality key or bucket suffix.

mcq.q: What changes minds fastest when rejecting an anti-pattern in review?
options: A dated, numbered prediction of the failure
A link to a best-practices document
A firm 'no' from a senior engineer
A list of companies that failed this way
mcq.why: A specific cost tied to the team's own roadmap is checkable, which turns a debate into arithmetic.

section: How to present a storage decision
hook: 'We should use Cassandra' starts an argument. What kind of sentence would end it instead?
title: Lead with the requirement, not the product
body: Open with a product name and every reviewer has a favourite alternative. Open with the requirement instead. 'We need 20,000 writes per second per region, a p99 under 10 ms, and 7-year retention' is a sentence everyone can check. 'We should use Cassandra' is one everyone can argue with. Then **show the numbers**: capacity, durability and cost estimates, with every assumption labelled.
takeaway: Requirements get checked. Product names get argued.
deeper:
**Why requirements first:** A storage decision affects many teams for many years. Stated requirements give everyone the same test: does the proposal meet 20,000 writes per second per region, p99 under 10 ms, 7-year retention? Product preferences then have to argue against numbers, not against each other.

**Why labelled assumptions:** Reviewers trust a wrong estimate with clear assumptions more than a vague claim, because they can fix the assumptions. The photo capacity sketch works this way: 10 percent of users, 2 MB photos, 25 percent for resizes, 1.4× for erasure coding. Change one input and recompute.

**What to show:** Capacity today, in 1 year and in 3. Durability from redundancy and repair time. Cost per GB-month and per request, including replicas and backups.

**The payoff:** Once the requirement is agreed, the product choice often follows from it.

quiz.q: Your proposal's first slide says 'Use DynamoDB', and the review stalls in a debate about Cassandra. How would you rewrite the opening?
quiz.a: Lead with checkable requirements, such as writes per second per region, a p99 target and retention, then show capacity, durability and cost numbers with assumptions labelled, and let the product follow.

mcq.q: Why do reviewers trust a wrong estimate with labelled assumptions over a vague claim?
options: They can fix the assumptions and recompute
Wrong estimates are usually close enough
Labelled estimates are always conservative
Vague claims hide the product name
mcq.why: Visible inputs let reviewers correct one number and rerun the math instead of arguing about the conclusion.

section: How to present a storage decision
hook: Admitting what your design gives up sounds like weakness in a review. Why does it do the opposite?
title: Name what you give up, then show the exit
body: Every storage choice gives up something: consistency, cost, latency, flexibility or operational simplicity. Leave it out and reviewers will find it for you. **Name what you give up** first: it shows you understood the trade. Then **show the exit**: explain how data would move out if the choice turns out wrong. That lowers the stakes of the decision, and lower stakes mean faster approval.
takeaway: A reversible decision is an easy decision to approve.
deeper:
**Why naming the cost helps:** Reviewers will find the weakness anyway. Saying it first moves the conversation from 'did they notice?' to 'is the trade worth it?', which is the conversation you want.

**The five usual costs:** Consistency (stale reads), cost (replicas, egress), latency (cross-region writes), flexibility (key-only access) and operational simplicity (one more system to run).

**Why the exit speeds approval:** A decision that can't be undone deserves maximum scrutiny. One with a credible exit, built on a routing layer, CDC, open formats and versioned records, is safer to try, so reviewers can say yes sooner.

**It closes the loop:** The four presentation rules are lead with the requirement, show the numbers, name what you give up, and show the exit. The last one answers the question every review should ask: how would we leave this system?

quiz.q: Two proposals for the same store are equally sound. One ends with a migration-out plan; the other calls the choice permanent. Which gets approved faster, and why?
quiz.a: The one with the exit. A credible way to move data out if the choice is wrong lowers the stakes, so reviewers can approve without demanding certainty.

mcq.q: Why does showing the exit speed up approval of a storage decision?
options: It lowers the stakes if the choice is wrong
It proves the chosen product is the best
It removes the need for a cost model
It guarantees no migration will be needed
mcq.why: A recoverable decision needs less certainty, so reviewers can approve it sooner.

hook: Interview answers and real storage designs look like different skills. What do they have in common?
title: Interviews and real designs share one five-part shape
body: Candidates often jump straight to boxes and arrows. Strong answers, in interviews and in real design docs, follow one **shape**: state the requirements, make estimates, present a design, walk through failure modes, discuss trade-offs. Each step constrains the next. Practise the shape on model problems and you build the muscle production design reviews use. Any single outline is one good answer, not the only one.
takeaway: Requirements, estimates, design, failures, trade-offs. In that order, every time.
deeper:
**Why requirements first:** They define what good means. An S3-like store needs an 11 nines durability target and strong read-after-write consistency, and those two lines drive most of the design.

**Why estimates second:** Numbers eliminate options. At 250 TB of new photos a day, tiering policy matters more than the object store. At 100 Gbps, 50 PB takes about 46 days to move, so a migration planned in weeks is wrong.

**Why failure modes:** A design that only works on the happy path isn't finished. Name disk, node, zone and region loss, hot keys, bad deploys and corrupt writes, and say how each is detected and recovered.

**Why trade-offs last:** Saying what you gave up, and when you would choose differently, shows judgment. It is also where interviewers and reviewers probe hardest.

quiz.q: An interviewer asks you to design chat storage, and you start drawing partitions immediately. What did you skip, and why does it matter?
quiz.a: Requirements and estimates. Without write rates, read patterns, retention and encryption needs, you can't justify the partition key, the engine or the tiering.

mcq.q: What order does a strong storage design answer follow?
options: Requirements, estimates, design, failure modes, trade-offs
Design, estimates, requirements, trade-offs, failure modes
Estimates, design, trade-offs, requirements, failure modes
Failure modes, design, requirements, estimates, trade-offs
mcq.why: Requirements define success, estimates rule options out, and the design is then stressed by failures and justified by trade-offs.

hook: An object store must list everything under a prefix across billions of keys. What makes that cheap?
title: An S3-like store is three services: API, metadata, data
body: Design an object store with PUT, GET, DELETE and LIST by prefix, an 11 nines durability target and strong read-after-write consistency. Split it in three. A stateless **front end** runs API servers, auth and routing. A **metadata service** maps bucket and key to object location in a sharded, replicated key-value store, range-partitioned by (bucket, key) so LIST works. A **data service** of storage nodes holds chunks, with large objects erasure-coded across failure domains.
takeaway: Keep the front end stateless and the metadata sorted.
deeper:
**Why range partitioning:** Keys sorted by (bucket, key) keep every object under a prefix next to each other, so LIST is a range scan over one or a few shards. Hash partitioning would scatter them across every shard.

**The catch:** Sorted keys create hot prefixes. If everyone writes under one prefix, one shard takes the load, so shards must split automatically.

**Large vs small objects:** Large objects are split into chunks and erasure-coded, for example RS(10,4), across failure domains. Small objects can be replicated, or packed into larger files to save metadata, which was Haystack's idea.

**Why stateless front ends:** Any server can take any request, so the tier scales by adding machines and loses nothing when one dies.

**The trade-off:** Erasure coding cuts cost but makes small reads and repair more expensive.

quiz.q: Your object store hash-partitions its metadata by key, and customers complain that LIST on a prefix is painfully slow. Why, and what does fixing it cost?
quiz.a: Hashing scatters a prefix's keys across every shard, so LIST must query them all. Range partitioning by (bucket, key) fixes it but creates hot prefixes, so shards must split automatically.

mcq.q: Why is the metadata range-partitioned by (bucket, key)?
options: So LIST by prefix becomes a range scan
So writes spread evenly by hash
So objects can be erasure-coded
So the front end can stay stateless
mcq.why: Sorted keys keep a prefix's objects together, so listing them reads one contiguous range.

hook: An S3-like store writes a new object's data across a dozen disks. At what exact moment does the object exist?
title: The metadata commit is the instant an object exists
body: A PUT writes chunks to many storage nodes, and a reader could arrive halfway through. So the write path has a strict order: write data fragments first, then commit metadata. The **metadata commit** is the **linearization point**. Before it, readers see the old object or none; after it, every reader sees the new one. That single atomic step is what gives strong read-after-write consistency.
takeaway: Write the bytes first; let one metadata commit make them real.
deeper:
**Why that order:** If metadata were committed first, a reader could follow it to fragments that don't exist yet. Writing data first means a crash leaves, at worst, orphan fragments nobody points to.

**The background crew:**
1. Scrubbers read data and verify checksums, catching silent corruption.
2. Repair workers rebuild lost fragments in parallel.
3. A garbage collector removes chunks no metadata references, including orphans from failed writes.

**Where it strains:** The metadata store, range-partitioned by (bucket, key), gets hot prefixes, so shards must split automatically. Erasure coding cuts cost but makes small reads and repairs more expensive.

**The general lesson:** Consistency doesn't need every node to agree at once. It needs one place where the decision becomes true, and a write order that never lets readers get ahead of it.

quiz.q: A PUT has written 12 of 14 erasure-coded fragments when the front-end server crashes before committing metadata. What does a reader see, and what happens to the fragments?
quiz.a: The reader sees the old object or none, because metadata was never committed. The written fragments are unreferenced, so the garbage collector eventually removes them.

mcq.q: What gives an S3-like store strong read-after-write consistency?
options: The metadata commit acts as the linearization point
Every fragment is written synchronously to three regions
Readers always query the storage nodes directly
Scrubbers verify checksums before each read
mcq.why: Once metadata commits atomically, every later read sees the new object; before it, none do.

hook: A billion users upload photos, then view them far more often. Which layer should serve most of those views?
title: Photo serving: CDN first, origin cache second, store last
body: Users add about 250 TB of photos a day, and reads are dominated by recent and viral photos. So layers in front of the store absorb them. The upload service writes the original to an object store, then an async pipeline makes resized versions. **Metadata** (owner, time, privacy, locations of each size) lives in a sharded database keyed by photo ID. Serving goes through a **CDN**, then an origin cache, then the object store.
takeaway: Serve the hot few from the edge; keep the store for the long tail.
deeper:
**Why async resizing:** The upload returns once the original is safe. Thumbnails and other sizes are derived data, so a pipeline can make them later and remake them if they are lost.

**Why metadata is separate:** Owner, privacy and the location of each size get queried and changed; the bytes never change. A sharded database keyed by photo ID handles the first, the object store the second.

**How the layers split the load:**
1. The CDN serves popular photos from edge caches near users.
2. The origin cache catches what the CDN misses.
3. The object store handles the long tail of older photos.

**Why it works:** Access drops sharply with age, so a small set of recent and viral photos takes most reads. Caching that set covers most traffic, while the store is sized for durability, not peak views.

quiz.q: A photo goes viral with 50 million views in an hour. Which layer should absorb them, and what could go wrong if the owner makes it private mid-spike?
quiz.a: The CDN absorbs the hot object. It may keep serving the photo under stale privacy settings for a short time unless the change triggers an invalidation.

mcq.q: Where does photo metadata live in this design?
options: A sharded database keyed by photo ID
Inside the object, next to the bytes
In the CDN's edge caches
In the async resizing pipeline
mcq.why: Owner, time, privacy and size locations change and get queried, so they live in a sharded database, apart from the immutable bytes.

hook: A user deletes a photo and it vanishes instantly. Are the bytes actually gone?
title: Photos: replicate hot, re-encode cold, delete in two steps
body: Photos cool fast, so their storage should change with age. Replicate hot data for fast reads for the first days, then **re-encode** to wider erasure codes, which is what Meta did going from Haystack to f4, and later inside Tectonic. Deletion takes two steps. A **soft delete** in metadata makes the photo disappear at once; compaction removes the bytes later, within the compliance window. A viral photo is a hot object the CDN absorbs.
takeaway: Disappearing is instant; destruction runs on a compliance clock.
deeper:
**Why replicate first:** New photos get most of their reads early. Full replicas serve those reads from one node, fast. Once reads drop, wider erasure codes cut the bytes stored per photo.

**Why two-step deletion:** Rewriting packed, erasure-coded storage for every single delete would be ruinous. Marking the photo deleted in metadata hides it immediately; compaction reclaims the space in bulk. The gap must stay inside the compliance window, and it doubles as protection against mistaken deletes.

**Region loss:** Keep erasure-coded fragments or replicas across regions for durability.

**The privacy catch:** A CDN may keep serving a photo under stale privacy settings for a short time after the owner changes them, unless the change triggers an invalidation. Durability and freshness are separate problems, solved in separate layers.

quiz.q: Legal requires deleted photos to be physically erased within 30 days, but your compaction runs every 45 days. What's wrong, and why not delete the bytes immediately?
quiz.a: Physical deletion lands outside the compliance window, so compaction must run more often. Deleting bytes immediately would force costly rewrites of packed, erasure-coded storage for every delete.

mcq.q: What happens first when a user deletes a photo in this design?
options: A soft delete in metadata hides it
Compaction rewrites the file holding it
The CDN re-encodes the photo
Every fragment is overwritten with zeros
mcq.why: The metadata soft delete makes the photo disappear at once; compaction removes the bytes later, within the compliance window.

hook: A key-value store must work across three continents. One question decides the whole design. Which one?
title: Multi-region KV: home region, multi-leader or consensus
body: Before any design, ask: must writes be accepted in every region, or only in a home region? **Option A**: each key has a home region, one leader per shard, async replicas elsewhere. Simple, consistent per key, small RPO on failover. **Option B**: multi-leader, always writable, but last-writer-wins can lose concurrent updates. **Option C**: Paxos across regions per shard, Spanner-style. Strong consistency, but every write pays a cross-region round trip.
takeaway: Default to a home region; pay for more only where it matters.
deeper:
**Option A, home region:** Raft or Paxos runs inside the region for each shard, and other regions hold async replicas for local reads. Losing a region means failover with a small RPO. Pick it for most products.

**Option B, multi-leader:** Every region accepts writes and replicates asynchronously, resolving conflicts with last-writer-wins timestamps or CRDTs. Dynamo and Cassandra follow this family. Pick it for always-writable carts or presence.

**Option C, global consensus:** Paxos runs on a majority of each shard's replicas, and those replicas are spread across regions, so a commit waits on another region. Pick it for money and uniqueness constraints.

**Under all three:** An LSM tree per node, partitioned by consistent hashing or by range with automatic splitting.

**The short version:** Pick A until a requirement forces B or C.

quiz.q: A global username service must never let two users claim the same name, even during a region outage. Which option fits, and what does it cost?
quiz.a: Option C, global consensus: Paxos across regions per shard gives the strong consistency uniqueness needs. The cost is a cross-region round trip on every write.

mcq.q: Which option suits an always-writable shopping cart?
options: Multi-leader with conflict resolution
A home region per key
Global consensus per shard
A single global leader
mcq.why: Multi-leader keeps every region writable; conflicts are resolved with last-writer-wins or CRDTs, which suits carts and presence.

predict.q: For most multi-region products, which key-value design is the recommended default?
options: A home region per key
Multi-leader in every region
Global consensus per shard

hook: A user asks to be deleted. Their data sits in systems nobody remembers building. How do you find every copy?
title: GDPR deletion starts with 'no declaration, no deploy'
body: A user's data is in databases, caches, object stores, search indexes, logs, the lake, ML training sets and backups. GDPR Article 17 requires erasure without undue delay. You can't delete what you can't find, so start with a **data inventory**: every dataset declares whether it holds personal data and which column holds the user ID. No declaration, no deploy. Then a **deletion orchestrator** fans each request out to every registered store.
takeaway: You can only delete what you've inventoried.
deeper:
**What the orchestrator does:**
1. Receives the request.
2. Writes a durable deletion job, so a crash doesn't lose it.
3. Fans out to every registered store.
4. Tracks completion and retries failures.
Meta's DELF is a published example of framework-driven deletion.

**Per-store handling:** Online stores delete by key, and caches are invalidated. The lake and backups need their own techniques, because they are built to be immutable.

**Verification:** Periodic scanners look for deleted user IDs and alert if any turn up. Deletion nobody checks is deletion that silently failed somewhere.

**Why the inventory is the hard part:** The orchestrator is ordinary engineering. Knowing every dataset that holds a user ID, including the one created last week, is organizational. 'No declaration, no deploy' makes it a gate instead of a hope.

quiz.q: A new team ships an analytics table containing user emails but never registers it. A deletion request arrives. What happens, and what process would have prevented it?
quiz.a: The orchestrator never reaches the table, so the user's data survives deletion. An inventory gate, where no declaration of personal data and user-ID column means no deploy, would have blocked the launch.

mcq.q: Why does the deletion orchestrator write a durable job first?
options: So the request survives crashes and can be retried
So the user can cancel the request later
So backups can be skipped entirely
So caches refill faster afterwards
mcq.why: Fan-out across many stores takes time and can fail midway; a durable job lets the orchestrator track and retry until done.

hook: Deleting one user from a year of immutable backups would mean rewriting all of them. What's the shortcut?
title: Crypto-shredding: delete the key, not the backups
body: Backups and logs are built to be immutable, and rewriting a year of them per deletion request is absurd. So use **crypto-shredding**: encrypt each user's data with a per-user key, and to delete the user, delete the key. Every copy, backups included, becomes unreadable without rewriting anything. The lake gets a different fix: partition or index tables by user, so Iceberg or Hudi deletes plus compaction touch rows, not whole tables.
takeaway: When you can't destroy every copy, destroy the only key.
deeper:
**How the shred works:**
1. On write, encrypt the user's data with that user's key.
2. Store the ciphertext anywhere: databases, logs, backups.
3. On deletion, destroy the key.
The bytes remain, but they are now unreadable noise.

**The lake:** Tables partitioned or indexed by user let deletes be row-level instead of full rewrites. Iceberg and Hudi record the deletes, and compaction later rewrites the affected files.

**The costs:** Per-user keys add key-management load, and the key store itself must be durable and must truly delete. Deleting from immutable formats needs a compaction budget.

**Why it matters:** Deletion must reach primary stores, caches, replicas, backups and the lake. Crypto-shredding is the practical way to reach the backups without restoring or rewriting them.

quiz.q: Your deletion system clears a user from every online store within a day, but nightly backups hold 90 days of history. An auditor asks whether the user's data is still readable. What design lets you answer no?
quiz.a: Crypto-shredding: encrypt each user's data with a per-user key and delete the key on request. The backups still exist, but that user's data in them is unreadable.

mcq.q: How does crypto-shredding delete a user's data from backups?
options: By destroying the user's encryption key
By rewriting every backup without the user
By marking the user deleted in metadata
By expiring backups older than 30 days
mcq.why: Without the per-user key, every encrypted copy, backups included, becomes unreadable with no rewrite needed.

predict.q: How do you delete one user from a year of immutable backups without rewriting them?
options: Destroy that user's encryption key
Mark the user deleted in each backup's index
Revoke the user's access to the backups

hook: You have a 100 Gbps link and 50 PB to move. How long will the migration take?
title: Moving 50 PB at 100 Gbps takes about 46 days
body: Teams plan migrations in weeks. The arithmetic disagrees. At 100 Gbps sustained, 50 PB takes 50e15 × 8 / 1e11 = 4 million seconds, about 46 days, and that is pure transfer on a perfectly used link. Verification, retries and production traffic sharing the pipe all stretch it. So plan for months, and for **bandwidth limits**.

stat.label: to copy 50 PB at a sustained 100 Gbps

takeaway: Do the transfer math before you promise a date.
deeper:
**The arithmetic:**
1. 50 PB = 50 × 10¹⁵ bytes.
2. × 8 = 4 × 10¹⁷ bits.
3. ÷ 10¹¹ bits per second = 4 × 10⁶ seconds.
4. ÷ 86,400 ≈ 46 days.

**Why reality is slower:** The link is never fully yours. User traffic needs bandwidth, and so does repair. Every object must also be checksummed, counted and compared.

**What the number changes:** A migration this long spans deploys, schema changes and incidents. Writes keep arriving during those 46 days, so the plan needs dual writes or CDC, and deletes made mid-migration must be replayed to the new system.

**Where to start:** Backfill the oldest and coldest data first, because it changes least.

**The short version:** Physics sets the floor, and everything else only adds.

quiz.q: A VP asks you to move 20 PB between systems in two weeks over a 100 Gbps link. What do you answer?
quiz.a: Pure transfer alone takes about 18.5 days at full line rate: 20e15 × 8 / 1e11 = 1.6 million seconds. With verification and shared bandwidth, plan for well over a month.

mcq.q: Why does a 50 PB migration need dual writes or CDC?
options: Writes keep arriving during weeks of copying
The link can't carry reads and writes together
Object stores reject bulk copies
Checksums only work on live data
mcq.why: Copying takes weeks, so new writes and deletes must also reach the new system, through dual writes or change data capture.

predict.q: How long does it take to copy 50 PB over a sustained 100 Gbps link?
options: About 46 days
About 5 days
About 1 year

hook: How do you move 50 PB between storage systems while users keep reading and writing, with zero downtime?
title: Zero-downtime migration runs in eight careful steps
body: Big-bang cutovers fail because you can't test them until it's too late. The pattern that works moves traffic in small, reversible steps. Put a **routing layer** in front. Dual-write new data, or write new and read through to old. Backfill the oldest, coldest data first. Verify with checksums and counts. Run **shadow reads** and log mismatches. Cut reads over gradually. Keep the old system read-only for rollback. Then decommission.
takeaway: Every step stays reversible until the last one.
deeper:
**The full sequence:**
1. Routing layer, so clients don't know which system serves a key.
2. Dual-write, or write new and read through to old.
3. Backfill in batches, oldest and coldest first.
4. Verify: checksums per object, counts per prefix.
5. Shadow reads: read both, compare, log mismatches.
6. Cut over reads by percentage of keys or tenants.
7. Keep the old system read-only for a rollback window.
8. Decommission.

**Who used it:** Meta for MyRocks, Uber for GCP, Dropbox for Magic Pocket.

**Why coldest first:** Old data changes least, so it is least likely to be modified after it is copied.

**The two traps:** Deletes during migration must be replayed to the new system, or deleted data comes back. Objects mutated after being copied need CDC or version checks, or the new system keeps the stale copy.

quiz.q: Midway through a migration, a user deletes a file that was already backfilled to the new system. After cutover, the file reappears. What was missing?
quiz.a: Deletes during migration weren't replayed to the new system. CDC or dual writes must carry deletes, like every other mutation, to the new store.

mcq.q: What does the shadow-read step do?
options: Reads both systems and logs mismatches
Sends every read to the new system at once
Copies the oldest data first
Keeps the old system read-only
mcq.why: Shadow reads compare answers from the old and new systems on real traffic before any user depends on the new one.

hook: Moving small objects to a cheaper storage tier can raise your bill. How?
title: Tier by the access curve, but never below a size floor
body: A **tiering policy** starts from access logs, object sizes, per-tier costs (storage, retrieval, minimum duration) and latency needs. Keep objects hot for N days, where N is the **knee** of the access curve. Warm after that. Cold or archive after M days without reads. But never tier objects below a size floor, because per-object overhead can exceed the savings. Respect minimum storage durations, and allow pinning for known-hot data and legal hold.
takeaway: Tiering saves money per byte and costs money per object.
deeper:
**Finding N:** Plot reads against age. Before the knee, data is hot, and moving it would trigger retrieval costs. After the knee, reads fall off and a cheaper tier pays.

**The size floor:** Every object carries fixed overhead in every tier: metadata, transition requests, sometimes per-object charges. For tiny objects, that overhead outweighs the per-byte saving, so moving them loses money.

**Minimum durations:** Colder tiers charge early-delete fees if an object leaves before its minimum storage duration. Moving data that will be deleted soon can cost more than leaving it.

**Pinning:** Some data is hot for known reasons, like a featured item, and some can't be moved or deleted, like data under legal hold. The policy needs an override for both.

**The catch:** Every tier boundary is a move, and every move is a chance to lose or duplicate data.

quiz.q: A team moves every object older than 30 days, including billions of 2 KB thumbnails, to an archive tier. The bill goes up. Why?
quiz.a: The thumbnails are below any sensible size floor: per-object transition and overhead costs exceed their tiny per-byte savings. Exclude small objects, or pack them into larger files first.

mcq.q: What should set how long objects stay in the hot tier?
options: The knee of the access curve
A fixed 90-day rule
The object's size
The number of replicas
mcq.why: Data should stay hot until reads fall off; after the knee, a cheaper tier pays for itself.

predict.q: You move millions of tiny objects to a cheaper storage tier. What can happen to the bill?
options: It can go up
It drops by the tier's price gap
It stays exactly the same

hook: An archive tier costs a fraction of the hot tier. When does moving data there lose money anyway?
title: Move data only if savings beat transition plus retrieval
body: Cheaper per GB is not the same as cheaper. The rule: tiering saves money only if the storage saving per month, times months stored, is greater than the **transition cost** plus the expected **retrieval cost**. Data read again soon, or deleted soon, can lose money in a cheap tier. S3 Intelligent-Tiering automates this per object; explicit lifecycle rules are better when you already know the lifecycle.
takeaway: A cheap tier is only cheap if you leave the data there.
deeper:
**The inequality:** Saving per month × months stored > transition cost + expected retrieval cost. Every term matters.

**Short stays lose:** If an object will be deleted in two months, the saving has only two months to repay the transition fee, and minimum-duration charges may apply on top.

**Surprise reads lose:** Retrieval from cold tiers costs money and time. A dataset re-read for a yearly audit can erase the saving in one pass.

**Automatic vs explicit:** Intelligent-Tiering watches each object's access and moves it, which suits unknown patterns. When you know the lifecycle, say logs deleted after 90 days, an explicit lifecycle rule is simpler and predictable.

**The review question:** What share of stored data hasn't been read in 90 days? That share is the candidate pool; the inequality decides which of it should move.

quiz.q: Logs are kept 60 days, then deleted. A teammate proposes moving them to archive on day 7 to save money. What do you check first?
quiz.a: Whether 53 days of savings beat the transition cost plus any retrieval and early-delete charges. With deletion so soon, the move may lose money.

mcq.q: When do explicit lifecycle rules beat S3 Intelligent-Tiering?
options: When you already know the data's lifecycle
When access patterns are unknown
When objects are read constantly
When data has no retention rule
mcq.why: Automatic tiering suits unknown patterns; when the lifecycle is known, explicit rules do the job directly.

hook: A celebrity updates their profile and 100,000 requests miss the cache at once. What stops the stampede?
title: Profile cache: CDC invalidation and leases against herds
body: A read-heavy profile service needs a cache that stays fresh and survives spikes. Use a look-aside cache keyed by user ID. Invalidate on write via **CDC** from the database, not only from the app, so no writer can forget. When a popular key expires, use **leases** or request coalescing, so one request refills it while the rest wait. Replicate hot keys. Run regional pools with cross-region invalidation.
takeaway: Invalidate from the database, and let one request refill the key.
deeper:
**Why CDC, not the app:** App-driven invalidation depends on every code path remembering. A batch job, a migration script or a new service will eventually forget. The database's change stream sees every write, whoever made it.

**The thundering herd:** A popular key expires, and thousands of requests miss at once and hit the database together. Meta's memcache paper uses leases: the first miss gets a token to refill the key, and the others wait briefly or take a slightly stale value.

**Hot keys:** Replicate them across cache nodes, so one node isn't the bottleneck.

**What to measure:** Hit rate, and stale-read rate, not only latency. A cache that is fast and wrong looks perfectly healthy on a latency-only dashboard, so measure both.

quiz.q: A nightly batch job updates profiles directly in the database, bypassing the app. Users see old profile data for hours afterwards. What's the fix?
quiz.a: Drive invalidation from the database's CDC stream instead of the app, so every write, including the batch job's, invalidates the cache. Alert on stale-read rate to catch misses.

mcq.q: What stops a thundering herd when a popular cache key expires?
options: Leases or request coalescing
Invalidation via CDC
Regional cache pools
Measuring the hit rate
mcq.why: A lease lets one request refill the key while the others wait, so the database isn't hit by every miss at once.

hook: Two people send messages to the same chat at the same instant. Who decides which came first?
title: Chat ordering comes from one leader per conversation
body: Clocks on phones and servers disagree, so timestamps can't reliably order a chat. The design gives each conversation **per-conversation sequence numbers** from a single leader. Partition by conversation ID; cluster by message time or sequence number. Writes append to an LSM-based store, replicated within the region with **quorum writes**. Recent messages are cached, and old ones tier to cheaper storage.
takeaway: Order needs one authority; give each conversation its own.
deeper:
**Why one leader per conversation:** A single authority hands out 1, 2, 3 for that chat, so every reader sees the same order. Scoping it per conversation keeps the leader from becoming a global bottleneck.

**Why quorum writes:** A message is acknowledged once a quorum of replicas in the region has it, so one replica failing doesn't lose it.

**Why LSM:** Chat is write-heavy. LSM trees buffer writes and flush sorted files, turning many small writes into sequential I/O.

**The encryption catch:** With end-to-end encryption, the server stores ciphertext only. It cannot build a search index over text it can't read, so search must happen on the device.

**Tiering:** Recent messages are read constantly and cached. Old messages are rarely opened, so they move to cheaper storage.

quiz.q: Product wants server-side full-text search across all messages in an end-to-end encrypted chat app. What do you tell them?
quiz.a: The server stores only ciphertext, so it can't index message text. Search must run on the device, or the product must give up end-to-end encryption for searchable data.

mcq.q: What gives messages in one conversation a single agreed order?
options: Sequence numbers from one leader per conversation
Timestamps from each sender's phone
Last-writer-wins across regions
Clustering messages by size
mcq.why: One authority per conversation assigns increasing numbers, so every reader sees the same order.

predict.q: In an end-to-end encrypted chat app, where must message search run?
options: On the user's device
On a regional search cluster
Inside the message database

hook: Millions of events arrive every second, and analysts want them as tables within the hour. How?
title: Events become tables: Kafka, Parquet, Iceberg snapshots
body: Producers write to **Kafka**, durable and ordered per partition. Consumers write compressed Parquet files to object storage every few minutes, committed as **Iceberg snapshots**. Small files get compacted into large ones. Tables are partitioned by date and event type. Raw events are kept 30 to 90 days, aggregates longer. Personal fields are tokenized or kept in separate columns, so a deletion doesn't mean rewriting everything.
takeaway: Buffer in a log, land in open files, compact relentlessly.
deeper:
**Why Kafka in front:** Producers are bursty, and object storage prefers large files. Kafka absorbs the bursts and lets consumers batch events into sensible file sizes.

**Why snapshots:** An Iceberg commit makes a whole batch of new files visible at once through the table's manifest. Readers see either the old snapshot or the new one, never half a batch.

**Why compaction:** Writing every few minutes still creates many small files, and small files kill systems sized by bytes. Merging them keeps queries fast and metadata small.

**Why separate personal fields:** A deletion request then touches a token map or one column instead of rewriting whole files.

**Retention is part of the design:** Raw events for 30 to 90 days, aggregates longer. Without that rule, the lake becomes retention by nobody.

quiz.q: A lake writes one file per event, keeps everything forever, and stores emails inline in every row. Name three problems and their fixes.
quiz.a: Too many small files: batch and compact. No retention: keep raw events 30 to 90 days, aggregates longer. Inline emails: tokenize or separate personal fields so deletion is cheap.

mcq.q: Why commit the Parquet files as Iceberg snapshots?
options: Readers see a whole batch or none of it
Snapshots compress the files further
Snapshots remove the need for Kafka
Snapshots expire old events automatically
mcq.why: An Iceberg snapshot commit makes a batch of files visible atomically, so queries never see half-written data.

hook: A file system holds a billion files. What keeps its directory tree from piling onto one metadata server?
title: Shard directories by hash of parent ID
body: A billion-file file system fails first at metadata, not disks. Separate the **namespace**, the directory tree, from block locations, and store both in a sharded, replicated key-value store. Shard directory entries by **hash of parent ID**. Directories spread across shards instead of piling onto one, and a rename within a directory stays on one shard, so it's cheap. Clients cache hot directories with leases. This is the Colossus and Tectonic pattern.
takeaway: Key metadata by parent, and a directory's work stays on one shard.
deeper:
**Why split namespace from locations:** They answer different questions and change at different rates. The namespace answers 'what's in this directory?'; block locations answer 'where are this file's bytes?'. Separating them lets each scale on its own.

**Why a key-value store:** One master holding everything in memory is what limited GFS and HDFS. Colossus moved metadata to Bigtable and Tectonic to ZippyDB, both sharded and replicated.

**Why parent ID:** Entries keyed by their parent's ID keep one directory's children together, so listing it or renaming within it touches a single shard. Hashing the parent ID scatters different directories across the cluster.

**Why client leases:** A lease is a time-limited right. Clients serve hot directory lookups from their own cache until the lease expires, taking load off the metadata store without serving stale entries forever.

quiz.q: Your file system's metadata runs on one master, and file creates stall at 800 million files. Sketch the fix.
quiz.a: Split the namespace from block locations, store both in a sharded, replicated key-value store, shard entries by hash of parent ID, and let clients cache hot directories under leases.

mcq.q: What does sharding by hash of parent ID keep cheap?
options: Renames within a single directory
Renames across the whole tree
Reads of file contents
Erasure-coding new blocks
