mcq.why: A directory's entries share one parent ID, so they sit on one shard, and renaming within that directory stays a single-shard operation.

hook: A transfer debits one account, then the server crashes before crediting the other. What must the database do?
title: ACID: four promises that make a transaction safe
body: Money moves in two steps, and a crash between them must not make money vanish. That is what **ACID** guarantees for a transaction. Atomicity: all of it happens or none of it does. Consistency: rules such as uniqueness hold before and after. Isolation: concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-done work. Durability: once committed, it survives crashes. When multi-row changes must agree, a design needs these.
takeaway: All or nothing, rules intact, no peeking, and it sticks.
deeper:
**Where durability comes from:** The write-ahead log. Changes are logged before being applied, and fsync forces the log to durable media, so a committed transaction can be replayed after a crash.

**Where it shows up in storage design:** Choosing between relational and key-value starts with one question: do you need multi-row transactions or joins? Profiles need transactional updates and secondary indexes, so they sit in Spanner, Aurora or MySQL. An application-maintained index without transactions is an anti-pattern precisely because it lacks atomicity: a crash between two writes leaves them inconsistent forever.

**At scale:** Distributed SQL systems such as Spanner, CockroachDB and TiDB keep transactions across shards, using consensus, at the cost of latency. Strong consistency is recommended for money, identity, inventory and uniqueness, which is where ACID earns its price.

quiz.q: A service writes an order row and decrements inventory in two separate calls, with no transaction. The process crashes between them. Which ACID property was missing, and what's the result?
quiz.a: Atomicity. The order exists but inventory was never decremented, so the two disagree. One transaction around both writes makes them happen together or not at all.

mcq.q: Which ACID property ensures a committed transaction survives a crash?
options: Durability
Atomicity
Isolation
Consistency
mcq.why: Durability means committed data persists, typically by logging changes to a write-ahead log forced to disk before acknowledging.

hook: The easiest data to replicate, cache and erasure-code all shares one property. What is it?
title: Data you never overwrite is data you can copy freely
body: Overwrites are where storage gets hard: every copy must change together, and caches go stale. **Append-only** storage only adds data at the end and never overwrites. **Immutable** data is never changed after being written. Both remove that coordination. A new version becomes a new object or a new record, and old copies are never wrong, only older.
takeaway: Never overwrite, and every copy stays correct forever.
deeper:
**Where immutability pays:** Photos and videos are immutable blobs, which is why erasure coding and CDN caching work so well for them. An S3-like store writes fragments, then commits metadata, and the fragments never change. LSM trees write immutable sorted files, SSTables, and merge them later instead of editing in place.

**Where append-only pays:** Logs and events are append-only, huge and read in bulk, so they suit sequential writes to Kafka and cheap object storage. The first cut of storage selection gives append-only events their own branch for this reason.

**The cost:** Nothing is freed in place. Old versions and deletes pile up until compaction or garbage collection reclaims them. Deleting a user from immutable formats needs a compaction budget, or crypto-shredding for backups.

**The short version:** Immutability moves the hard work from write time to cleanup time.

quiz.q: A team wants to let users edit uploaded videos in place to save storage. What would the system lose, and what's the usual alternative?
quiz.a: Immutability: erasure-coded fragments and CDN copies would need coordinated updates and could serve stale versions. Instead, write each edit as a new object and repoint the metadata.

mcq.q: What is the main cost of append-only, immutable storage?
options: Old versions pile up until compaction reclaims them
Replicas can disagree about the latest value
CDN caches serve stale object versions
Writes must lock every copy at once
mcq.why: Nothing is freed in place, so deleted and superseded data takes space until compaction or garbage collection runs.

hook: Some data will probably never be read again, yet you must keep it for years. Where should it live?
title: Archival storage: cheapest to keep, slowest to read
body: Frozen data is kept for law or insurance and may never be read. Paying hot or even warm prices for it wastes money for years. **Archival storage** is the lowest-cost tier, built for data rarely or never read. The trade is retrieval: getting data back is slow and can cost extra, and archive tiers can charge early-delete fees for data that leaves before a **minimum storage duration**.
takeaway: Archive what you must keep and hope never to read.
deeper:
**Where it fits the lifecycle:** Data is born, read a lot, read less, then archived or deleted. Frozen data, kept for law or insurance only, is archival's natural tenant, because its only reader may be an auditor years later.

**How data gets there:** A tiering policy moves data to cold or archive after M days without reads. The reference architecture ends in an archive tier after the retention window.

**When archiving loses money:** Tiering pays only if the storage saving over the months stored beats the transition cost plus expected retrieval cost. Tiny objects can cost more in per-object overhead than they save, and data deleted soon after archiving may trigger early-delete fees.

**The catch:** Archived personal data still counts for deletion requests. Crypto-shredding erases a user from archives and backups without restoring them.

quiz.q: Compliance requires keeping transaction records for 7 years, and they're almost never read after month two. Where should they live, and what must you check before moving them?
quiz.a: An archival tier after the access curve's knee. Check that savings over the months stored beat transition and expected retrieval costs, and respect minimum-duration fees and any legal holds.

mcq.q: What is the main trade-off of archival storage?
options: Very low cost, but slow and costly retrieval
Very fast reads, but high storage cost
Strong consistency, but weak durability
Unlimited writes, but no deletes
mcq.why: Archive tiers are the cheapest place to keep bytes, but reading them back is slow and can carry retrieval and early-delete charges.

hook: One store goes down for an hour and loses nothing. Another stays up and loses a file. Which failed worse?
title: Availability is answering; durability is not losing
body: Two numbers get confused constantly. **Availability** is the fraction of time a system answers requests correctly. **Durability** is the probability that stored data is not lost. An outage hurts availability, then ends; lost data is gone for good. A system can be highly available and still lose data, or be down for an hour with every byte safe. So designs set a target for each, separately.
takeaway: Downtime ends. Data loss doesn't.
deeper:
**Durability targets:** An S3-like store aims for 11 nines of durability. That comes from redundancy across failure domains and, above all, fast repair: loss risk scales with the repair window squared for 3-way replication.

**Availability targets:** A design doc states an SLO, the region layout and what happens during a partition. Availability depends on how fast reads and writes can move to healthy replicas.

**Where they pull apart:** Synchronous cross-region replication protects the last writes, RPO zero, but every write waits on another region. Asynchronous replication keeps writes fast but may lose the last few seconds in a region loss.

**Recovery language:** RPO is how much data you may lose, a durability promise. RTO is how long recovery may take, an availability promise. A backup that takes a week to restore protects durability and wrecks availability.

quiz.q: A team boasts 99.99 percent availability, but the only copy of some data lives on one disk. What would you point out?
quiz.a: Availability measures answering requests, not keeping data. With one copy, a single disk failure loses data permanently, so durability is poor however good the uptime is.

mcq.q: Which recovery target is a durability promise?
options: RPO: how much data you may lose
RTO: how long recovery may take
SLO: the share of successful requests
p99: the tail latency target
mcq.why: RPO bounds lost data, a durability matter; RTO bounds downtime, an availability matter.

hook: Why do photos, videos, lake files and backups almost always end up in the same kind of store?
title: Object storage: flat keys to blobs, over HTTP
body: Large files don't need a directory tree or row-level updates. They need cheap, durable storage reachable from anywhere. **Object storage** is flat key-to-blob storage over HTTP, like S3 and GCS. A **bucket** is its top-level container of objects. A **blob** is a large binary object with no internal structure the store cares about. You PUT, GET, DELETE, and LIST by prefix.
takeaway: Give up editing in place, and storage gets simple enough to scale.
deeper:
**Where it fits:** The first question in choosing storage is whether data is large immutable blobs over 1 MB. If so, it goes to an object store: S3, GCS, Blob, Ambry or a Tectonic blob tenant. Photos and videos, lake files and backups all land here.

**How one is built:** A stateless front end, a metadata service mapping (bucket, key) to object location in a sharded key-value store, and a data service of storage nodes. Large objects are chunked and erasure-coded; small ones can be packed into larger files to save metadata.

**Its limits:** Object storage fits workloads that tolerate 100 ms or more. Billions of tiny objects are its weak spot, because LIST cost and per-request cost dominate.

**Why it wins anyway:** Immutable blobs make erasure coding, CDN caching and tiering straightforward, so object stores are the cheapest durable home for bulk bytes.

quiz.q: A team proposes storing each chat message as its own S3 object, billions of 500-byte objects. What's wrong, and what's better?
quiz.a: Per-object overhead dominates: request charges, LIST cost and metadata. Messages belong in an LSM or wide-column store partitioned by conversation, or packed into larger files.

mcq.q: What is a bucket in object storage?
options: A top-level container of objects
A fixed-size piece of an object
A replica of an object in another region
A file listing a table's data files
mcq.why: Buckets are the top-level containers; keys inside them name objects, and chunks are pieces of objects.

hook: Your database expects a raw disk, but it runs on a cloud VM. What is it actually writing to?
title: Block storage: a disk the network pretends is local
body: Databases and file systems expect a disk: numbered, fixed-size blocks they can read and overwrite in place. In the cloud, that disk often lives across the network. **Block storage** exposes fixed-size blocks, like a disk, through services such as EBS and Persistent Disk. The file system or database on top decides what the blocks mean; the storage just reads and writes them.
takeaway: Block storage knows blocks, not files. Meaning lives above it.
deeper:
**Coupled vs disaggregated:** Local disk gives the lowest, most predictable latency, since there is no network hop. Network block storage lets compute scale and move independently of data. The trade-off catalog picks coupled for predictable, latency-critical workloads and disaggregated for elastic compute.

**The latency ladder:** A p99 under 1 ms means memory or local flash, with no network hop. Network block storage adds that hop, so it suits workloads whose latency targets leave room for it.

**How it differs from object storage:** Blocks are small and overwritten in place, and the storage has no idea what a file is. Objects are whole blobs addressed by key over HTTP and never edited in place.

**Durability still matters:** fsync forces data to durable media, and databases call it before acknowledging a commit.

quiz.q: A latency-critical database on network block storage keeps missing its sub-millisecond p99 target. What does the latency ladder suggest?
quiz.a: Sub-millisecond p99 needs memory or local flash. Move hot data to local flash or memory, accepting coupled storage and compute, or relax the target to what networked SSD can meet.

mcq.q: What does block storage expose to the system above it?
options: Fixed-size blocks, like a disk
Whole objects addressed by key
Rows with secondary indexes
Files in a directory tree
mcq.why: Block storage presents numbered fixed-size blocks; file systems or databases on top give them meaning.

hook: A tiny structure can say 'definitely not here' but never 'definitely here'. Why is that so useful?
title: A Bloom filter says 'definitely not' or 'maybe'
body: An LSM tree may keep a key in any of many sorted files, and checking each one on disk is slow. A **Bloom filter** is a compact structure, kept in memory, that answers 'definitely not present' or 'maybe present'. A 'no' is always right, so the read skips that file entirely. A 'maybe' can be a false positive, costing one wasted lookup but never a wrong answer.
takeaway: Skip the disk whenever the filter says no.
deeper:
**How it works:** Hash the key several ways and set those bits in a bit array. To check a key, test the same bits. If any bit is clear, the key was never added. If all are set, it probably was, though other keys may have set those bits.

**Where it shows up:** LSM trees buffer writes in memory, flush sorted files and compact them later. A read may need to check several SSTables; per-file Bloom filters let it skip files that can't hold the key. That is how LSM engines keep read amplification in check.

**The tuning knob:** More bits per key means fewer false positives and more memory. There are no false negatives at any size.

**The catch:** A standard Bloom filter can't delete a key, since clearing a bit might erase evidence of other keys. Filters are rebuilt when files are rewritten, which suits immutable SSTables.

quiz.q: An LSM store's point reads touch six files each, and most lookups are for keys that don't exist. What cheap structure fixes this, and why does it help misses most?
quiz.a: Per-file Bloom filters in memory. A 'definitely not present' answer skips the file without disk I/O, so lookups for missing keys rarely touch disk at all.

mcq.q: Which Bloom filter answer can be wrong?
options: Maybe present
Definitely not present
Both answers, equally
Neither answer
mcq.why: Bloom filters have false positives but no false negatives, so 'maybe' can be wrong while 'definitely not' never is.

hook: The index behind most relational databases edits data right where it sits. What does that cost on writes?
title: B-trees update pages in place
body: Relational databases need fast point reads, range scans and updates. A **B-tree** is a balanced tree index that updates pages in place. Every lookup walks a few levels from root to leaf, and a range scan walks neighbouring leaves. The cost shows on writes: each update rewrites a page wherever it lives on disk, so heavy random writes mean heavy random I/O.
takeaway: B-trees make reads cheap by making writes land in place.
deeper:
**Where the choice appears:** Heavy overwrites favour B-trees; heavy writes and appends favour LSM trees. The trade-off catalog puts it as B-tree for read-heavy workloads with in-place updates and range scans, LSM for write-heavy workloads, compression and flash.

**Why balanced matters:** Every leaf is the same distance from the root, so a lookup takes a predictable number of page reads whichever key you ask for.

**The write cost in detail:** Updating one row means rewriting its whole page. Random updates scatter those rewrites across the disk. Pages split as they fill, and the database writes changes to a write-ahead log first, so a crash mid-update can be recovered.

**Versus LSM:** An LSM tree makes writes sequential and compresses well, but pays with compaction and reads that may check several files. Neither wins in general; the workload decides.

quiz.q: A user-settings table is read constantly, updated occasionally in place, and queried by ranges of user ID. B-tree or LSM, and why?
quiz.a: B-tree. Read-heavy work with in-place updates and range scans is its sweet spot; an LSM tree's advantages show up under heavy writes.

mcq.q: Which workload favours a B-tree over an LSM tree?
options: Read-heavy, in-place updates, range scans
Write-heavy, append-mostly ingestion
Compressed data on flash at high write rates
Time-series inserts that are never updated
mcq.why: B-trees update pages in place and keep keys sorted, which suits reads, updates and range scans.

hook: Some databases never update data in place, even on an overwrite. So how do they find the latest value?
title: LSM trees buffer writes, flush sorted files, then merge
body: Random writes are slow on disk and wear out flash. An **LSM tree**, a log-structured merge tree, avoids them: it buffers writes in memory, flushes them as sorted, immutable files called **SSTables**, and compacts those files in the background. A read checks memory first, then files from newest to oldest, so the newest version of a key always wins.
takeaway: Write sequentially now, merge later, read the newest first.
deeper:
**Where LSM appears:** Messages are write-heavy, so LSM engines like Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Bigtable and MyRocks suit them. The multi-region key-value design runs an LSM tree per node. The trade-off catalog picks LSM for write-heavy workloads, compression and flash.

**The write path:**
1. Append to a write-ahead log for durability.
2. Insert into the in-memory buffer.
3. When it fills, flush it as a sorted SSTable.
4. Compaction merges SSTables, dropping old versions and tombstones.

**The costs:** Reads may check several SSTables, which is read amplification; Bloom filters skip most of them. Compaction rewrites data repeatedly, which is write amplification, and old versions take space until merged.

**The origin:** O'Neil and colleagues described the log-structured merge-tree in 1996, a design that later proved a natural fit for flash.

quiz.q: A chat service's LSM store shows rising read latency and disk usage, and compaction is falling behind. What's happening?
quiz.a: SSTables are piling up: reads must check more files, and old versions and tombstones aren't being merged away. Give compaction more budget or reduce the write rate.

mcq.q: What is an SSTable?
options: An immutable sorted file in an LSM tree
A page updated in place in a B-tree
An in-memory write buffer
A marker that records a delete
mcq.why: LSM trees flush buffered writes as sorted string tables, which are never modified, only merged by compaction.

hook: You delete a row in an LSM database, yet disk usage doesn't drop. Where did the data go?
title: Deletes write a tombstone; compaction does the deleting
body: In immutable files you can't erase a row, only record that it's gone. A **tombstone** is a marker that records a delete until compaction removes the data. **Compaction** merges and rewrites files, dropping old versions and deleted records. Until it runs, the deleted bytes still sit on disk, and reads must skip them. In LSM trees and lakes, deletion is really two events: the tombstone and the compaction.
takeaway: In immutable storage, delete means mark now, erase at compaction.
deeper:
**In LSM trees:** Reads see the tombstone and treat the key as gone. Compaction later merges SSTables and drops both the tombstone and the older values it hides.

**In lakes:** Iceberg or Hudi record row-level deletes, and compaction rewrites the affected files. Partitioning tables by user keeps those rewrites small. The log pipeline also compacts many small files into large ones.

**In photo storage:** A soft delete in metadata hides a photo at once; physical deletion by compaction follows within the compliance window.

**Why it matters for compliance:** The deletion request isn't finished when the tombstone lands. It's finished when compaction removes the bytes, so compaction needs a budget and a deadline.

**The catch:** Compaction costs disk I/O and competes with user traffic, just like repair does.

quiz.q: Legal requires deleted user rows to be physically gone within 30 days. Your LSM store writes tombstones at once, but some SSTables haven't been compacted in 60 days. Are you compliant?
quiz.a: No. The tombstone hides the data from reads, but the bytes remain until compaction. Schedule compaction so affected files are rewritten inside the 30-day window.

mcq.q: What physically removes deleted data in an LSM tree?
options: Compaction
The tombstone
A Bloom filter
The write-ahead log
mcq.why: The tombstone only marks the delete; compaction rewrites files and drops the deleted and superseded data.

predict.q: You delete a row in an LSM-based database. When are its bytes actually removed from disk?
options: When compaction runs
Immediately
When the next backup completes

hook: Your app wrote 1 GB, read 1 GB and stores 1 GB. The disks did far more. What are the hidden multipliers?
title: Three hidden multipliers: read, write and space
body: The bytes your app asks for are rarely the bytes the disks handle. **Read amplification** is reading more bytes than requested. **Write amplification** is physical bytes written divided by logical bytes written. **Space amplification** is storing more bytes than the logical data size. Every storage engine trades these against each other, and none gets all three low at once.
takeaway: Every engine picks which amplification to pay; know which yours pays.
deeper:
**LSM trees:** Compaction rewrites data many times, raising write amplification. A read may check several SSTables, raising read amplification, which Bloom filters cut. Old versions and tombstones wait for compaction, raising space amplification.

**B-trees:** Updating one row rewrites a whole page, a form of write amplification, but a read walks one tree.

**Redundancy is space amplification by design:** Triple replication stores 3 bytes per logical byte; RS(10,4) stores 1.4. The photo sketch turns 250 TB a day logical into 350 TB raw this way.

**Erasure coding's read side:** Repairing one lost RS(10,4) fragment reads 10 fragments, a read amplification paid at repair time.

**Why name them:** When a system is slower or bigger than expected, one of these three is usually the reason.

quiz.q: A team moves an ingest-heavy table from a B-tree engine to an LSM engine. Writes get faster, but disk usage grows and point reads slow down. Which amplifications moved?
quiz.a: Space and read amplification rose: old versions wait for compaction, and reads check several SSTables. Writes became sequential, which is why they sped up.

mcq.q: How is write amplification defined?
options: Physical bytes written over logical bytes written
Bytes read over bytes requested
Bytes stored over logical data size
Replicas written over replicas acknowledged
mcq.why: Write amplification compares what the device physically writes with what the application logically wrote.

hook: A cache serves 99 percent of reads. Is that good news, or could it be hiding a problem?
title: Hit rate says how fast; stale-read rate says how wrong
body: **Cache hit rate** is the share of reads served by the cache, and a high one means the backing store is protected. It says nothing about whether those hits were correct. A cache that stays stale looks perfect on hit rate. A **CDN**, content delivery network, is a cache near users for static content. For both, measure hit rate and stale reads, not only latency.
takeaway: A fast wrong answer still counts as a hit.
deeper:
**Where hit rate matters:** The storage flowchart adds a cache only when the workload is read-heavy and can tolerate staleness. Read-heavy means each hit saves real load on the database.

**Where staleness bites:** The profile cache design invalidates on write via CDC, so no writer can forget, and alerts on stale-read rate rather than only latency. A review question asks whether cache invalidations are reliable, or whether the cache can stay stale forever.

**CDNs in the reference design:** Photos and videos are served through a CDN, then an origin cache, then the object store. A viral photo becomes a hot object the CDN absorbs. Immutable blobs are ideal CDN content, since the object itself never changes.

**The CDN catch:** Metadata can change even when bytes don't. A CDN may serve a photo under stale privacy settings for a short time unless the change triggers an invalidation.

quiz.q: A profile cache reports a 99 percent hit rate, yet users keep seeing names they changed yesterday. What's wrong with the monitoring, and with the cache?
quiz.a: Hit rate can't see staleness. Invalidation is unreliable, likely app-driven with some writer skipping it. Invalidate via CDC from the database and alert on stale-read rate.

mcq.q: Why do immutable photos make ideal CDN content?
options: The cached object can never be an old version
They always fit in a single server's memory
CDNs accept only immutable files
They never need invalidation for any reason
mcq.why: Bytes that never change can't go stale in a cache, though related metadata such as privacy settings still can.

hook: A disk flips one bit in a stored photo and reports no error at all. Who notices?
title: Checksums catch corruption; scrubbing goes looking for it
body: Some corruption is silent: no error, no alert, just wrong bytes. A **checksum** is a small value computed from data, used to detect corruption: recompute it on read and compare. **Scrubbing** is background reading of data to find corruption before a user or a repair needs that data. Together they turn silent damage into a found, repairable fault, while enough healthy copies still exist.
takeaway: Corruption you don't look for is corruption you'll serve.
deeper:
**End-to-end, or it doesn't count:** A review question asks how silent corruption is detected and whether checksums are end-to-end. A checksum computed by the writer and verified by the reader catches damage anywhere in between: disk, network, memory or software.

**Where scrubbers run:** In the S3-like design, scrubbers verify checksums in the background while repair workers rebuild lost fragments. Scrubbing matters most for cold data, which may sit unread for years; without it, a bad fragment is found only when you need it most.

**Where checksums travel:** Moving a blob to an object store means keeping a pointer and a checksum in the database row, so the reader can verify it fetched the right bytes. Migrations verify with checksums per object and counts per prefix.

**Why replication isn't enough:** Replicas faithfully copy corrupt writes. Detection has to come from checking the data itself.

quiz.q: An archive holds erasure-coded data that nobody reads for years, and disks silently corrupt fragments over time. What keeps this from becoming data loss?
quiz.a: Scrubbing: background reads verify checksums and find bad fragments while enough healthy ones remain, so repair can rebuild them before more fail.

mcq.q: Why should checksums be end-to-end?
options: They catch corruption anywhere between writer and reader
They make replication faster
They remove the need for backups
They reduce storage overhead
mcq.why: Computed at the writer and checked at the reader, a checksum detects damage from disks, networks, memory or software.

hook: A 5 GB video must survive disk failures and be read in parallel. What's the first thing the store does to it?
title: Big objects get cut into fixed-size chunks
body: One huge object on one disk is slow to read and painful to repair. So storage systems split it. A **chunk** is a fixed-size piece of a file or object. Chunks spread across many nodes, can be read in parallel, and can be erasure-coded across failure domains. When a disk dies, only its chunks need rebuilding, and many nodes can share that work.
takeaway: Cut big data into pieces so many machines share every job.
deeper:
**In the object store design:** Large objects are split into chunks and erasure-coded, for example RS(10,4), across failure domains. The metadata service records where each chunk lives, storage nodes hold the chunks, and a garbage collector removes chunks nothing references.

**Why fixed size:** Placement, repair and accounting all get simpler when every piece is the same size. A node's load is roughly its chunk count.

**Why it helps repair:** Durability is a repair-speed problem. When the chunks from a failed disk have copies scattered across hundreds of nodes, as in Dropbox's Magic Pocket, reconstruction runs in parallel instead of funnelling into one replacement disk.

**Small objects are the opposite problem:** They are far smaller than a chunk. Packing many into larger files, Haystack's idea, saves metadata instead of multiplying it.

quiz.q: A storage node holding 40,000 chunks dies. Why does spreading those chunks' copies across hundreds of nodes make recovery faster?
quiz.a: Every node holding a surviving copy can rebuild a few chunks in parallel, so repair uses hundreds of disks and links at once instead of one replacement disk.

mcq.q: Why do storage systems split large objects into chunks?
options: To spread, parallelize and repair them piece by piece
To avoid computing checksums
To store small objects more cheaply
To make objects mutable in place
mcq.why: Chunks spread across nodes, so reads and repairs run in parallel and a failure affects only some pieces.

hook: A query sums one column across a billion rows. Why should it never read the other 49 columns?
title: Columnar files and manifests turn files into tables
body: Row storage makes a one-column aggregate read every column of every row. A **columnar format** stores each column together, which is good for scans, as Parquet and ORC do. The query reads only the columns it needs, and similar values compress well. A **manifest** is a file listing the data files that make up a table snapshot, which is how a pile of Parquet files becomes one consistent table.
takeaway: Store by column for scans; list files in a manifest for truth.
deeper:
**Where columnar appears:** The first cut sends mostly-scan workloads to a columnar lake or warehouse: Iceberg, BigQuery or Redshift. Google uses Capacitor on Colossus; open source uses Parquet on object storage.

**What manifests do:** An Iceberg commit writes new data files, then a new manifest and snapshot pointing at them. Readers follow the snapshot, so they see the whole batch or none of it. The log pipeline commits Parquet files as Iceberg snapshots every few minutes this way.

**Why it enables open formats:** Because the table is defined by files and manifests on object storage, Trino, Spark and Presto can all read the same table. That is what makes future migrations cheap.

**The catch:** Columnar files are poor at single-row updates. Deletes become row-level markers plus compaction, which is why lakes partition tables by user when deletion matters.

quiz.q: Analysts' queries on a row-oriented log table scan terabytes to compute one metric. What storage change helps most, and why?
quiz.a: Rewrite the logs as columnar files such as Parquet, partitioned by date and event type. Queries then read only the columns they need, and similar values compress well.

mcq.q: What does a table manifest list?
options: The data files that make up a table snapshot
Every row's primary key
The columns and their compression codecs
The replicas holding each file
mcq.why: A manifest names the files in a snapshot, so readers see one consistent version of the table.

hook: Three replicas must agree on the order of writes, and any one of them might crash mid-vote. How?
title: Consensus picks one order; the leader enforces it
body: Replicas that each order writes their own way drift apart. **Consensus** is a protocol for nodes to agree on a value despite failures; Paxos and Raft are the classics. A **leader** is the replica that orders writes for a shard. In practice, consensus elects the leader and commits its log entries once a majority accepts them, so the group survives the failure of a minority.
takeaway: One leader orders; a majority makes it stick.
deeper:
**Where consensus shows up:** Strong consistency needs a single leader or consensus per key; that is the price of readers never seeing stale data. Distributed SQL systems such as Spanner, CockroachDB and TiDB replicate with consensus.

**Inside one region:** The home-region key-value design runs Raft or Paxos inside the region for each shard. Majority round trips stay short, so writes stay fast.

**Across regions:** Spanner-style global consensus runs Paxos on a majority of each shard's replicas, spread across regions. Every write then includes a cross-region round trip, which is why it is reserved for money and uniqueness.

**Leaders elsewhere:** Chat storage uses a single leader per conversation to hand out sequence numbers. The single-leader option buys simple reasoning and transactions; leaderless and multi-leader buy always-writable, multi-region writes.

**The catch:** A majority must be reachable. Lose it, and the group stops accepting writes rather than risk two orders.

quiz.q: A 5-replica Raft group runs in one region. Two replicas crash. Can it still accept writes? What if a third crashes?
quiz.a: With two down, three of five remain, a majority, so writes continue. With three down, no majority exists, so the group stops accepting writes rather than risk divergence.

mcq.q: What does a shard's leader do?
options: Orders the writes for that shard
Stores the only copy of the data
Serves every read for every shard
Runs compaction for the cluster
mcq.why: The leader is the replica that orders writes for a shard; consensus keeps the followers applying the same order.

predict.q: A 5-replica consensus group loses 3 replicas. What happens to writes?
options: They stop until a majority returns
They continue on the 2 survivors
They continue with weaker durability

hook: Three replicas, and you wait for only two on every write and two on every read. Why is that enough?
title: W + R > N: why overlapping quorums see the latest write
body: Waiting for every replica lets one slow node slow everything. A **quorum** is the minimum number of replicas that must respond, for example W plus R greater than N. With three replicas, W = 2 and R = 2 overlap, so every read quorum includes at least one replica holding the latest write. **Read repair** fixes stale replicas when a read notices they disagree.
takeaway: Overlap the quorums and at least one witness always knows.
deeper:
**The overlap:** N = 3, W = 2, R = 2. Any two replicas you read share at least one with any two you wrote, because 2 + 2 > 3. The read compares versions and returns the newest.

**Read repair:** When that read sees a replica holding an older version, it writes the newer value back. Frequently read keys heal themselves; rarely read ones rely on other background mechanisms.

**Where quorums show up:** Chat storage replicates within the region with quorum writes, so one failed replica doesn't lose a message. Dynamo-family leaderless stores rely on quorums instead of a single leader.

**The trade-off:** Lower W speeds writes but weakens each acknowledgment. Lower R speeds reads but risks missing the latest write. Tuning W and R is choosing where to spend latency.

**The catch:** Quorums alone don't resolve two concurrent writes to the same key. Something else, such as last-writer-wins or a CRDT, must decide.

quiz.q: A store runs N = 3 with W = 1 and R = 1 to be fast. Users sometimes read an old value right after writing. Why, and what setting fixes it?
quiz.a: W + R = 2 is not greater than 3, so a read can hit a replica that missed the write. Use W = 2 and R = 2, or any W + R > N.

mcq.q: What does read repair do?
options: Updates stale replicas that a read finds
Rebuilds lost fragments after a disk dies
Merges SSTables to drop old versions
Rolls back a failed transaction
mcq.why: When a read sees replicas disagree, it writes the newest version back to the stale ones.

hook: Add one server to a cluster that places keys by hash mod N, and almost every key moves. How do you avoid that?
title: Consistent hashing moves few keys when nodes change
body: With hash(key) mod N, adding one node changes N, and almost every key maps somewhere new. That is a cluster-wide reshuffle for one server. **Consistent hashing** moves few keys when nodes join or leave. Nodes and keys sit on the same hash ring, and each key belongs to the next node along it. A new node takes over only the keys between it and its neighbour.
takeaway: Change one node, move one node's worth of keys.
deeper:
**Why mod N fails:** With 10 nodes, key k lives on node hash(k) mod 10. Add an eleventh and mod 11 sends most keys elsewhere, so nearly all data moves at once.

**Why the ring works:** Only the arc between the new node and its predecessor changes owner. Roughly 1/N of the keys move, all from one neighbour. Real systems place several virtual points per node to even out the arcs.

**Where it shows up:** The multi-region key-value design partitions by consistent hashing or by range with automatic splitting. Dynamo, one of the core papers, is the best-known example of consistent hashing in a leaderless store.

**Hash vs range:** Hashing spreads load evenly but scatters neighbouring keys, so prefix scans touch every shard. That is why an S3-like store range-partitions metadata by (bucket, key): LIST needs sorted neighbours, and pays for it with hot prefixes and automatic splits.

quiz.q: A cache cluster places keys by hash mod N. Adding one node at peak causes a near-total miss rate and a database meltdown. What would have limited the damage?
quiz.a: Consistent hashing: adding a node would move only the keys on one arc, roughly 1/N of them, so most keys keep hitting the same cache node.

mcq.q: Why does an S3-like store range-partition metadata instead of hashing it?
options: LIST by prefix needs sorted neighbouring keys
Hashing cannot spread load evenly
Range partitioning never creates hot spots
Consistent hashing needs a central master
mcq.why: Range partitioning keeps a prefix's keys together for LIST; hashing would scatter them across every shard.

predict.q: A 10-node cluster places keys by hash mod N. You add one node. Roughly what share of keys move?
options: Most of them
About 10 percent
Almost none

hook: Your biggest shard is full while its neighbours sit half empty. Which two operations fix that, and how differ?
title: Resharding changes the split; rebalancing moves the pieces
body: Data outgrows one machine, so it gets split. A **shard** is a horizontal slice of a dataset; a **partition** is a subset owned by one group of nodes, and the word also means a network split. **Resharding** changes how data is split into shards. Rebalancing moves data between nodes to even out load. Both copy data under live traffic, which is why neither can be an afterthought.
takeaway: An untested resharding plan becomes an outage on the day you need it.
deeper:
**Why the review asks:** 'What is the resharding plan, and has it been tested?' Every growing dataset reshards eventually, and doing it for the first time under load is how outages happen.

**Where bad keys force it:** Unbounded partition keys such as 'country' or 'day' produce one partition that is hot and too large to move. The fix is a high-cardinality key or a bucket suffix, ideally chosen before the data exists.

**Automatic splitting:** Range-partitioned stores split shards when they grow hot or large. S3-like metadata needs this because range partitioning by (bucket, key) creates hot prefixes.

**Rebalancing's cost:** Small cells and stamps need rebalancing as load shifts, part of the stranded-capacity trade-off. Moving data uses the same disks and links that serve users, just like repair does.

**The two meanings of partition:** One is ownership of data. The other is a network split, which a design doc must address: what happens during a partition?

quiz.q: An events table uses 'day' as its partition key, and today's partition is too hot and too large to move. Which fix is resharding, and which is only rebalancing?
quiz.a: Switching to a high-cardinality key or adding a bucket suffix is resharding: it changes how data is split. Moving the hot partition to a bigger node is rebalancing, and won't fix the skew.

mcq.q: What does resharding change?
options: How data is split into shards
Which node holds a given replica
The number of replicas per shard
How often compaction runs
mcq.why: Resharding redefines the split itself; rebalancing only moves the existing pieces between nodes.

hook: Two regions update the same cart at once and can't reach each other. How do they merge without losing an item?
title: Vector clocks spot conflicts; CRDTs merge them
body: Multi-leader stores accept writes everywhere, so two updates to one key can happen concurrently. Last-writer-wins keeps one and silently drops the other. A **vector clock** is a set of per-replica counters used to detect that two updates were concurrent rather than one after the other. A **CRDT**, a conflict-free replicated data type, merges without coordination, so every replica converges on the same result.
takeaway: Detect concurrency honestly, then merge instead of picking a winner.
deeper:
**How vector clocks detect:** Each replica increments its own counter on a write. If one version's counters are all greater than or equal to another's, it came later. If each is ahead somewhere, the writes were concurrent, and the store knows it has a conflict instead of guessing.

**How CRDTs merge:** The data type is designed so merges don't depend on order. A set that only adds, or a counter where each replica tracks its own increments, gives the same answer whatever order updates arrive in.

**Where they show up:** The multi-leader key-value design resolves conflicts with last-writer-wins timestamps or CRDTs, and suits always-writable carts and presence. Dynamo, part of this family, used vector clocks to detect concurrent versions.

**The trade-off:** Last-writer-wins is simple but can lose data under concurrent updates. CRDTs keep every update, but only for data types that can merge; a bank balance with a floor can't simply be merged.

quiz.q: An always-writable cart uses last-writer-wins across regions, and support keeps hearing that added items vanish. What's happening, and what's the fix?
quiz.a: Concurrent adds in two regions conflict, and LWW keeps only one. Detect concurrency with vector clocks and merge with a CRDT, such as an add-wins set, so both items survive.

mcq.q: What does a vector clock tell you about two versions of a key?
options: Whether one came after the other, or both were concurrent
Which version the leader wrote
How many replicas hold each version
The wall-clock time of each write
mcq.why: Comparing per-replica counters shows the order, or reveals that neither update saw the other.

hook: Replication copies every write to three regions. A law says this data can't leave the country. Now what?
title: Data residency pins data, and pins its copies too
body: Replication spreads data for durability, and that can quietly break the law. **Data residency** is a rule that data must stay in a given country or region. It constrains where every copy lives: primaries, replicas, caches, backups and the lake. Compliance requirements call for **residency pinning** alongside deletion by user ID and per-tenant keys, and a review question asks what actually enforces it.
takeaway: Residency is enforced by placement rules, not by promises.
deeper:
**The review question:** Which regions may this data live in, and what enforces it? 'The team knows' is not enforcement. Placement rules in the storage layer are.

**What it collides with:** Cross-region replication for durability or failover must stay inside the allowed set of regions. A CDN or a regional cache pool can put copies near users in places the rule forbids.

**Where it sits in design:** The design doc's compliance review covers the personal data inventory, residency, retention, deletion and legal hold. The compliance modifier for choosing storage lists residency pinning as a direct consequence of storing personal data.

**Related tools:** Per-tenant keys let one customer's key be revoked. Deletion by user ID needs every dataset to declare its user-ID column.

**The catch:** Durability plans often assume copies in distant regions. With residency, independent failure domains must be found inside the allowed area.

quiz.q: A backup job copies an EU-only dataset to a US region for disaster recovery. What rule is broken, and how should recovery be designed instead?
quiz.a: Data residency: backups are copies too. Keep recovery copies in other allowed regions or zones inside the permitted area, enforced by placement rules.

mcq.q: Which copies does a data residency rule constrain?
options: All of them, including replicas, caches and backups
Only the primary copy
Only data in the lake
Only unencrypted data
mcq.why: Residency applies to every copy, so replicas, caches and backups must also stay in allowed regions.

hook: A new storage system handles full production traffic for weeks, and no user ever sees its answers. Why?
title: Dark launch: real traffic, invisible results
body: Staging never has production's load, key skew or strange data. So you let the new system meet the real thing, safely. A **dark launch** runs a new system on real traffic without users seeing its results. Migrations use it as **shadow reads**: read from both old and new, compare, and log mismatches. By cutover day, the new system has already survived production.
takeaway: Let production test the new system before users depend on it.
deeper:
**Where it fits in a migration:**
1. Routing layer in front.
2. Dual-write new data.
3. Backfill old data, oldest and coldest first.
4. Verify with checksums and counts.
5. Shadow reads: the dark launch.
6. Cut over reads gradually by keys or tenants.

**What it catches:** Encoding differences, missed deletes, stale copies after backfill, and performance under real key skew. Each logged mismatch is a bug found without a user seeing it.

**Why it lowers risk:** Gradual cutover by percentage, plus a read-only rollback window, means a problem missed in the dark still has a small blast radius.

**The cost:** Every shadowed read runs twice, so a dark launch adds read load on the old and new systems for the paths it covers.

quiz.q: A team plans to cut all reads over to a new store in one step after a successful backfill. What would you add first, and why?
quiz.a: Shadow reads, a dark launch: read both systems on real traffic, compare and log mismatches. Then cut over gradually by percentage, keeping the old store read-only for rollback.

mcq.q: What makes a launch dark?
options: Real traffic runs through it, but users never see its results
It runs only at night on synthetic data
It is hidden from the on-call team
It uses a copy of production data in staging
mcq.why: A dark launch exercises the new system on real requests while users still get answers from the old one.

hook: Two users upload the same file. Why might a store keep only one copy, and when is that impossible?
title: Deduplication stores identical data once, if it can see it
body: Millions of users upload the same popular files, and storing each copy wastes space. **Deduplication** stores identical data only once: detect duplicates, usually by content hash, and keep one copy with many references. It saves bytes but adds bookkeeping, since a shared copy can be deleted only when nothing references it. And it only works on data the store can compare, which encryption can prevent.
takeaway: Dedup saves bytes until encryption or deletion makes copies unequal.
deeper:
**Reference counting:** Once copies are shared, deleting one user's file must not delete everyone's. The store tracks references, and garbage collection reclaims the data only when nothing points to it, the same job it does for unreferenced chunks in an object store.

**Where encryption blocks it:** Crypto-shredding encrypts each user's data with a per-user key, so two users' identical files become different ciphertexts, and there is no dedup across per-user keys. End-to-end encrypted chat stores only ciphertext, so identical content under different keys looks different to the server.

**Where deletion complicates it:** GDPR deletion must remove a user's data, but a deduplicated block may also belong to others. Remove the user's reference, and delete the block only when the count reaches zero.

**The trade-off:** Space saved versus metadata, reference tracking and weaker isolation between users. Where privacy requires per-user keys, dedup across users is off the table.

quiz.q: A backup service wants both cross-user deduplication and per-user crypto-shredding for the same files. Why can't it have both?
quiz.a: Per-user keys make identical files encrypt to different ciphertexts, so the store can't detect them as duplicates. Dedup then only works within one key's data.

mcq.q: When can a deduplicated block be physically deleted?
options: When no remaining reference points to it
When the first uploader deletes it
After a fixed 30-day window
When its checksum changes
mcq.why: Shared copies serve many owners, so garbage collection frees the block only when its reference count reaches zero.

predict.q: Two users upload the same file, each encrypted with their own key. Can the store deduplicate it?
options: No, the ciphertexts differ
Yes, by comparing content hashes
Only if both files are small

hook: Storing data is only part of the cloud bill. Which line item grows every time data leaves?
title: Egress: you pay again every time data leaves
body: Storage is billed once a month. Movement is billed every time. **Egress** is data leaving a cloud or region, and it is often billed. A read path serving users from another region, cross-region replication, a lake queried from a different cloud and a migration out all pay it. That is why a storage cost model lists network egress right next to storage and requests.
takeaway: Put data where it's read, or pay for every trip.
deeper:
**The review question:** What is the egress cost of the main read path? A cheap storage tier can still be an expensive design if every read crosses a region or cloud boundary.

**Where it hides:**
1. Cross-region replication copies every write out of its region.
2. Users served far from their data.
3. Analytics engines in another cloud reading the lake.
4. Migrations: moving 50 PB means paying to move 50 PB.

**What absorbs it:** A CDN serves hot content from edge caches near users, so the origin sends each popular object out far fewer times. Regional cache pools do the same for database reads.

**Why defaults matter:** If default replication is cross-region, cost doubles for data that never needed it, and egress is part of that bill.

**The cost model line:** Storage, requests, network egress, replication, backup and people. Leaving egress out is a common way to underestimate a design.

quiz.q: A team stores data cheaply in one region but serves most users from another, and the bill is triple the forecast. What did the forecast miss, and what are two fixes?
quiz.a: Egress on the main read path. Put a CDN or regional cache in front of reads, or place the data, or replicas of hot data, in the region where it is read.

mcq.q: Why does a CDN reduce egress costs?
options: Popular objects leave the origin far fewer times
CDN traffic is never billed by anyone
It compresses objects to a tenth of their size
It moves data into a cheaper storage tier
mcq.why: Edge caches serve repeat requests near users, so the origin sends each hot object out only occasionally.

hook: You post a comment, refresh, and it's gone. A second later it's back. Which guarantee did the system skip?
title: Strong, eventual, linearizable: what a read may see
body: Seeing your own comment vanish is eventual consistency at work. **Eventual consistency** means replicas converge if writes stop, but reads may be stale. **Strong consistency** means every read sees the latest committed write. **Linearizability** is the strictest form: every operation appears to happen at one instant, in real-time order. Stronger guarantees cost latency, especially across regions.
takeaway: Pay for strong where stale is wrong; accept eventual where stale is harmless.
deeper:
**Who needs which:** Strong for money, identity, inventory and uniqueness. Eventual for feeds, counters, caches and analytics. A comment briefly disappearing is annoying; a double-spent balance is an incident.

**What strong requires:** A single leader or consensus per key, so one authority orders writes. Across regions, that means a round trip per write.

**Where linearizability shows up:** An S3-like store gets strong read-after-write consistency by making the metadata commit its linearization point. After the commit, every reader sees the new object.

**The multi-region menu:** A home region per key gives consistency per key. Multi-leader stays writable everywhere but can lose concurrent updates under last-writer-wins. Global consensus, Spanner-style, is strongly consistent and pays cross-region latency.

**The catch:** A cache in front turns a strong store eventual unless invalidation is reliable.

quiz.q: A ticketing service must never sell the same seat twice, but its seat store is eventually consistent across regions. What goes wrong, and what does it need?
quiz.a: Two regions can both see a seat as free and sell it. Uniqueness needs strong consistency, a single leader or consensus per seat, accepting slower cross-region writes.

mcq.q: What does linearizability guarantee?
options: Every operation appears at one instant, in real-time order
Replicas converge once writes stop
Each transaction reads a consistent snapshot
Reads come from the nearest replica
mcq.why: Linearizability places each operation at a single point in time consistent with real-time order, the strictest of these guarantees.

hook: A report reads a table for ten minutes while writes keep landing. How does it get numbers that add up?
title: Snapshots freeze a moment; isolation reads from one
body: A long read against changing data can see half of one update and all of another, and the totals won't add up. A **snapshot** is a point-in-time view of data. **Snapshot isolation** means each transaction reads a consistent snapshot, as of when it started, while other writes continue. The report sees one coherent moment instead of a blur.
takeaway: Read from one frozen moment and the numbers always add up.
deeper:
**How databases do it:** Keep old versions of changed rows as long as some transaction might need them. A reader picks versions no newer than its start time. Writers don't block readers, and readers don't block writers.

**Not quite serializable:** Snapshot isolation can still allow anomalies such as write skew, where two transactions each read a snapshot, check a rule and write different rows that together break it. Serializable isolation prevents that, at more cost.

**Snapshots in lakes:** Iceberg commits new Parquet files as a table snapshot listed by a manifest. Queries read one snapshot, so they never see a half-written batch.

**Snapshots and blobs:** Blobs stored in database rows bloat every backup, replica and snapshot. Keeping blobs in an object store keeps snapshots small.

**The catch:** Old versions take space until nothing needs them, a form of space amplification.

quiz.q: Two on-call doctors each check that another doctor is on call, then both sign off at once under snapshot isolation. What anomaly is this, and what prevents it?
quiz.a: Write skew: each read a consistent snapshot showing another doctor on call, then wrote different rows. Serializable isolation, or locking the rows that were read, prevents it.

mcq.q: What does snapshot isolation give each transaction?
options: A consistent view as of its start
Exclusive locks on every row it reads
Protection from every anomaly, write skew included
The newest committed value on each read
mcq.why: Each transaction reads one consistent snapshot, but snapshot isolation is weaker than serializable and can allow write skew.

hook: Three replicas on three separate servers, all on one power feed. How many copies do you really have?
title: Three copies in one failure domain are one copy
body: Replicas protect you only if they don't fail together. A **failure domain** is a set of components that can fail together: a rack, a zone, a region. A **zone** is an isolated data center or group within a region; a **region** is a geographic area with several data centers. Copies must sit in independent failure domains, or a single event takes them all.
takeaway: Count copies by failure domain, not by server.
deeper:
**The review question:** How many failures can one item survive, and are copies in independent failure domains? Three replicas on one rack survive disk failures but not a rack power loss.

**Where it shapes design:** An S3-like store erasure-codes large objects, RS(10,4) for example, across failure domains, so losing one domain costs only a few fragments. Photo storage keeps fragments or replicas across regions to survive region loss.

**The failure-mode list:** A design doc walks through disk, node, rack, zone and region loss, and for each states detection, impact and recovery.

**The trade-off:** Wider domains cost more. Cross-region copies add latency and egress, and synchronous cross-region writes should be an explicit, RPO-driven choice.

**Blast radius is the same idea turned around:** Cells and stamps are failure domains you build on purpose, so a bad deploy stays inside one.

quiz.q: A team spreads RS(10,4) fragments over 14 servers, but in only two racks, seven each. One rack loses power. Is the data safe?
quiz.a: No. The rack takes 7 fragments with it, but RS(10,4) survives only 4 losses. Fragments must be spread so no single failure domain holds more than 4.

mcq.q: What is a failure domain?
options: A set of components that can fail together
A shard that has lost its leader
A region with no replicas
A disk with a high error rate
mcq.why: Racks, zones and regions are failure domains: everything inside can fail in one event, so copies must span them.

predict.q: RS(10,4) fragments are split 7 and 7 across two racks. One rack fails. What happens?
options: The data can't be read
Nothing, since 4 failures are allowed
Reads slow down but succeed

hook: Your database says 'committed', then the power goes out. Is the data really there?
title: Log it, fsync it, then say committed
body: A write sitting in the operating system's memory is not on disk yet, and a power cut erases it. **Fsync** is the system call that forces data to durable media. A **write-ahead log** (WAL) records changes before they are applied. Together they make commits safe: append the change to the log, fsync, then acknowledge. After a crash, replaying the log restores every committed change.
takeaway: Committed means logged and fsynced, never merely written.
deeper:
**The sequence:**
1. Append the change to the WAL.
2. Fsync the log to durable media.
3. Acknowledge the commit.
4. Apply the change to data pages or memory later.
A crash after step 3 is safe, because the log is replayed on restart.

**Why a log:** Appending to one file is sequential and fast. Updating data pages in place is random and slow. The log lets the slow part happen later without risking committed data.

**Where it shows up:** B-trees log changes before rewriting pages. LSM trees write to a WAL before inserting into the in-memory buffer, so buffered writes survive a crash. ACID's durability rests on this pair.

**The cost:** Fsync is slow, and a commit waiting on its own fsync caps throughput. Group commit batches many transactions into one fsync to win it back.

**The catch:** Replication can't replace fsync. Replicas in one failure domain that acknowledge from memory can all lose power together.

quiz.q: A team disables fsync to double write throughput, reasoning that three replicas protect the data. What scenario breaks this?
quiz.a: A power event across the failure domain: all three replicas held acknowledged writes only in memory, so they vanish together. Group commit recovers throughput without giving up fsync.

mcq.q: Why does a write-ahead log make commits both safe and fast?
options: Sequential appends are fast and replayable after a crash
It keeps committed data only in memory
It skips fsync for small writes
It replicates every write to three regions
mcq.why: Appending and fsyncing one log is cheap and durable; slow in-place updates happen later, and the log replays them after a crash.

hook: A failed upload leaves fragments on 14 disks that nothing points to. Who cleans them up?
title: Garbage collection reclaims what nothing references
body: Storage systems that never overwrite leave debris: orphan fragments from failed writes, old versions, deleted data. **Garbage collection** reclaims space from deleted or unreferenced data. In an S3-like store, a collector removes chunks no metadata references. It relies on a strict write order: data first, metadata second, so a crash leaves harmless orphans, never dangling pointers.
takeaway: Write data before pointers, and let a collector sweep the orphans.
deeper:
**Why orphans are safe:** If the store writes fragments and crashes before committing metadata, nothing refers to those fragments. Readers can't see them, and the collector removes them later. The reverse order would leave metadata pointing at missing data, which is far worse.

**Where it shows up:** Blobs moved out of database rows follow the same pattern: write the object first, then the row pointing to it. Deduplicated data is freed only when its reference count reaches zero. Compaction does a similar job for LSM trees and lakes, dropping old versions and deleted records.

**What it costs:** Scanning for unreferenced data takes I/O that competes with user traffic, like repair and compaction.

**The safety question:** A collector that frees something still referenced is a data-loss bug. Many systems add a delay before physical deletion, the same idea as soft delete: purge later, so a mistake can be caught.

quiz.q: A photo service writes the metadata row first, then uploads the image. Occasionally users see broken images. Why, and what's the fix?
quiz.a: A crash between the steps leaves metadata pointing to a missing object. Upload the image first, then commit the row; a crash then leaves only an orphan for garbage collection.

mcq.q: Why write data before metadata in an object store?
options: A crash leaves orphans to collect, not dangling pointers
Metadata writes are slower than data writes
Garbage collection only scans metadata
Readers query storage nodes directly
mcq.why: Unreferenced data is invisible and collectable; metadata pointing at missing data breaks reads.

hook: A cluster has 1,000 shards and plenty of spare capacity, yet one shard is on fire. Why?
title: One hot key can melt one shard in an idle cluster
body: Spreading data evenly doesn't spread traffic evenly. A **hot key** is a key receiving far more traffic than others: a celebrity profile, a viral photo, today's partition. All its requests land on one shard, however many shards exist. The review question asks for it directly: what is the hottest key, and what is its QPS at peak? Averages hide it.
takeaway: Capacity is per shard; your hottest key sets the limit.
deeper:
**Fixes by layer:**
1. CDN: a viral photo becomes a hot object the edge absorbs.
2. Cache: replicate hot keys across cache nodes, and use leases or request coalescing so an expiring key doesn't trigger a thundering herd.
3. Keys: add a bucket suffix to spread one logical key over several partitions.

**Where hot keys come from:** Unbounded partition keys like 'day' make every current write hit one key range. Range partitioning by prefix creates hot prefixes, which is why S3-like metadata shards must split automatically.

**In the design doc:** The failure modes list a hot key alongside disk, node and region loss, each with detection, impact and recovery.

**The catch:** Splitting can't help a single key; one key lives on one shard. Only caching, replication or changing the key spreads its load.

quiz.q: A profile store sits at 20 percent average load, but one celebrity's profile saturates its shard every evening. What are two fixes?
quiz.a: Replicate the hot key across cache nodes, with leases to stop thundering herds, or serve it from a cache layer in front. Resharding alone won't help, since one key lives on one shard.

mcq.q: Why can't splitting shards fix a single hot key?
options: One key always lives on one shard
Splitting only works on cold data
Hot keys are stored only in the cache
Splitting raises the replication factor
mcq.why: Splitting divides ranges of keys, but one key's traffic still lands on whichever shard owns it.

predict.q: A cluster has 1,000 shards at 20 percent load, yet one shard is saturated. What's the most likely cause?
options: One hot key
Too few disks in the cluster
A slow network link

hook: A client times out and retries a payment write. Did the customer just pay twice?
title: Idempotent operations make retries safe
body: Networks fail after a request is processed but before the reply arrives, so clients retry. An **idempotent** operation has the same effect if repeated: 'set balance to 50' is idempotent, 'add 10' is not. Distributed storage is full of retries, from clients, repair workers, deletion orchestrators and migration backfills, so each needs idempotent steps to be safe.
takeaway: Assume every request runs twice, and design so twice is harmless.
deeper:
**Where retries are built in:** A deletion orchestrator fans out to every store, tracks completion and retries; deleting an already-deleted key must be harmless. Migration backfills run in batches and get restarted; copying an object that already arrived must not corrupt it.

**Versions make writes idempotent:** A version or timestamp on every record lets a replay recognize a change it has already applied, which is how dual writes and backfills are reconciled.

**Making a non-idempotent write safe:** Attach a unique request ID and record it with the result. A retry with the same ID gets the stored result instead of applying the change again.

**Where it isn't enough:** Idempotence handles repeats, not ordering. Two different updates racing still need a leader, a version check or a merge rule.

**The design test:** For every write path, ask what happens if this exact request arrives twice.

quiz.q: A backfill copies 10 million objects, crashes at 6 million, and restarts from the beginning. What property must each copy step have, and how do versions help?
quiz.a: Idempotence: recopying an object must leave the same result. Versions let the copier skip safely, and stop a stale backfilled copy from replacing a newer dual-written one.

mcq.q: Which operation is idempotent?
options: Set the user's email to a given value
Add 10 to the account balance
Append a row to the event log
Increment the page-view counter
mcq.why: Setting a value gives the same result however many times it runs; adding, appending or incrementing changes it each time.

hook: One page load makes 50 storage reads. Why does the slowest of them decide how fast the page feels?
title: IOPS limit throughput; tail latency sets the feel
body: Averages hide the requests users remember. **IOPS**, input/output operations per second, measures how many reads and writes a device can do. **Tail latency** is high-percentile latency such as p99: how slow the slowest 1 percent of requests are. When one request touches many reads, it waits for the slowest, so the tail, not the average, sets what the user feels.
takeaway: Design for the p99; users live in the tail.
deeper:
**Where IOPS runs out first:** A review question asks which resource runs out first: IOPS, capacity, CPU, memory or metadata. Hot random reads can exhaust IOPS while disks are half empty.

**The latency ladder:** A p99 under 1 ms means memory or local flash. Under 10 ms means SSD-backed key-value storage. 100 ms and up allows object storage. The p99 target is often the first filter on the storage choice.

**What hurts the tail:** Background repair and compaction use the same disks and links as users, which is why repair traffic must be rate-limited. A noisy tenant in a shared cluster without quotas pushes everyone's p99 up.

**DynamoDB's goal:** Its single primary goal was predictable p99 latency. Naming the tail as the goal shaped the whole design.

**Measure it:** Alert on the p99, not the average.

quiz.q: A service's median read is 2 ms but its p99 is 400 ms, and each page makes 50 reads. Why do users complain when the median looks great?
quiz.a: About 40 percent of page loads include at least one read from the slowest 1 percent (1 − 0.99⁵⁰), so users feel the tail. Fix what drives the p99, such as background work or noisy tenants.

mcq.q: What does p99 latency measure?
options: The latency that 99 percent of requests stay under
The average latency across all requests
The latency of the fastest 99 requests
The time to write 99 percent of the data
mcq.why: p99 is the 99th percentile: only 1 percent of requests are slower, and that tail is what users notice.

predict.q: Each page load makes 50 reads. What share of page loads include at least one read slower than p99?
options: About 40 percent
About 1 percent
About 5 percent

hook: A leader goes silent. It might be dead, or just cut off. How can anyone safely replace it?
title: A lease is authority that expires on its own
body: Authority that lasts until revoked is dangerous, because a silent holder can't be reached to revoke it. A **lease** is a time-limited right, used for leaders and cache fills. When it runs out, the authority is gone without any message from the holder. So a silent leader can be replaced safely: wait for its lease to expire, then grant a new one.
takeaway: Wait out the lease, plus a margin, and two leaders never overlap.
deeper:
**Why expiry is the point:** If authority lasted until revoked, a crashed or cut-off holder would keep it forever, and granting it again would create two leaders. With a lease, time does the revoking. Real systems add a safety margin, because clocks drift.

**Leases for cache fills:** When a popular key expires, thousands of requests can miss at once. Meta's memcache paper uses leases so one request earns the right to refill the key while the others wait, stopping the thundering herd.

**Leases for client caching:** A billion-file metadata service lets clients cache hot directories with leases. Clients serve lookups locally until the lease expires, so the metadata store sheds load without clients serving stale entries forever.

**The trade-off:** Short leases mean faster failover and more renewal traffic. Long leases mean less traffic and longer waits when a holder dies.

quiz.q: A primary holds a 10-second lease and stops responding. An engineer wants to promote a new primary immediately. What's the risk, and what's the safe move?
quiz.a: The old primary may still be alive and serving, giving two leaders. Wait for its lease to expire, then promote; after expiry the old primary knows it has no authority.

mcq.q: How does a lease help stop a cache thundering herd?
options: Only the request holding the lease refills the key
It keeps the key from ever expiring
It sends each miss to a different database
It copies the key to every region
mcq.why: The first miss gets a lease to refill the key while others wait, so the database sees one query instead of thousands.

hook: A compromised admin account tries to delete every backup. What can make that impossible, even for an admin?
title: Object lock makes deletion impossible for a set time
body: Soft delete protects against mistakes, but a determined operator, a bug or an attacker can still purge. **Object lock** is WORM protection that prevents deletion for a period; **WORM** means write once, read many. **Legal hold** is a block on deletion for legal reasons, lasting until it is lifted. Both override normal deletion, including the automated kind.
takeaway: Some data must be undeletable, even by you.
deeper:
**The review question:** Can an operator or a bug delete everything? What stops it: soft delete, delayed purge or object lock? Object lock is the one aimed at a deleter with full permissions: in its strictest mode, not even an admin can remove locked data early.

**Where legal hold collides:** GDPR deletion pipelines must respect legal hold. The design doc's compliance review lists both the deletion path by user ID and legal hold, because one removes data and the other forbids removing it.

**Where tiering collides:** A tiering policy must allow pinning for legal hold, so lifecycle rules don't move or expire held data.

**Backups:** A backup that the production account can delete offers little protection. Locked backups survive the very incident they exist for.

**The trade-off:** Locked data can't be removed early, even when you want it gone, so lock periods need care. Hard delete, soft delete, object lock: each step trades flexibility for safety.

quiz.q: A deletion orchestrator receives a GDPR request for a user whose records are under legal hold. What should happen?
quiz.a: The held records must not be deleted while the hold lasts. The orchestrator should skip or defer them, record why, and finish the deletion once the hold is lifted.

mcq.q: What does WORM mean?
options: Write once, read many
Write often, read minimally
Write-only replicated media
Wide object replication model
mcq.why: WORM storage lets data be written once and read many times, but not changed or deleted during the lock period.

hook: Thousands of customers share one storage cluster. What stops one of them from ruining it for everyone?
title: Many tenants, one system: quotas, keys and blast radius
body: Sharing hardware across customers is what makes cloud storage cheap. **Multi-tenancy** means many customers sharing one system. The danger is the noisy neighbour: one tenant's batch job saturates the disks and every online service slows. So shared storage needs per-tenant quotas and priority classes, and often per-tenant encryption keys, so one tenant can be throttled or revoked without touching the rest.
takeaway: Share the hardware, never the failure.
deeper:
**The anti-pattern:** One giant shared cluster with no quotas. Tectonic avoids it with traffic classes, per-tenant quotas and priorities, so batch work yields to online traffic.

**The isolation spectrum:** Cells and stamps split tenants across independent units, so a bad deploy or a hot tenant hits one slice. Giant pools share everything and fix stranded capacity. Pick by which risk dominates.

**Per-tenant keys:** Customer-managed keys allow per-tenant revocation and crypto-shredding. A review question asks who holds the keys and whether one tenant's key can be revoked, and compliance calls for per-tenant keys where personal data is involved.

**Tenants at Meta:** Tectonic serves photos as a blob tenant, one of many workloads on the same large clusters, which is exactly why its traffic classes matter.

**The catch:** Isolation costs capacity. Every quota and every separate cell leaves some resources idle.

quiz.q: A SaaS storage platform must let one customer leave and have all their data made unreadable, without touching anyone else. What does its multi-tenancy design need?
quiz.a: Per-tenant, customer-managed encryption keys. Revoking or destroying that tenant's key crypto-shreds their data, backups included, while other tenants are unaffected.

mcq.q: What protects tenants in a shared cluster from a noisy neighbour?
options: Per-tenant quotas and priority classes
A larger replication factor
Erasure coding with wider stripes
Longer retention periods
mcq.why: Quotas cap each tenant's share of I/O, and priorities let online traffic go ahead of batch work.

hook: Renaming one directory in a billion-file system can be instant or take hours. What decides which?
title: The namespace is the set of names, and it's hard to scale
body: Bytes scale by adding disks; names don't. A **namespace** is the set of names, paths or keys, in a storage system. Every create, list, rename and stat is a namespace operation, and at billions of files those operations hit metadata, not disks. Whether a rename is cheap depends on how names are stored: kept together on one shard, or scattered as separate keys.
takeaway: Scale the names, and the bytes will follow.
deeper:
**Where it breaks first:** GFS and HDFS kept the namespace in one master's memory and hit its limits. Review questions ask for the metadata operation rate for list, rename and stat, and which operation is O(number of files).

**How big systems store it:** A billion-file metadata service separates the namespace, the directory tree, from block locations, stores both in a sharded, replicated key-value store, and shards directory entries by hash of parent ID. One directory's entries share a shard, so renaming within it stays cheap. Colossus and Tectonic follow this pattern.

**Flat namespaces:** Object stores use flat keys in buckets instead of a tree. LIST by prefix emulates directories, which is why S3-like metadata is range-partitioned by (bucket, key).

**The trade-off:** A tree makes directory rename natural but needs careful metadata sharding. A flat keyspace makes lookup simple, but 'renaming a directory' means rewriting every key under the prefix.

quiz.q: A team moves from a file system to an object store and plans to 'rename a folder' of 10 million objects nightly. What's wrong?
quiz.a: Object stores have a flat namespace, where a folder is just a key prefix. Renaming it means copying and deleting 10 million objects, not one metadata update.

mcq.q: What is a namespace in a storage system?
options: The set of names, paths or keys it holds
The set of disks it spans
The set of regions it replicates to
The set of tenants sharing it
mcq.why: The namespace is every name the system knows; operations on it hit metadata, which is why it limits scale before bytes do.

hook: Triple replication survives two failures and triples your bytes. Is there a cheaper way to get more?
title: Replication factor: every copy costs a full copy
body: Each extra copy buys failure tolerance at the price of storing everything again. **Replication factor** is the number of full copies of data. Three copies survive two failures at 3× the bytes. RS(10,4) erasure coding survives four failures at 1.4×, but its repairs cost more. So hot, small, latency-sensitive data is replicated, while warm or cold large data is erasure-coded.
takeaway: Copies buy speed; codes buy space; fast repair buys durability.
deeper:
**Why replicate at all:** A full copy serves a read from one node and repairs by copying one replica. That makes replication right for hot data where latency matters.

**Why the factor isn't the whole story:** Durability depends less on how many copies you keep than on how fast you rebuild a lost one. With three replicas, halving repair time cuts loss probability about four times.
