**Where copies must live:** Copies in one failure domain fail together. A replication factor of 3 on one rack is not three independent copies.

**Hidden multipliers:** Every replica and backup counts toward cost; a review question asks for cost per GB-month including replicas and backups. Blobs stored in database rows are multiplied by every replica too.

**Derived data:** Data that can be rebuilt can accept lower durability, as derived-data platforms like LinkedIn's Venice show.

quiz.q: A team stores 2 PB of rarely read video archives at a replication factor of 3. What would you suggest, and what does it cost them?
quiz.a: Erasure-code the archive, for example RS(10,4): 1.4× instead of 3× cuts raw storage from 6 PB to 2.8 PB and tolerates more failures. The cost is slower small reads and costlier repair.

mcq.q: With a replication factor of 3, how many failures can data survive?
options: Two
Three
One
Four
mcq.why: Three full copies survive losing any two; the remaining copy still holds the data.

hook: A region goes down. The business immediately asks two questions. What are they?
title: RPO is data you may lose; RTO is time you may be down
body: Disaster plans fail when nobody agreed on what 'recovered' means. **RPO**, recovery point objective, is how much data you may lose in a disaster. **RTO**, recovery time objective, is how long recovery may take. Zero RPO needs synchronous replication to another region; a few seconds allows async. RTO depends on how fast failover or restore really is, not on what the plan says.
takeaway: Agree on RPO and RTO before the disaster, not during it.
deeper:
**RPO drives replication:** Synchronous cross-region replication fits when RPO must be zero; asynchronous fits when latency matters more than the last few seconds of data. Making synchronous the default for everything is an anti-pattern; it should be backed by an RPO requirement per dataset.

**The review question:** What happens to in-flight writes if a region is lost? What is the RPO? A home-region design with async replicas elsewhere accepts a small RPO on failover.

**RTO drives restore:** The design doc's durability section lists backups and their restore time. When did we last restore, and how long did it take? A backup that takes four days to restore sets a four-day RTO, whatever the plan claims.

**Why both:** RPO is a durability promise, RTO an availability promise. A system can meet one and miss the other.

quiz.q: A payments ledger has an RPO of zero and an RTO of 15 minutes; an analytics store has an RPO of 1 hour and an RTO of 1 day. How should their replication and recovery differ?
quiz.a: The ledger needs synchronous cross-region replication and tested fast failover. The analytics store can replicate asynchronously and recover from backups or by rebuilding.

mcq.q: Which replication choice does an RPO of zero require?
options: Synchronous cross-region replication
Asynchronous cross-region replication
Nightly backups to another region
A cache in every region
mcq.why: Only waiting for another region to confirm each write guarantees no acknowledged write is lost with a region.

hook: Users log in by email, but your table is keyed by user ID. What does every login query need?
title: Secondary indexes must stay in step with the data
body: A primary key answers one question fast; every other lookup needs help. A **secondary index** is an index on a field other than the primary key, such as email or username. It speeds those queries but adds a second write for every change. The danger comes when data and index writes aren't atomic: a crash between them leaves the two inconsistent, and nothing fixes it on its own.
takeaway: An index that can disagree with its data is worse than none.
deeper:
**The review question:** Which queries need a secondary index, and is that index transactional with the data? The second half is where designs go wrong.

**The anti-pattern:** Application-maintained indexes without transactions mean two writes with no atomicity. Pinterest named this a key reason for moving its graph store to TiDB.

**Why profiles sit in SQL:** Profiles need secondary indexes and updates, which is why the reference architecture puts them in Spanner, Aurora or MySQL rather than a pure key-value store, with caches absorbing reads.

**Where it shapes the store choice:** Single-key reads under 10 ms at huge QPS go to key-value stores. Once queries need other fields with consistent indexes, relational or distributed SQL fits better.

**The cost:** Each index adds write work and storage, so index only what real queries need.

quiz.q: A NoSQL store keyed by user ID gets an email lookup table, written by the app after each user write. After an outage, some emails point to deleted users. Why?
quiz.a: Data and index writes weren't atomic, so crashes left them out of step. Use a store with transactional secondary indexes, or write both in one transaction.

mcq.q: Why do profiles in the reference architecture sit in SQL-style stores?
options: They need secondary indexes and transactional updates
They are too large for key-value stores
They are append-only data
They must be erasure-coded
mcq.why: Lookups by email or username need indexes kept consistent with the row, which transactional stores provide.

hook: A dataset should live 30 days. Who deletes it on day 31 if nobody writes a cleanup job?
title: TTL: data that deletes itself on schedule
body: Cleanup jobs get forgotten, and data kept by accident is kept forever. A **TTL**, time to live, is automatic expiry after a duration. The store itself deletes the data when time runs out, so nobody has to remember. Short retention favours TTL-based stores, and a platform that sets a sensible TTL by default turns retention by nobody into retention by design.
takeaway: The best deletion job is the one nobody has to run.
deeper:
**Where it shows up:** The retention modifier says long retention needs tiering and archival, while short retention favours TTL-based stores. The design doc's lifecycle section lists TTLs alongside tiering rules, archival and deletion.

**The anti-pattern it prevents:** Retention by nobody: no TTL, no lifecycle rule, no owner, and a dataset that grows until it becomes a cost or compliance incident.

**Defaults matter:** If the default retention is forever, storage grows forever. A default TTL makes the safe, cheap choice the one teams get by doing nothing.

**Pipelines:** Keeping raw events 30 to 90 days and aggregates longer is a TTL policy, set per table.

**The catch:** Expiry in immutable stores usually means tombstones plus compaction, so bytes linger until compaction runs. And a TTL must yield to legal hold.

quiz.q: Session data should live 24 hours, but the table holds three years of sessions because the cleanup cron broke in year one. What would have prevented this?
quiz.a: A TTL-based store, or a TTL on the table, so expiry happens automatically with no job that can fail silently. Pair it with an owner and a lifecycle rule.

mcq.q: Which retention need best fits a TTL-based store?
options: Short retention, such as days
Seven-year compliance retention
Indefinite retention under legal hold
Data that must never be deleted
mcq.why: TTLs expire data automatically, which suits short retention; long retention calls for tiering and archival.

hook: One transaction touches two databases in two regions. How do both commit, or neither?
title: Two-phase commit: everyone votes, then everyone commits
body: A change that spans two systems must not half-happen. **Two-phase commit** is a protocol for atomic commit across participants. In phase one, a coordinator asks every participant to prepare and vote. Only if all vote yes does phase two tell them to commit; otherwise all abort. The price is waiting: every participant is held until the slowest one answers.
takeaway: Atomic across systems means waiting for the slowest one.
deeper:
**The two phases:**
1. Prepare: each participant makes the change durable but not visible, and votes yes or no.
2. Commit or abort: if every vote is yes, the coordinator says commit; any no means abort everywhere.

**The blocking problem:** A participant that voted yes must wait for the decision. If the coordinator crashes at that moment, the participant holds its locks until it learns the outcome.

**The latency cost:** Across regions, each phase adds a cross-region round trip. That cost helps explain why a design doc might list cross-region transactions as a non-goal, the checklist's own example of one.

**Where atomicity matters:** Application-maintained indexes fail precisely because two writes lack atomic commit. Distributed SQL systems such as Spanner, CockroachDB and TiDB provide transactions across shards, so applications don't have to build this themselves.

quiz.q: A team proposes transactions spanning databases in Europe and Asia for every checkout. What cost should they expect, and what might the design do instead?
quiz.a: Each commit waits on cross-region round trips in both phases, and a coordinator failure can block participants. The design could make cross-region transactions a non-goal and keep each checkout in one region.

mcq.q: What happens in two-phase commit if one participant votes no?
options: Every participant aborts
The others commit without it
The coordinator retries forever
Only the no-voter rolls back
mcq.why: Atomic commit means all or nothing: a single no vote aborts the transaction everywhere.

hook: Most storage ideas you use at work first appeared in a single paper. Which ones are worth reading first?
title: The storage canon: papers, books and conferences
body: Most systems in large-scale storage trace back to a handful of papers. **The core canon**: GFS (SOSP 2003), Bigtable (OSDI 2006), Dynamo (SOSP 2007), Haystack (OSDI 2010), Windows Azure Storage (SOSP 2011), Spanner (OSDI 2012), f4 (OSDI 2014), Aurora (SIGMOD 2017), Tectonic (FAST 2021) and DynamoDB (USENIX ATC 2022). **Books**: Kleppmann's Designing Data-Intensive Applications and Petrov's Database Internals.
takeaway: Read the papers behind the systems you run.
deeper:
**More papers:** Erasure Coding in Windows Azure Storage (USENIX ATC 2012), TAO and Scaling Memcache at Facebook (2013), Ceph (OSDI 2006), the FoundationDB Record Layer (SIGMOD 2019), DELF on deletion correctness (USENIX Security 2020), ShardStore (SOSP 2021) and O'Neil's Log-Structured Merge-Tree (1996).

**Blogs and data:** Google's 'A peek behind Colossus' (2021), Dropbox's 'Inside the Magic Pocket' (2016), Backblaze's drive statistics for real disk failure rates, and the AWS Builders' Library on cells, shuffle sharding and retries.

**More books:** Site Reliability Engineering (O'Reilly, 2016), free online; read its data-integrity chapter. Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces, free online, for file systems, RAID and crash consistency.

**Conferences to follow:** USENIX FAST, OSDI and ATC, ACM SOSP, plus VLDB and SIGMOD for database systems.

quiz.q: You're about to design a warm blob tier using erasure coding. Which two papers from the canon are most directly relevant, and why?
quiz.a: f4 (OSDI 2014), Meta's warm blob storage tier, and Erasure Coding in Windows Azure Storage (USENIX ATC 2012), which introduced LRC for cheaper repairs.

mcq.q: Which paper describes Meta's warm BLOB storage tier?
options: f4, OSDI 2014
Haystack, OSDI 2010
Tectonic, FAST 2021
TAO, USENIX ATC 2013
mcq.why: f4 is the warm tier built once photo reads fell; Haystack was the earlier hot store, and Tectonic later replaced both.

hook: Four sentences sum up how a senior staff engineer thinks about storage. What do they count first?
title: Shape first, repair fast, count objects, set safe defaults
body: Four rules carry most storage judgment. Start from **data shape** and access pattern, not product names; the same app needs several stores. Durability comes from fast, parallel repair as much as from copy count; halving repair time helps as much as adding redundancy. Metadata, not bytes, usually breaks first, so count objects, not only terabytes. And **defaults are policy**: make the safe, cheap choice the one teams get by doing nothing.
takeaway: Describe the data, speed the repair, count the objects, fix the defaults.
deeper:
**Shape first:** Blobs go to object stores, logs to Kafka and lakes, scans to columnar warehouses, transactions to SQL, and huge-QPS key lookups to key-value stores. A billion-user app uses all of them.

**Repair fast:** Loss needs further failures inside the repair window, so risk scales with the window squared for 3-way replication. Dropbox's Magic Pocket spreads reconstruction across hundreds of nodes to keep that window short.

**Count objects:** GFS and HDFS hit single-master metadata limits; Colossus and Tectonic moved metadata to sharded key-value stores. A million 1 KB files cost far more metadata than one 1 GB file.

**Fix defaults:** Forever-retention grows storage forever, and cross-region replication by default doubles cost for data that never needed it. AWS making encryption at rest the S3 default in 2023 shows the good version.

quiz.q: A team plans one Postgres for logs, photos and profiles, sized only by terabytes, with retention left at forever. Which rules does it break?
quiz.a: Shape first, with one store for three shapes; count objects, since it's sized only by bytes; and defaults are policy, since forever-retention grows cost and compliance risk without limit.

mcq.q: Halving repair time helps durability about as much as what?
options: Adding redundancy
Doubling disk size
Adding a cache
Switching to SSDs
mcq.why: Loss depends on failures inside the repair window, so shrinking the window buys durability comparable to adding copies.

hook: Every storage system you build will be replaced one day. What should you build into it on day one?
title: Bound blast radius, plan the exit, write deletion first
body: Four more rules close the loop. Limit **blast radius** with cells or stamps, but know that smaller units strand capacity. Every system will be migrated, so build in abstraction, CDC, versions and open formats from day one. Deletion and migration are the design-doc sections most often missing, so write them first. And interview answers and real designs share one shape: requirements, estimates, design, failure modes, trade-offs.
takeaway: Contain failure, plan the exit, design deletion, then show your work.
deeper:
**Blast radius:** AWS cells and Azure stamps confine a bad deploy or a hot tenant to one slice. Meta chose big Tectonic clusters to fix stranded capacity instead. Both are right for their constraints.

**Plan the exit:** Every system is replaced within 5 to 10 years. A stable API, change data capture, a version on every record and open formats such as Parquet and Iceberg make that move a project, not a rewrite.

**Write deletion and migration first:** Both are easy on day one and very hard in year three. GDPR deletion must reach databases, caches, object stores, logs, the lake, ML training sets and backups; crypto-shredding handles the backups.

**One shape:** State requirements, estimate, design, walk the failure modes, name the trade-offs. A strong interview answer and a strong design doc are the same document at different lengths.

quiz.q: You're reviewing a design with no deletion section, no migration plan, and every tenant in one shared cluster with no quotas. Which takeaways does it break, and what do you ask for?
quiz.a: Write deletion and migration first, plan the exit, bound blast radius. Ask for a deletion path by user ID, an exit plan with CDC and open formats, and cells or per-tenant quotas.

mcq.q: What is the cost of limiting blast radius with small cells or stamps?
options: Stranded capacity
Weaker durability
Higher write amplification
Staler cache reads
mcq.why: Each small unit keeps its own headroom, so capacity one cell can't use sits idle while another runs out.
